regions.name: Bordeaux
regions.summary: Bordeaux is one of the world's most famous fine wine regions, on France's Atlantic coast, renowned for red blends of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from the Left and Right Banks, plus dry and sweet whites. Its 1855 Classification and château system underpin a global benchmark for age-worthy claret.
regions.climate: Maritime climate moderated by the Atlantic Ocean and the Gironde estuary, giving mild winters and warm, humid summers; vintage variation is significant due to unpredictable rain, especially around harvest. The Landes forest to the west offers some protection from Atlantic storms. The Gironde, Garonne, and Dordogne rivers moderate temperature and have shaped the region's key gravel and clay soils.
regions.soils: The Left Bank (Médoc, Graves) has gravel-dominated soils that retain heat and drain well, favoring Cabernet Sauvignon; the Right Bank (St-Émilion, Pomerol) has more clay and limestone, favoring Merlot, which ripens better in these cooler, damper soils.
regions.classification: Bordeaux uses the AOC system layered with regional (Bordeaux, Bordeaux Supérieur), sub-regional (Médoc, Graves), and commune-level appellations (Margaux, Pauillac, St-Émilion). Separately, the 1855 Classification ranks top Médoc and Sauternes châteaux (Premier Cru through Cinquième Cru), essentially unchanged since its creation apart from one 1973 promotion; St-Émilion maintains its own classification (Premier Grand Cru Classé A/B, Grand Cru Classé) which is periodically revised, and Graves/Pessac-Léognan has a separate cru classé list.

subRegions.name: Médoc
subRegions.notes: Left Bank, Cabernet Sauvignon-dominant, home to most 1855-classified châteaux including Margaux, Pauillac, St-Estèphe, and St-Julien.

subRegions.name: Graves / Pessac-Léognan
subRegions.notes: Left Bank south of the city, known for both classified reds and Bordeaux's finest dry whites.

subRegions.name: St-Émilion
subRegions.notes: Right Bank, Merlot/Cabernet Franc-based, limestone plateau, with its own periodically revised classification.

subRegions.name: Pomerol
subRegions.notes: Small Right Bank appellation with clay-rich soils, no formal classification, home to Pétrus and other top Merlot-based wines.

subRegions.name: Sauternes / Barsac
subRegions.notes: Sweet, botrytized whites from Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, aided by autumn mists off the Ciron river.

subRegions.name: Entre-Deux-Mers
subRegions.notes: Land between the Garonne and Dordogne rivers, source of everyday dry whites and value reds.

regions.styles: Reds range from structured, tannic, cedar-and-blackcurrant Left Bank wines built for long ageing to plusher, plum-and-red-fruit Right Bank Merlot-based wines that can be more approachable young; top wines can age for decades. Dry whites from Graves/Pessac-Léognan blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon for citrus, green fruit, and oak-derived texture. Sauternes and Barsac produce lusciously sweet, botrytis-affected whites with honey, apricot, and marmalade notes and considerable ageing potential.
notes: The 1855 Classification covers only the Médoc (plus one Graves château, Haut-Brion) and Sauternes/Barsac; St-Émilion and Pomerol are classified separately or not at all.
"Claret" is the traditional English term for red Bordeaux.
Botrytis cinerea (noble rot), encouraged by autumn mists off the Ciron River, is essential to Sauternes production.
Bordeaux is the birthplace of the château system and en primeur (wine futures) trading.
Bordeaux blends are typically labeled by place and producer rather than by grape variety.

regions.name: Burgundy — Côte d'Or & Côte Chalonnaise
regions.summary: The heartland of Burgundy, the Côte d'Or is the source of the world's most sought-after Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, produced from a narrow, fragmented patchwork of vineyards ranked by a strict climat-based hierarchy. The Côte Chalonnaise, just to the south, offers the same grape varieties in more affordable, still excellent expressions.
regions.climate: Continental climate with cold winters and warm summers, at the northern edge of reliable ripening for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, which makes vintage variation significant. The Côte d'Or is a narrow, east-facing escarpment that benefits from morning sun and some shelter from westerly weather provided by higher ground behind it. Spring frost and hail are recurring risks that can drastically cut yields in an unlucky year.
regions.soils: Predominantly limestone and marl from Jurassic-era seabeds, with the precise mix and depth of clay, limestone, and scree varying vineyard by vineyard (climat by climat), which underlies Burgundy's famous concept of terroir. Villages, Premier Cru, and Grand Cru sites are distinguished largely by subtle differences in soil composition, slope, and aspect.
regions.classification: A strict four-tier hierarchy: regional appellations (e.g. Bourgogne), village appellations (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin, Meursault), Premier Cru (named individual vineyards within a village), and Grand Cru (the very top individual vineyards, each with its own AOC, e.g. Romanée-Conti, Le Montrachet). Ownership is highly fragmented, with many growers holding tiny parcels within the same climat.

subRegions.name: Côte de Nuits
subRegions.notes: Northern half of the Côte d'Or, almost entirely red, home to most Grand Cru red vineyards including Chambertin, Musigny, and Romanée-Conti.

subRegions.name: Côte de Beaune
subRegions.notes: Southern half, produces both great reds (Pommard, Volnay) and the top white Grand Crus (Montrachet, Corton-Charlemagne).

subRegions.name: Côte Chalonnaise
subRegions.notes: South of the Côte d'Or, includes villages like Mercurey, Rully, Givry, and Montagny, offering good-value Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

regions.styles: Red wines are pale to medium ruby, medium-bodied, and high in acidity, with red fruit (cherry, raspberry) and earthy, floral, or spicy complexity that develops further with bottle age; top wines can age for decades. White wines range from lean, mineral, appley village-level wines to rich, complex, nutty, oak-aged Grand Cru whites with great ageing potential. Style is heavily shaped by producer winemaking choices, such as oak use and whole-cluster fermentation, in addition to the site itself.
notes: Burgundy's vineyard fragmentation stems partly from Napoleonic inheritance laws splitting holdings among heirs over generations.
"Climat" is the Burgundian term for a precisely delimited, named vineyard parcel with its own recognized characteristics; the Climats of Burgundy are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Négociants, who buy grapes or wine from multiple growers, play a historically central role in Burgundy alongside grower-producers (domaines).
Chablis is administratively part of Burgundy but lies well to the north and is treated as its own distinct wine region.
The same Grand Cru vineyard can be bottled by dozens of different producers, with quality and style varying considerably between them.

regions.name: Chablis
regions.summary: Chablis is an isolated outpost of Burgundy in the far north of the region, producing 100% Chardonnay wines defined by high acidity, minerality, and a distinctive lean, flinty style shaped by its cool climate and unique Kimmeridgian soils.
regions.climate: Cool continental climate, one of the most northerly wine regions in France, with a high risk of spring frost that has historically driven the use of aspersion (water sprinklers) and smudge pots or candles (bougies) for frost protection. The region's marginal warmth keeps acidity high and produces the characteristically lean, taut Chablis style; hail is also a recurring risk in some vintages.
regions.soils: Kimmeridgian limestone and clay, rich in fossilized oyster shells, dominate the best (Premier Cru and Grand Cru) slopes, while a younger, less prized Portlandian limestone is found elsewhere in the appellation. Kimmeridgian soil is closely associated with Chablis's characteristic minerality and is a defining feature of its top sites.
regions.classification: Four-tier AOC hierarchy: Petit Chablis (lesser sites, often flatter or higher land), Chablis (the largest category), Premier Cru (numerous named vineyards on Kimmeridgian slopes), and Grand Cru (a single contiguous hillside of seven climats on the right bank of the Serein, facing southwest).

subRegions.name: Grand Cru
subRegions.notes: Seven adjoining climats (Les Clos, Vaudésir, Valmur, Grenouilles, Blanchots, Preuses, Bougros) on one south/southwest-facing slope near the town of Chablis.

subRegions.name: Premier Cru
subRegions.notes: Over 40 named climats, often grouped under umbrella names such as Fourchaume or Montmains, on varied slopes around the appellation.

regions.styles: Bone-dry, high-acid white wines with green apple, citrus, and characteristic flinty, steely minerality; Petit Chablis and Chablis are typically unoaked or lightly oaked and drunk relatively young, while Premier and especially Grand Cru wines are richer and more textured, sometimes partly barrel-aged, and capable of ageing for a decade or more.
notes: Chablis is made exclusively from Chardonnay, unlike much of the rest of Burgundy, which also grows Pinot Noir.
The region's Kimmeridgian soil is geologically distinct from the limestone found in the Côte d'Or further south.
Traditional oak use (large old foudres, or none at all) is more restrained here than in the Côte d'Or, emphasizing fruit and minerality over oak character.
Chablis lies closer to Champagne than to the rest of Burgundy, both geographically and in its high-acid, cool-climate style.
Frost protection methods such as wind machines, water sprinklers, and candles are a defining part of viticulture here due to the region's frost-prone climate.

regions.name: Beaujolais
regions.summary: Beaujolais, at the southern end of Burgundy, is France's leading region for Gamay, producing everything from simple, fruity Beaujolais Nouveau to serious, age-worthy reds from its ten named Crus in the granite hills of the north.
regions.climate: Semi-continental climate, somewhat warmer than the Côte d'Or to the north, with hills to the west providing some shelter. The hillier, granite-based north, where the ten Crus are located, is generally cooler and more structured in style than the flatter, clay-limestone south, which produces simpler, fruitier wines. Overall warmth is sufficient for Gamay to ripen fully, giving fresh, fruit-forward wines.
regions.soils: The northern Cru zone is dominated by granite and schist, giving more structured, mineral wines, while the flatter southern part of Beaujolais has more clay and limestone, suited to lighter, fruitier styles. Soil type is a key factor differentiating the ten Crus both from each other and from basic Beaujolais.
regions.classification: Three-tier AOC system: Beaujolais (basic, largely from the south), Beaujolais-Villages (from designated villages mainly in the north, with fuller flavor), and the ten Crus (Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié, Saint-Amour), each its own appellation without further internal tiering. Beaujolais Nouveau is a separate designation for wine released on the third Thursday of November following harvest.

subRegions.name: Moulin-à-Vent
subRegions.notes: Considered the most structured and age-worthy Cru, from manganese-rich soils.

subRegions.name: Fleurie
subRegions.notes: Known for perfumed, elegant, floral wines.

subRegions.name: Morgon
subRegions.notes: Powerful, structured wines, especially from the Côte du Py slope.

subRegions.name: Chiroubles
subRegions.notes: The lightest and most fragrant of the Crus, from high-altitude vineyards.

subRegions.name: Brouilly / Côte de Brouilly
subRegions.notes: Brouilly is the largest, fruitiest Cru; Côte de Brouilly, a hill within it, gives more concentrated wines.

regions.styles: Predominantly light-to-medium-bodied red wines with vibrant red fruit (cherry, strawberry, raspberry) and low tannin, often made partly or wholly by carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration for freshness and fruitiness; Beaujolais Nouveau is very light and meant for immediate drinking, while Cru Beaujolais can be more structured, savory, and age-worthy over several years. A small amount of white (Chardonnay) and rosé is also produced.
notes: Beaujolais Nouveau, released just weeks after harvest, was a major marketing phenomenon from the 1970s through the 1990s ("Le Beaujolais Nouveau est arrivé").
Carbonic maceration, historically strongly associated with Beaujolais, produces distinctive banana and bubblegum aromatics in simple wines.
The ten Crus never carry the word "Beaujolais" on the label, only the Cru name itself, such as "Morgon".
Beaujolais lies immediately south of the Mâconnais and is administratively linked to greater Burgundy despite its distinct grape and style identity.
Interest in serious, terroir-driven Cru Beaujolais, often from old-vine, low-intervention producers, has grown significantly since the 2000s.

regions.name: Champagne
regions.summary: Champagne is the archetypal fine sparkling wine region, in a cool, northerly part of France, whose traditional-method blends of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and Pinot Meunier set the global benchmark for quality sparkling wine and give the region its name as a protected term.
regions.climate: Cool, marginal continental climate at the northern limit of successful grape ripening, giving grapes with naturally high acidity, which is essential for sparkling wine, and relatively low sugar and alcohol. Chalk subsoil helps with drainage and heat retention, moderating an otherwise challenging climate, while frost and uneven ripening remain recurring vintage risks, which is part of why non-vintage blending across multiple years is central to the region's style.
regions.soils: Predominantly chalk, with clay and marl in places, which provides excellent drainage, reflects sunlight to aid ripening, and retains moisture during dry periods; the chalk cellars carved beneath many houses also provide ideal, temperature-stable conditions for the prolonged bottle ageing traditional-method sparkling wine requires.
regions.classification: AOC Champagne governs the whole region; within it, the historically significant Échelle des Crus rated villages, and Grand Cru (17 villages) and Premier Cru (over 40 villages) status is still referenced on labels. Style is further defined by dosage level (from Brut Nature to Doux), vintage versus non-vintage status, and blend type such as Blanc de Blancs, Blanc de Noirs, or rosé.

subRegions.name: Montagne de Reims
subRegions.notes: Known especially for Pinot Noir, giving structure and power.

subRegions.name: Vallée de la Marne
subRegions.notes: Pinot Meunier stronghold, producing fruitier, earlier-drinking wines.

subRegions.name: Côte des Blancs
subRegions.notes: Almost entirely Chardonnay, on pure chalk, prized for finesse and ageability.

subRegions.name: Côte des Bar (Aube)
subRegions.notes: Southernmost and warmest subzone, mainly Pinot Noir, historically less prestigious but increasingly respected.

regions.styles: The great majority is non-vintage Brut, blended across multiple base years and often multiple villages and grape varieties for a consistent house style, typically pale gold with a fine mousse, citrus and orchard fruit, and brioche or biscuit autolytic character from lees ageing, alongside refreshing high acidity. Vintage Champagne, made only in strong years from a single harvest, is richer and more age-worthy; Blanc de Blancs (Chardonnay only) is lighter and more citrus-driven, Blanc de Noirs (dark grapes only) fuller-bodied, and rosé Champagne, made by blending in red wine or brief maceration, adds red-fruit character.
notes: "Champagne" is a legally protected name in the EU and many other countries, usable only for sparkling wine made in this delimited region by the traditional method.
Minimum lees-ageing requirements here (longer for vintage than non-vintage wines) are stricter than the EU's general traditional-method minimum.
Grower-producer Champagnes (Récoltant-Manipulant), made by growers from their own fruit rather than by large houses (Négociant-Manipulant), have gained prominence as an alternative to major brands.
Dom Pérignon, a Benedictine monk, is popularly, if partly mythically, credited with advancing the region's early sparkling winemaking methods.
The three main grapes contribute differently to blends: Chardonnay for finesse and acidity, Pinot Noir for structure and body, and Pinot Meunier for fruitiness and early approachability.

regions.name: Northern Rhône
regions.summary: The Northern Rhône is a narrow strip of steep, terraced vineyards along the Rhône river producing some of France's most powerful and age-worthy Syrah-based reds, notably Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie, alongside distinctive Viognier-based whites from Condrieu.
regions.climate: Continental climate with some Mediterranean influence, tempered by the cooling mistral wind that funnels down the Rhône valley and helps keep vineyards healthy by reducing disease pressure. Steep, often south-facing terraced slopes maximize sun exposure, which is needed to ripen Syrah at this relatively northerly latitude, though the terrain makes mechanization extremely difficult and viticulture very labor-intensive.
regions.soils: Granite is the defining soil, especially on the steepest terraces of Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage, giving structured, mineral wines; Hermitage hill also has areas of loess and limestone, and Condrieu's granite-based soils, with decomposed mica locally called "arzelle", suit aromatic Viognier.
regions.classification: A collection of separate AOCs rather than a single hierarchical system: prestigious crus such as Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage, and Cornas (all red only), Condrieu and Château-Grillet (white only, Viognier), and the larger, more affordable Crozes-Hermitage and St-Joseph appellations for both colors, with regional Côtes du Rhône covering lesser sites. Unlike Burgundy, there is no Premier or Grand Cru tier within these individual appellations.

subRegions.name: Côte-Rôtie
subRegions.notes: Steep terraced slopes (Côte Brune and Côte Blonde); reds may include up to 20% co-fermented Viognier.

subRegions.name: Hermitage
subRegions.notes: Single large hill producing powerful, long-lived Syrah, plus a small amount of white from Marsanne and Roussanne.

subRegions.name: Condrieu
subRegions.notes: Dedicated exclusively to aromatic, full-bodied Viognier whites.

subRegions.name: Cornas
subRegions.notes: All red, full-bodied, powerful, tannic Syrah; no white permitted.

subRegions.name: Crozes-Hermitage
subRegions.notes: The largest Northern Rhône appellation, flatter land, more approachable and affordable style.

subRegions.name: St-Joseph
subRegions.notes: A long, narrow strip on the west bank with variable quality, producing both red and white wine.

regions.styles: Reds are Syrah-based, deep in color, medium to full-bodied, with dark fruit, black pepper, smoked meat, and floral violet notes, firm tannins, and, from top sites, strong ageing potential over decades. Whites from Viognier, as in Condrieu, are full-bodied and aromatic with peach, apricot, and floral notes, typically drunk relatively young; Marsanne/Roussanne-based whites from Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage are richer and nuttier and can age well.
notes: Syrah is believed to originate in the Northern Rhône; Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage are among its most historic and prestigious expressions.
Co-fermenting a small percentage of Viognier with Syrah in Côte-Rôtie is a traditional practice that can add aromatic lift and soften color and tannin.
The mistral, a strong, cold wind from the north, is an important climatic feature that helps protect vineyards from disease.
Vineyards are often terraced and worked by hand on very steep slopes, making labor costs and viticulture especially demanding.
Unlike the Southern Rhône, Grenache plays essentially no role here; Syrah dominates red production almost exclusively.

regions.name: Southern Rhône
regions.summary: The Southern Rhône is a broad, warm expanse of vineyards producing the great majority of Rhône wine by volume, from everyday Côtes du Rhône to powerful, Grenache-dominant blends like Châteauneuf-du-Pape, typically made from several grape varieties.
regions.climate: Mediterranean climate, warmer and drier than the Northern Rhône, with abundant sunshine that reliably ripens Grenache and the region's other varieties; the mistral wind is also present here, reducing disease pressure and stressing vines in ways that can contribute to fruit concentration. Drought stress in dry years is a growing concern, though the region's overall warmth generally supports full ripeness and produces wines with higher alcohol levels than those of the north.
regions.soils: Highly varied, including the famous large, heat-retaining galets roulés (rounded stones) of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, which store daytime heat and release it at night; elsewhere sand, clay, and limestone predominate, with soil type influencing which of the permitted grape varieties perform best on a given site.
regions.classification: A pyramid similar in spirit to Burgundy's but based on villages rather than climats: basic Côtes du Rhône (region-wide), Côtes du Rhône-Villages (better sites, some entitled to add a named village), and top individual village appellations such as Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas, and Vacqueyras. Châteauneuf-du-Pape uniquely permits up to 13 traditionally counted grape varieties in its blend and has stricter rules, including a minimum alcohol level and mandatory hand-harvesting.

subRegions.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
subRegions.notes: The region's most famous appellation, Grenache-dominant, powerful, full-bodied reds and a small amount of white, from galets roulés soils.

subRegions.name: Gigondas
subRegions.notes: Grenache-based, structured reds, often compared to a more affordable Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

subRegions.name: Vacqueyras
subRegions.notes: Similar profile to Gigondas, slightly lighter, good value.

subRegions.name: Côtes du Rhône-Villages
subRegions.notes: Villages with typically better sites and lower yields than basic Côtes du Rhône; some, such as Cairanne, now stand as their own appellation.

subRegions.name: Tavel
subRegions.notes: Dedicated entirely to rosé, one of France's few AOCs producing only rosé wine.

regions.styles: Predominantly medium-to-full-bodied red blends, warm and generous, with ripe dark and red fruit, garrigue herb notes such as thyme and lavender, pepper and spice, moderate-to-high alcohol, and tannins ranging from soft to firm depending on the proportion of Mourvèdre and Syrah; top Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Gigondas can age for a decade or more. The region also produces significant amounts of dry rosé, notably Tavel, and some white blends from Grenache Blanc, Clairette, and Roussanne.
notes: Châteauneuf-du-Pape's name references the historic residence of Avignon-based Popes nearby in the 14th century.
Grenache is the backbone of most Southern Rhône reds, prized for ripeness and generous fruit, but is often blended with Syrah and Mourvèdre for structure and color.
Large, heat-storing galets roulés stones are a signature, though not universal, feature of Châteauneuf-du-Pape vineyards.
Côtes du Rhône is one of France's largest and most widely exported AOC categories by volume.
Tavel is one of very few French AOCs producing exclusively rosé wine.

regions.name: Loire Valley
regions.summary: Stretching along France's longest river, the Loire Valley is a diverse region spanning cool, crisp Muscadet near the Atlantic, aromatic Sauvignon Blanc and Chenin Blanc in the center, and light reds in Touraine and Anjou, unified by high acidity and freshness.
regions.climate: The long west-to-east span means significant climatic variation: the western Pays Nantais end has a maritime climate moderated by the Atlantic, the central sections (Anjou, Touraine) are semi-maritime and transitional, and the easternmost vineyards around Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé are more continental. The river itself moderates temperature and helps reduce frost risk along its banks, and the region's overall coolness preserves high acidity across its wines.
regions.soils: Highly varied along the river's length: schist and gneiss around the Muscadet area of the Pays Nantais, tuffeau limestone and flint (silex) around Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé giving the region's flinty, mineral character, and a mix of clay, tuffeau limestone, and sand or gravel in Anjou-Touraine, influencing both its reds and Chenin-based whites.
regions.classification: The Loire is not a single hierarchy but a collection of distinct AOCs grouped by sub-region, each with its own rules on grape variety and style, such as Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, which permits optional "sur lie" ageing, Vouvray and Savennières for Chenin Blanc in still or sparkling styles, Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé for Sauvignon Blanc, and Chinon, Bourgueil, and Saumur-Champigny for Cabernet Franc reds. Some appellations, such as Vouvray, permit a range of sweetness levels from dry to sweet within the same AOC.

subRegions.name: Pays Nantais (Muscadet)
subRegions.notes: Coastal, Melon de Bourgogne based, dry and saline, often aged "sur lie" for added texture.

subRegions.name: Anjou-Saumur
subRegions.notes: Chenin Blanc heartland producing dry, sweet, and sparkling styles, plus Cabernet Franc reds such as Saumur-Champigny.

subRegions.name: Touraine
subRegions.notes: Includes Vouvray (Chenin Blanc) and the Cabernet Franc reds of Chinon and Bourgueil.

subRegions.name: Central Vineyards (Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé)
subRegions.notes: Sauvignon Blanc heartland producing flinty, mineral, aromatic whites; Sancerre also makes Pinot Noir reds and rosés.

regions.styles: Whites dominate and range from bone-dry, briny Muscadet, through zesty, herbaceous, gooseberry-and-citrus Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé Sauvignon Blanc, to Chenin Blanc wines spanning dry, off-dry, sparkling (Crémant de Loire, Vouvray Mousseux), and lusciously sweet botrytized styles (Coteaux du Layon, Quarts de Chaume). Reds, mainly Cabernet Franc from Chinon, Bourgueil, and Saumur-Champigny, are light-to-medium-bodied with red fruit and characteristic leafy, herbaceous notes; rosé production, such as Rosé d'Anjou and Cabernet d'Anjou, is also significant.
notes: The Loire covers the widest range of styles of any single major French river valley: dry, sweet, sparkling, red, white, and rosé.
"Sur lie" ageing, on the lees without racking until bottling, is a signature Muscadet technique adding texture and a slight spritz.
Chenin Blanc's high natural acidity allows Loire producers to make everything from bone-dry to intensely sweet botrytized wines from the same grape.
Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé sit opposite each other across the river and share very similar Sauvignon Blanc styles rooted in flinty (silex) soils.
The Loire is sometimes called the "Garden of France" for its historic château-studded landscape as well as its diverse produce.

regions.name: Alsace
regions.summary: Alsace, on France's northeastern border with Germany, is unusual among French regions for its Germanic grape varieties and single-varietal labeling tradition, producing predominantly aromatic, dry-to-off-dry white wines of great purity from Riesling, Gewurztraminer, and Pinot Gris.
regions.climate: Cool continental climate, but one of the driest and sunniest in France thanks to the rain-shadow effect of the Vosges Mountains to the west, which block Atlantic weather systems. This combination of coolness and low rainfall allows for long, slow ripening that preserves aromatic intensity and acidity while still achieving good sugar levels.
regions.soils: Extremely varied and fragmented geology, including granite, limestone, sandstone, marl, volcanic, and schist soils, which can all be found within short distances along the eastern foothills of the Vosges; this underpins Alsace's strong sense of site-specific terroir, especially in its Grand Cru vineyards.
regions.classification: Three-tier system: regional Alsace AOC, which is varietally labeled and accounts for the great majority of production, Alsace Grand Cru (51 individually delimited vineyards, restricted mostly to Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, and Muscat, with stricter yields), and separate designations Crémant d'Alsace for traditional-method sparkling wine and Vendanges Tardives/Sélection de Grains Nobles for late-harvest and botrytized sweet wines respectively.

subRegions.name: Alsace Grand Cru
subRegions.notes: 51 named single vineyards, such as Schlossberg and Rangen, each with defined permitted grapes and often distinct soil and climate character.

subRegions.name: Bas-Rhin (northern Alsace)
subRegions.notes: Generally cooler, producing a lighter wine style.

subRegions.name: Haut-Rhin (southern Alsace)
subRegions.notes: Warmer, home to most Grand Cru vineyards and richer wine styles.

regions.styles: Predominantly still white wines, most commonly labeled by grape variety, ranging from bone-dry and steely Riesling with citrus, stone fruit, and mineral character, to opulently aromatic, off-dry-leaning Gewurztraminer with lychee and rose petal notes, to rich, weighty Pinot Gris. Vendanges Tardives are intense late-harvest sweet wines and Sélection de Grains Nobles are botrytized, very sweet dessert wines; Crémant d'Alsace provides fresh, traditional-method sparkling wine, and a small amount of Pinot Noir red and rosé is also made.
notes: Alsace is the only major French AOC region to routinely label wines by grape variety rather than by place name, reflecting its Germanic winemaking heritage.

Despite the traditional association with sweetness, Alsace wines are increasingly made dry, and sweetness level can be hard to predict from the label alone, a point of ongoing debate among producers and regulators.
Alsace Grand Cru wines, with rare exceptions that allow blends, must generally be 100% of a single permitted variety.
The Vosges Mountains' rain-shadow effect makes Alsace one of the driest regions in France despite its northerly, cool-climate location.
Alsace has changed sovereignty between France and Germany several times historically, which shaped both its grape varieties and its winemaking and labeling traditions.

regions.name: Languedoc-Roussillon
regions.summary: Stretching along the Mediterranean coast in southern France, Languedoc-Roussillon is France's largest wine-producing region by area, historically known for bulk production but now also a major source of good-value and increasingly high-quality reds, whites, and rosés, plus traditional fortified vins doux naturels.
regions.climate: Classic Mediterranean climate, with hot, dry summers and mild winters, and abundant sunshine that reliably ripens a wide range of grape varieties and supports organic and biodynamic viticulture through reduced disease pressure. Drought stress can be a challenge in the driest years, and proximity to the coast versus inland or hillside sites creates meaningful variation in wind exposure and diurnal temperature range across the region.
regions.soils: Highly diverse, including limestone and clay on the garrigue-covered hillsides, schist in areas such as Faugères and the higher ground of Roussillon, and alluvial or sandy soils nearer the coastal plain; hillside, lower-yielding sites on poorer soils are generally associated with the region's higher-quality appellations.
regions.classification: A large, evolving patchwork of AOCs, including Languedoc AOC as an umbrella designation and more specific appellations such as Faugères, Saint-Chinian, Minervois, Corbières, and Picpoul de Pinet, alongside a very large volume of IGP Pays d'Oc wines, which allow varietal labeling and greater flexibility than AOC rules. Roussillon also has distinct AOCs for fortified vins doux naturels, including Banyuls, Maury, and Rivesaltes.

subRegions.name: Minervois / Corbières
subRegions.notes: Large, historic AOCs on garrigue-covered hills, producing Grenache/Syrah/Carignan-based reds.

subRegions.name: Faugères / Saint-Chinian
subRegions.notes: Schist-influenced areas increasingly recognized for quality reds.

subRegions.name: Picpoul de Pinet
subRegions.notes: A coastal appellation dedicated to crisp, saline Picpoul white wine.

subRegions.name: Banyuls / Maury
subRegions.notes: Roussillon's fortified vins doux naturels, mainly from Grenache, sweet and often deliberately oxidative in style.

subRegions.name: Limoux
subRegions.notes: Known for both still Chardonnay/Chenin and traditional-method sparkling wine, including Blanquette de Limoux, an early precursor to Champagne's method.

regions.styles: Predominantly warm-climate, fruit-forward red blends of Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, and Carignan that are medium-to-full-bodied with ripe dark fruit and garrigue herbal notes; there is also a large volume of easy-drinking, often varietally labeled IGP Pays d'Oc reds, whites, and rosés aimed at the value and export market. Whites range from crisp coastal styles like Picpoul de Pinet to richer blends, and Roussillon's vins doux naturels are sweet, fortified wines with dried fruit, raisin, and sometimes deliberately oxidative (rancio) character.
notes: Languedoc-Roussillon is the single largest wine-growing area in France, and one of the largest in the world, by vineyard area.
The region has shifted substantially over recent decades from high-volume bulk production toward quality-focused, terroir-driven winemaking.
IGP Pays d'Oc is one of France's most successful and widely exported IGP designations, valued for its varietal labeling flexibility.
Blanquette de Limoux is sometimes claimed as the origin of traditional-method sparkling winemaking, predating Champagne's adoption of the method.
Vins doux naturels, such as Banyuls and Maury, are fortified by adding grape spirit during fermentation (mutage), similar in principle to Port production.

regions.name: Piemonte
regions.summary: Piemonte, in Italy's northwest at the foot of the Alps, is home to the country's most prestigious red wines, Barolo and Barbaresco, both made from Nebbiolo. It is a region of small family estates and a hierarchy of single-vineyard and village-level distinctions that rivals Burgundy in complexity and prestige.
regions.climate: Piemonte has a continental climate, with cold winters, warm summers, and a significant risk of autumn fog (the 'nebbia' that may have given Nebbiolo its name) and rain at harvest. The Alps to the north and west provide some shelter from extreme weather, while the Ligurian Apennines to the south moderate maritime influence. Hillside sites with good sun exposure and drainage are essential, as Nebbiolo buds early and ripens very late, often not picked until mid-to-late October. Vintage variation is significant, particularly around flowering and harvest-time rain.
regions.soils: The Langhe hills, home to Barolo and Barbaresco, are divided broadly into calcareous marl soils (Tortonian era, found around Barolo villages like La Morra and Barolo itself, giving more perfumed, earlier-approachable wines) and sandier, more compact Helvetian-era soils (found around Serralunga and Monforte, producing more structured, tannic, age-worthy wines). This soil distinction underpins much of the stylistic variation between Barolo communes.
regions.classification: Piemonte's finest wines fall under DOCG, Italy's highest classification, including Barolo, Barbaresco, Barbera d'Asti, Barbera d'Alba, Gavi, Asti (for Moscato d'Asti and sparkling Asti), and Roero. Barolo and Barbaresco are increasingly defined by officially recognized single-vineyard sites (MGA, Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive), allowing producers to label wines with vineyard names such as Cannubi or Rabajà. Broader regional wines fall under DOC designations like Langhe DOC and Piemonte DOC.

subRegions.name: Barolo
subRegions.notes: Eleven communes producing powerful, tannic, age-worthy Nebbiolo with notes of tar, rose, and red fruit; often called 'the wine of kings, the king of wines.'

subRegions.name: Barbaresco
subRegions.notes: Smaller zone than Barolo, generally producing slightly softer, more elegant Nebbiolo due to warmer sites and shorter legal ageing requirements.

subRegions.name: Roero
subRegions.notes: Sandier soils across the Tanaro river from the Langhe, producing lighter, more perfumed Nebbiolo alongside the white grape Arneis.

subRegions.name: Asti
subRegions.notes: Zone for sweet, low-alcohol, aromatic Moscato d'Asti and fully sparkling Asti Spumante.

subRegions.name: Gavi
subRegions.notes: Southeastern zone making crisp, mineral, high-acid white wine from the Cortese grape.

regions.styles: Barolo and Barbaresco are full-bodied, high-tannin, high-acid dry reds with pale garnet color, prized for aromas of rose, tar, dried cherry, and truffle, and for their long ageing potential (often decades). Barbera produces medium-to-full-bodied, high-acid, lower-tannin reds with dark fruit character, ranging from everyday to serious oak-aged examples. Dolcetto gives soft, fruity, lower-acid reds meant for earlier drinking. Moscato d'Asti is a lightly sparkling (frizzante), low-alcohol, sweet white with intense grapey, floral aromatics, while Gavi offers dry, crisp, citrus-driven whites.
notes: Nebbiolo is notoriously site-sensitive and rarely succeeds outside a handful of Piemontese zones, unlike more globally planted varieties.

Traditional vs. modernist winemaking (long maceration and large old botti vs. shorter maceration and new French barriques) was a defining stylistic debate in Barolo and Barbaresco through the late 20th century.
Barolo requires a minimum of 38 months' ageing (18 in wood), with Riserva requiring 62 months; Barbaresco requires 26 months (9 in wood), with Riserva at 50 months.
Despite its low tannin and light color, Nebbiolo has notably high acidity and alcohol, contributing to its remarkable longevity.
Piemonte also produces the world's most famous sweet sparkling wine, Asti, using the tank (Charmat) method rather than traditional method.

regions.name: Tuscany
regions.summary: Tuscany, in central Italy, is the spiritual home of Sangiovese and one of the world's most iconic wine regions, producing Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino, and the Bordeaux-inspired 'Super Tuscans.' Its rolling hills, medieval hill towns, and centuries-old winemaking tradition make it central to Italy's wine identity.
regions.climate: Tuscany has a Mediterranean climate moderated by elevation, with most quality vineyards planted on hillsides between roughly 150 and 500 metres. Proximity to the Tyrrhenian Sea brings moderating maritime influence to coastal zones, while inland areas like Montalcino and Chianti Classico experience wider diurnal temperature swings that help preserve acidity in Sangiovese. Summers are warm and dry, with occasional drought stress a concern in warmer vintages, while spring frost and harvest rain remain the main viticultural risks.
regions.soils: Soils vary from the galestro (crumbly clay-schist) and alberese (compact limestone) of Chianti Classico, which give Sangiovese its characteristic structure and elegance, to the more varied clay, sand, and galestro mix found around Montalcino. Coastal areas such as Bolgheri have gravel and sandier soils better suited to the Bordeaux varieties used in Super Tuscan blends.
regions.classification: Tuscany's top wines are governed by DOCG status: Chianti and Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, and Vernaccia di San Gimignano. Chianti Classico has its own additional Gran Selezione tier above Riserva. Many premium wines, particularly Bordeaux-blend 'Super Tuscans' like Sassicaia and Tignanello, are labelled under the broader IGT Toscana designation because their blends fall outside traditional DOC/DOCG rules, despite commanding prices well above many DOCG wines.

subRegions.name: Chianti Classico
subRegions.notes: The original, historic heartland of Chianti between Florence and Siena, producing Sangiovese-dominant wines of greater structure and ageing potential than basic Chianti.

subRegions.name: Montalcino
subRegions.notes: Warmer, more southerly zone producing Brunello di Montalcino, a 100% Sangiovese wine required to age for at least five years before release.

subRegions.name: Montepulciano
subRegions.notes: Hill town producing Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, a Sangiovese-based (locally called Prugnolo Gentile) wine with slightly less stringent ageing rules than Brunello.

subRegions.name: Bolgheri
subRegions.notes: Coastal Maremma zone that pioneered Bordeaux-variety 'Super Tuscans' such as Sassicaia and Ornellaia.

subRegions.name: San Gimignano
subRegions.notes: Known for Vernaccia di San Gimignano, Tuscany's principal DOCG white wine.

regions.styles: Chianti ranges from light, cherry-fruited, high-acid everyday wine to structured, age-worthy Riserva and Gran Selezione bottlings with notes of sour cherry, dried herb, and leather. Brunello di Montalcino is fuller-bodied, more tannic and concentrated, with dark cherry, balsamic, and earthy complexity, built for extended ageing. Vino Nobile sits stylistically between the two. Super Tuscans, based on Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot (sometimes blended with Sangiovese), are full-bodied, richly fruited, and oak-influenced in an international style.
notes: Sangiovese is famous for high acidity and firm tannin but relatively pale colour, historically leading Chianti producers to blend in small amounts of other varieties for colour and softness.

The 'Super Tuscan' movement began in the 1970s when producers like Sassicaia used Bordeaux varieties outside DOC rules, forcing Italy to eventually create the IGT category to accommodate high-quality wines outside traditional regulations.
Brunello di Montalcino must be aged for a minimum of five years (six for Riserva) before release, with at least two years in oak.
A 2008 scandal ('Brunellogate') involved allegations that some producers illegally blended in non-Sangiovese grapes, prompting tighter enforcement.
Chianti Classico is marked by the Gallo Nero (black rooster) seal on the neck of the bottle, a historic symbol of the original Chianti League.

regions.name: Veneto
regions.summary: Veneto, in northeast Italy, is one of the country's most productive wine regions by volume and the source of Amarone della Valpolicella, Soave, and Prosecco. Its geography ranges from Alpine foothills to the Adriatic plain, supporting an unusually wide range of styles from a single region.
regions.climate: Veneto has a climate that transitions from continental in the interior hills to more moderate near the Adriatic coast and Lake Garda, which exerts a warming, stabilizing influence on nearby vineyards. The Alps to the north shelter the region from the coldest continental air. Autumn is typically dry enough in Valpolicella to allow the appassimento (grape-drying) process used for Amarone and Recioto without excessive rot risk, though humidity management is still a key viticultural concern.
regions.soils: Soave's best vineyards, particularly the Classico zone, sit on volcanic soils that lend minerality and structure to Garganega-based whites, contrasting with the more fertile alluvial plains that produce simpler, high-volume Soave. Valpolicella's hillside sites have a mix of limestone and volcanic soils offering good drainage, essential for the appassimento method where grapes are dried before pressing.
regions.classification: Veneto's top designations include several DOCG wines: Amarone della Valpolicella, Recioto della Valpolicella, Soave Superiore, and Prosecco Superiore di Conegliano Valdobbiadene. Prosecco itself is a large DOC spanning Veneto and Friuli, with the smaller, hillier Conegliano Valdobbiadene zone earning DOCG status for higher quality. Valpolicella DOC covers standard red wines, while Ripasso della Valpolicella (wine re-fermented on Amarone lees) sits stylistically and in price between basic Valpolicella and Amarone.

subRegions.name: Valpolicella Classico
subRegions.notes: The original, hillier heartland west of Verona, producing the finest Amarone and Valpolicella wines.

subRegions.name: Soave Classico
subRegions.notes: Historic volcanic-soil zone producing the most structured and age-worthy Soave whites from Garganega.

subRegions.name: Conegliano Valdobbiadene
subRegions.notes: Hilly DOCG zone for premium Prosecco, including the prized Cartizze subzone.

subRegions.name: Bardolino
subRegions.notes: Light, fruity red wine zone on the shores of Lake Garda, made from similar grapes to Valpolicella.

regions.styles: Amarone della Valpolicella is a full-bodied, high-alcohol, dry red made from dried grapes, with concentrated dried-fruit, fig, and raisin character and notable ageing potential. Recioto della Valpolicella uses the same drying method but is fermentation-stopped to retain sweetness, producing a rich, sweet red. Valpolicella and Ripasso range from light and cherry-fruited to medium-bodied and richer, respectively. Soave is a dry, medium-bodied white with almond and citrus notes, while Prosecco is typically an off-dry to dry, light, fruity sparkling wine made by the tank method, prized for fresh pear and green apple aromatics.
notes: Amarone is made using appassimento, drying harvested grapes on straw mats or in crates for months before pressing, which concentrates sugars and flavour.
Ripasso wine gets its name and character from being 're-passed' over the leftover Amarone grape skins (pomace) after pressing, adding body and complexity to standard Valpolicella.
Prosecco is made predominantly by the Charmat (tank) method, in contrast to the traditional method used for Champagne and most Cava, giving it a fresher, more overtly fruity character.
Glera is the primary grape of Prosecco, renamed from 'Prosecco' itself in 2009 partly to protect the geographical name for EU trade purposes.
The Veneto is one of Italy's largest wine-producing regions by volume, driven heavily by Prosecco's global commercial success.

regions.name: Sicily
regions.summary: Sicily, the largest island in the Mediterranean, is Italy's most planted wine region and has transformed in recent decades from a source of bulk wine into a producer of increasingly distinctive, terroir-driven wines, led by the indigenous red grape Nero d'Avola and the volcanic wines of Mount Etna.
regions.climate: Sicily has a warm Mediterranean climate with abundant sunshine, low disease pressure, and limited rainfall, making organic viticulture relatively easy across much of the island. However, this is offset by significant elevation variation: vineyards on Mount Etna can reach 1000 metres or more, creating a much cooler, more marginal climate with high diurnal temperature range that produces fresher, more structured wines than the warm coastal plains. Sea breezes moderate coastal and hillside sites across the island.
regions.soils: Etna's vineyards are planted on distinct volcanic soils from different historic lava flows, rich in minerals and offering excellent drainage, which strongly influence the site-specific character prized in Etna Rosso and Bianco. Elsewhere on the island, soils are more varied, including clay, limestone, and sand, generally supporting the higher-yielding, warmer-climate viticulture typical of western and southern Sicily.
regions.classification: Sicilia DOC, established in 2011, covers the whole island and has become a significant quality and export designation, alongside older, more specific DOCs and one DOCG, Cerasuolo di Vittoria (a blend of Nero d'Avola and Frappato). Etna DOC governs wines from the volcano's slopes, with red, white, and rosato versions and a growing culture of officially recognized contrade (single-vineyard sites), informally used much like Burgundian climats even though not yet a formal legal classification tier.

subRegions.name: Etna
subRegions.notes: Volcanic slopes producing Sicily's most distinctive, terroir-driven wines, especially elegant, high-acid Nerello Mascalese reds often compared to Burgundy or Barolo.

subRegions.name: Vittoria
subRegions.notes: Southeastern zone and home to Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG, blending Nero d'Avola's power with Frappato's perfume.

subRegions.name: Marsala
subRegions.notes: Western port city that gives its name to Sicily's historic fortified wine, once world-famous but now a small niche category.

subRegions.name: Pantelleria
subRegions.notes: Volcanic island between Sicily and Tunisia known for sweet, aromatic Passito wines from the Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria) grape.

regions.styles: Nero d'Avola produces medium-to-full-bodied, dark-fruited, moderately tannic red wines, generally warm and generous in style outside Etna. Etna Rosso, from Nerello Mascalese, is notably lighter in colour but structured, with high acidity, red fruit, and earthy, mineral character reminiscent of Nebbiolo or Pinot Noir. Grillo and Catarratto produce fresh, dry, citrus-driven whites, while Etna Bianco (Carricante-based) offers steely, high-acid, age-worthy whites. Marsala ranges from dry to sweet fortified styles, and Pantelleria's Passito is intensely sweet, raisined, and aromatic.
notes: Sicily has more land under vine than any other Italian region, though much historically went into bulk wine and Marsala production before a quality-focused shift beginning in the 1990s-2000s.
Etna's vineyards are often ungrafted (planted on their own roots) due to the volcanic soil's resistance to phylloxera, and many are farmed as old, low-trained alberello (bush) vines.
Marsala was historically fortified and shipped by British merchants (notably John Woodhouse) in the 18th century, once rivalling Port and Sherry in international fame.
Cerasuolo di Vittoria is Sicily's only DOCG, reflecting the island's otherwise relatively young formal quality hierarchy compared to mainland regions.
Grillo, originally prized as the backbone grape for Marsala, is now increasingly bottled as a fresh, standalone dry white.

regions.name: Rioja
regions.summary: Rioja, in north-central Spain, is the country's most historically prestigious wine region and the benchmark for Tempranillo-based red wine, long defined by extended barrel and bottle ageing under its Crianza, Reserva, and Gran Reserva classification system.
regions.climate: Rioja sits in a valley along the Ebro river, shielded from Atlantic weather by the Sierra de Cantabria mountains to the north, which create a transitional climate blending Atlantic influence (in the cooler, wetter Rioja Alta and Rioja Alavesa) with more Mediterranean, continental conditions further east and lower in elevation (Rioja Oriental, formerly Rioja Baja). This range of mesoclimates allows for considerable stylistic variation, with the mountains also providing some protection from extreme cold and excessive rain.
regions.soils: Rioja Alta and Alavesa feature calcareous clay soils, alongside iron-rich clay, which support balanced, age-worthy Tempranillo. Rioja Oriental has more alluvial, sandy soils and a warmer climate, historically favoring higher-yielding, riper, fuller-bodied wine, though quality-focused single-vineyard projects have emerged there too in recent years.
regions.classification: Rioja is a DOCa (Denominación de Origen Calificada), Spain's highest classification tier alongside Priorat. Traditional ageing categories are Joven (little to no oak ageing), Crianza (minimum two years total ageing with at least one in oak), Reserva (minimum three years with at least one in oak), and Gran Reserva (minimum five years with at least two in oak and two in bottle). Since 2017, Rioja also permits Vino de Zona (sub-zone wines), Vino de Municipio (village wines), and Viñedo Singular (single-vineyard wines meeting strict criteria), moving the region toward a more terroir-focused, Burgundy-style classification alongside its traditional ageing categories.

subRegions.name: Rioja Alta
subRegions.notes: Higher-elevation, cooler western zone producing structured, elegant, age-worthy Tempranillo, historically the heart of traditional Rioja.

subRegions.name: Rioja Alavesa
subRegions.notes: Basque-administered northern zone with calcareous soils and small plots, producing fresh, aromatic, increasingly single-vineyard-focused wines.

subRegions.name: Rioja Oriental
subRegions.notes: Warmer, lower eastern zone (formerly Rioja Baja), traditionally a source of riper, fuller-bodied Garnacha-influenced wine.

regions.styles: Traditional Rioja red is medium-to-full-bodied, with red fruit, vanilla, coconut, and dill notes from extended ageing in American oak, though French oak and more fruit-forward, modern styles are increasingly common. Gran Reserva wines are the most structured and age-worthy, with tertiary notes of leather, tobacco, and dried fruit developing over long cellaring. White Rioja (Viura-based) ranges from fresh and unoaked to rich, barrel-fermented styles capable of extended ageing. Rosado (rosé) is also produced in a fresh, fruity style.
notes: Rioja's traditional reliance on American oak, which imparts distinctive coconut and dill notes, historically distinguished it from most other European red wines aged in French oak.
The 2017 introduction of Viñedo Singular (single vineyard) status marked a significant shift toward terroir-based classification, a departure from Rioja's historic focus purely on ageing time.
Rioja and Priorat are Spain's only two DOCa regions, the country's highest official quality tier, above standard DO.
Garnacha and other varieties are increasingly used to produce fresher, single-varietal, less oak-driven 'modern' Rioja aimed at contemporary palates.
Rioja's wine industry was significantly shaped in the 19th century by Bordeaux winemakers fleeing phylloxera, who brought barrel-ageing techniques with them.

regions.name: Ribera del Duero
regions.summary: Ribera del Duero, in north-central Spain along the upper Duero river, is renowned for producing some of Spain's most powerful and age-worthy red wines from Tempranillo (locally called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País), anchored by iconic estates such as Vega Sicilia.
regions.climate: Ribera del Duero has a harsh continental climate at high elevation (vineyards commonly sit between 700 and 1000 metres), with very hot summer days, cold nights, and a wide diurnal temperature range that preserves acidity and aromatic freshness in the grapes despite high ripeness. Winters are cold and can bring frost risk, while the high altitude and low humidity generally keep disease pressure low, though the region is vulnerable to spring frosts and hail.
regions.soils: Soils are varied but generally well-drained, including limestone, chalk, and clay on higher ground and alluvial sand and gravel closer to the Duero river, contributing to the concentration and structure typical of Ribera del Duero's best reds.
regions.classification: Ribera del Duero is a DO (Denominación de Origen) that shares Rioja's traditional ageing hierarchy of Crianza, Reserva, and Gran Reserva, based on minimum oak and bottle ageing periods, though many top estates release wines without these terms, favoring bespoke or estate-specific labeling to emphasize a single-vineyard or house style over the classic ageing ladder.
regions.styles: Ribera del Duero reds are typically full-bodied, deeply coloured, high in tannin and alcohol, with concentrated black fruit, and often significant new oak influence, especially in top wines meant for long ageing. Compared to Rioja, Ribera wines tend to be riper, darker-fruited, and more powerfully structured, though styles vary from modern, fruit-forward, internationally styled wines to more traditional, elegant examples. A small amount of rosado is also produced.
notes: Vega Sicilia, founded in the 19th century, is Ribera del Duero's most famous estate and one of Spain's most prestigious producers, predating the DO's formal creation in 1982.
The local Tempranillo clone is often called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País, reflecting the grape's long local history distinct from Rioja's Tempranillo.
Ribera del Duero's extreme diurnal temperature swings, sometimes exceeding 20°C between day and night, are central to the region's ability to achieve full ripeness while retaining freshness.
The region's rapid rise to international fame largely dates to the late 20th century, following Vega Sicilia's long-standing reputation and the DO's 1982 establishment.
Unlike Rioja, Ribera del Duero has traditionally focused almost exclusively on red wine, with white wine only permitted more recently.

regions.name: Priorat
regions.summary: Priorat, in the rugged hills of Catalonia, is one of only two Spanish regions (with Rioja) to hold DOCa status, producing intensely concentrated, mineral, old-vine Garnacha and Cariñena wines from steep terraced vineyards on distinctive black slate soil.
regions.climate: Priorat has a Mediterranean climate moderated by elevation and mountainous terrain, with hot, dry summers and low rainfall creating naturally low yields and water-stressed old vines. Steep slopes and varied aspects allow growers to select cooler, higher sites to counteract the region's overall heat, though drought stress and difficulty mechanizing the terraced, mountainous vineyards remain defining viticultural challenges.
regions.soils: Priorat's defining feature is llicorella, a dark, heat-retentive slate and quartzite soil that provides excellent drainage and forces vine roots deep in search of water, concentrating flavour in the grapes and giving the region's wines their distinctive minerality. This poor, rocky soil severely limits yields, contributing directly to the wines' intensity.
regions.classification: Priorat is one of Spain's two DOCa regions (alongside Rioja), reflecting its status as a historically and qualitatively elite zone. The region also recognizes Vi de Vila (village wines) designating wines from specific villages, and increasingly single-vineyard bottlings, paralleling Burgundian and Rioja-style moves toward terroir specificity. Many top wines are labeled simply with estate and vineyard names rather than traditional ageing categories.

subRegions.name: Gratallops
subRegions.notes: One of Priorat's most prestigious villages, home to several of the region's founding modern estates.

subRegions.name: Porrera
subRegions.notes: Village known for particularly powerful, structured old-vine Cariñena.

subRegions.name: Torroja del Priorat
subRegions.notes: Small central village contributing to the region's core llicorella-soil vineyards.

regions.styles: Priorat wines are typically full-bodied, high in alcohol (often 14.5% or above), deeply concentrated, and firmly structured, with dark fruit, liquorice, herbal, and mineral character from old-vine Garnacha and Cariñena, frequently supplemented by international varieties like Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah. These are serious, age-worthy wines, generally more powerful and less overtly fruity than most other Spanish Garnacha-based reds, with the potential for decades of cellaring in top examples.
notes: Priorat's modern reputation was essentially built from the mid-1980s by a small group of producers (including René Barbier, Álvaro Palacios, and others) who revived old, near-abandoned vineyards on llicorella slate.
The name 'llicorella' refers to the region's characteristic black slate and mica-schist soil, considered central to Priorat's identity and wine style.
Many of Priorat's vineyards are extremely old, low-yielding, dry-farmed bush vines planted on steep, difficult-to-work terraces, limiting mechanization.
Priorat achieved DOCa status in 2009, decades after Rioja, reflecting its comparatively recent rise to prominence despite a much older winemaking history.
The neighbouring, larger Montsant DO surrounds Priorat and produces wines from similar grapes, often at a more accessible price point.

regions.name: Rías Baixas
regions.summary: Rías Baixas, in Galicia in Spain's cool, damp northwest, is the country's premier white wine region, celebrated for aromatic, high-acid Albariño that has become one of Spain's most successful modern export wine styles.
regions.climate: Rías Baixas has a cool, wet, Atlantic maritime climate, among the rainiest in Spain, with the ocean's proximity moderating temperatures and providing consistent humidity. This climate necessitates specific viticultural adaptations, most notably training vines on raised granite pergolas (parras) to maximize air circulation and sun exposure while keeping bunches away from damp ground, reducing rot risk in a climate that could otherwise be highly disease-prone.
regions.soils: Soils are predominantly granite-based, often sandy and well-drained, sitting over a granite bedrock; this free-draining profile helps offset the region's high rainfall and contributes to the bright, mineral-inflected character of Albariño wines.
regions.classification: Rías Baixas is a DO with several officially recognized sub-zones reflecting Galicia's fragmented coastal geography, each with slightly different mesoclimates and, in some cases, distinct permitted grape blends. Albariño must make up the overwhelming majority of blends in most sub-zones, and the DO strictly regulates yields and the traditional pergola trellising method.

subRegions.name: Val do Salnés
subRegions.notes: The original heartland of Rías Baixas and Albariño, closest to the Atlantic, producing the region's most classic, saline, high-acid style.

subRegions.name: Condado do Tea
subRegions.notes: Warmer, more inland zone along the Miño river bordering Portugal, producing slightly riper, fuller-bodied wines.

subRegions.name: O Rosal
subRegions.notes: Coastal zone near the Portuguese border permitting more blending with Loureira and Treixadura alongside Albariño.

regions.styles: Rías Baixas wines are almost entirely dry, light-to-medium-bodied whites with pronounced aromatic character, notes of stone fruit, citrus, and often a distinct saline or sea-spray minerality, and high, refreshing acidity. Most are designed for early drinking, though a growing number of producers are making more textured, sometimes lees-aged or barrel-fermented examples with greater ageing potential.
notes: Albariño's high acidity and aromatic intensity, alongside its genetic (though debated) links to Alvarinho in neighbouring Vinho Verde, have made it one of the most recognizable single-varietal Spanish white wine styles internationally.

The traditional pergola (parra) trellising system, raising vines on granite posts, is a direct response to the region's high humidity and rainfall, distinguishing Rías Baixas vineyards visually from most of Spain.
Rías Baixas takes its name from Galicia's characteristic 'rías,' drowned river valleys similar to fjords, which shape the region's fragmented coastal geography and sub-zones.
The DO was formally established in 1988, and Albariño's commercial success has since made Rías Baixas one of Spain's fastest-growing quality wine regions.
Unlike much of inland Spain, Rías Baixas is defined far more by maritime than continental climate influence, a rarity among Spanish DOs.

regions.name: Jerez (Sherry Country)
regions.classification: Jerez-Xérès-Sherry is a DO governing the production of Sherry, with styles legally defined by production method and required minimum ageing under the solera system: Fino and Manzanilla (aged biologically under flor, minimum two years, typically bottled young and fresh), Amontillado (aged first biologically then oxidatively after the flor dies away), Oloroso (aged fully oxidatively from the start, fortified to a higher strength that prevents flor formation), and Palo Cortado (a rarer style beginning like Fino but developing an Oloroso-like character). Sweet styles include Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel (made from sun-dried grapes) and blended sweetened styles like Cream and Pale Cream. VOS and VORS designations certify Sherries with an average age of at least 20 and 30 years respectively.
regions.summary: Jerez, in Spain's far southwest near Cádiz, is the home of Sherry, one of the world's great fortified wine styles, uniquely shaped by the biological ageing effect of flor yeast and the fractional blending solera system.
regions.climate: Jerez has a hot, sunny Mediterranean climate with strong maritime influence from the nearby Atlantic Ocean, moderated further by the poniente, a cooling, humid westerly wind that helps sustain the flor yeast layer essential to Fino and Manzanilla production. Manzanilla, produced specifically in the coastal town of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, benefits from particularly strong, consistent maritime influence and higher humidity, contributing to its characteristically saline, delicate character compared to Fino made further inland.
regions.soils: The region's defining soil is albariza, a bright white, highly chalky soil with excellent water retention that allows vines to survive Jerez's hot, dry summers without irrigation while reflecting sunlight to aid ripening; it is considered the finest soil for Palomino, the grape used for the great majority of Sherry.

subRegions.name: Jerez de la Frontera
subRegions.notes: The historic administrative and commercial centre of the Sherry trade, home to many of the largest bodegas.

subRegions.name: Sanlúcar de Barrameda
subRegions.notes: Coastal town with cooler, more humid conditions, exclusively producing Manzanilla, a distinctively saline, delicate Fino-style Sherry.

subRegions.name: El Puerto de Santa María
subRegions.notes: Coastal town also known for classic, elegant Fino-style Sherry production.

regions.styles: Fino and Manzanilla are pale, bone-dry, light-bodied wines with a distinctive tangy, yeasty, saline freshness from ageing under flor, best drunk young and chilled. Amontillado is amber-coloured, dry, nutty, and more complex, combining biological and oxidative character. Oloroso is dark, full-bodied, dry, and intensely nutty, with notes of walnut, dried fruit, and wood. Pedro Ximénez is extremely sweet, dark, thick, and raisiny, often used both as a standalone dessert wine and as a blending component for sweetened styles like Cream Sherry.
notes: The solera system, a fractional blending method moving wine through tiers of barrels (criaderas) of increasing age toward a final solera tier, ensures consistency of style across vintages and is unique among the world's major wine regions.

Flor, a layer of naturally occurring yeast that forms on the surface of ageing Fino and Manzanilla, protects the wine from oxidation and imparts its distinctive fresh, tangy character; its survival depends on humidity, temperature, and the wine's alcohol level.

Sherry is fortified with grape spirit after fermentation, with the level of fortification determining whether flor can survive (lower strength, around 15%, for Fino/Manzanilla) or not (higher strength, around 17%+, for Oloroso).
Manzanilla can legally only be made in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, even though it uses the same Palomino grape and base wine as Fino made elsewhere in the DO.

Once one of the most globally traded wine styles, Sherry has seen a significant decline in mainstream popularity since the mid-20th century but retains a strong following among sommeliers and wine enthusiasts for its complexity and food-pairing versatility.

regions.name: Penedès
regions.summary: Penedès, in Catalonia near Barcelona, is the historic heartland of Cava, Spain's leading traditional-method sparkling wine, and has also become an important centre for both indigenous and international still wine production.
regions.climate: Penedès has a Mediterranean climate that shifts from warm and dry near the coast to progressively cooler and wetter with increasing elevation and distance inland toward the Serralada Prelitoral mountains. This range allows growers to match grape variety and style to site: warmer coastal and lowland areas suit fuller-bodied still wines, while higher, cooler vineyards preserve the acidity needed for quality Cava base wine.
regions.soils: Soils are varied, including limestone, clay, and sandy-gravel deposits, generally well-drained and moderately fertile; higher-elevation, poorer soils are typically favoured for premium Cava production, helping to control vigour and preserve freshness in the base wine.
regions.classification: Cava is a DO that is not geographically confined to Penedès alone (it can legally be produced in several designated zones across Spain), but Penedès is by far its historic and volumetric centre. Cava must be made by the traditional method (second fermentation in bottle) and aged for a minimum of nine months on lees, with higher tiers—Cava de Guarda Superior, Reserva, and Gran Reserva—requiring longer lees ageing (18, 15, and 30 months respectively) and, since 2019 reforms, organic viticulture for the top tiers. Penedès DO separately covers the region's still wines.

subRegions.name: Penedès Superior
subRegions.notes: Higher-elevation inland zone with a cooler climate, favoured for quality Cava base wine and increasingly for still white wine.

subRegions.name: Baix Penedès
subRegions.notes: Warmer, lower coastal zone historically associated with bulk wine production.

subRegions.name: Sant Sadurní d'Anoia
subRegions.notes: The historic town and effective capital of Cava production, home to major producers including Codorníu and Freixenet.

regions.styles: Cava is typically a dry (Brut) to extra-dry sparkling wine with fine bubbles from traditional-method production, showing citrus, green apple, and characteristic bready or nutty autolytic notes from lees ageing, with quality and complexity increasing through the Reserva and Gran Reserva tiers. Rosado Cava, often made with Garnacha or Pinot Noir, offers red berry character. Penedès still wines range from crisp, fresh whites made from local varieties to fuller-bodied reds and international-variety wines, reflecting the region's varied terrain and long history of viticultural experimentation.
notes: Cava's traditional grape trio—Macabeo, Xarel-lo, and Parellada—each contributes distinct qualities to the blend: body, structure/acidity, and aromatic freshness respectively.

The Cava DO controversially spans multiple, non-contiguous regions of Spain, meaning not all Cava is Catalan, a point of ongoing debate that led some top Penedès producers to leave the DO and adopt the separate Corpinnat or Clàssic Penedès designations to emphasize terroir specificity.
Josep Raventós of Codorníu is traditionally credited with producing Spain's first traditional-method sparkling wine in Penedès in the 1870s, inspired by Champagne.

Penedès was also a pioneering region for Spanish still wine innovation, with producer Miguel Torres playing a major role from the 1960s-70s in introducing international grape varieties and modern winemaking techniques to Spain.

Corpinnat, launched in 2017 by a group of premium Penedès producers, requires organic farming, hand-harvesting, extended lees ageing, and production within the historic Penedès area, positioning itself as a stricter, terroir-focused alternative to Cava.

regions.name: Douro Valley
regions.summary: The Douro Valley is the birthplace of Port wine and one of the world's oldest demarcated wine regions, formally delimited in 1756. Steep terraced vineyards line the schist slopes above the Douro river, producing fortified wines ranging from everyday Ruby to decades-worthy Vintage Port, alongside a growing reputation for structured dry Douro DOC table wines.
regions.climate: The climate is continental and increasingly hot and dry moving inland, sheltered from Atlantic influence by the Serra do Marão and Montemuro mountain ranges. Summers are very hot with low rainfall and winters cold, creating significant stress on vines grown on poor, rocky soils. Elevation, aspect and proximity to the river moderate individual vineyard sites considerably. This combination of heat and drought stress concentrates fruit and sugar, which is essential for producing the ripe, alcohol-rich base wines used for fortification.
regions.soils: Schist bedrock dominates, and vine roots must penetrate its fractured layers to find water reserves during the dry summer, giving low yields of concentrated fruit. Small pockets of granite occur, particularly toward the western, cooler end of the region, generally producing lighter, less powerful wines than schist sites.
regions.classification: The Douro DOC covers both fortified Port and dry Douro table wines. Vineyards are individually rated under an official points-based classification (grades A to F) based on factors including altitude, aspect, soil, yield and vine age, which determines the annual quota (the Beneficio) each grower is permitted to fortify into Port. Port itself is further categorized by style and ageing regime: Ruby, Tawny, Vintage, Late Bottled Vintage, Colheita, Reserve, and aged Tawny with indicated age (10, 20, 30 or 40 years).

subRegions.name: Baixo Corgo
subRegions.notes: The westernmost and wettest, coolest sub-zone, historically supplying lighter styles and bulk production.

subRegions.name: Cima Corgo
subRegions.notes: The historic heartland of premium Port around Pinhão, home to many of the top-rated quintas.

subRegions.name: Douro Superior
subRegions.notes: The easternmost, hottest and driest sub-zone, more remote but increasingly prized for both Port and acclaimed dry reds.

regions.styles: Fortified wines dominate: youthful, fruity Ruby and Late Bottled Vintage; oxidative, nutty, caramelized Tawny aged in wood; and Vintage Port, declared only in exceptional years, built for decades of bottle ageing. Dry white and rosé Port also exist in smaller volumes. Douro DOC still wines are typically full-bodied, structured, dark-fruited reds with real ageing potential, alongside a smaller volume of increasingly polished whites.
notes: Traditional Rabelo boats once carried Port barrels down the Douro to the ageing lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, opposite Porto.
Vintage Port can only be declared in exceptional years and requires approval from the regulatory body (IVDP).
Foot-treading in stone lagares remains practiced by top quintas for gentle, effective extraction of colour and tannin.
The Alto Douro Wine Region has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001 for its historic terraced landscape.

regions.name: Vinho Verde
regions.summary: Vinho Verde is Portugal's largest DOC, located in the lush, rainy northwest, known for producing young, light, high-acid white wines, often with a gentle spritz. The name translates as 'green wine,' referring to its youthful style rather than its colour.
regions.climate: The climate is strongly Atlantic maritime, cool and notably wet, with high humidity that historically encouraged growers to train vines high off the ground (on pergolas or wire-and-post systems) to improve air circulation and reduce rot risk. Conditions become progressively warmer and drier moving inland and toward the Spanish border. This cool, damp climate preserves high natural acidity and keeps alcohol levels naturally low.
regions.soils: Granite-derived, sandy, well-draining and generally low in fertility, which helps offset the region's abundant rainfall by limiting excess vine vigour.
regions.classification: The DOC Vinho Verde is divided into nine officially recognized sub-regions with differing climates and grape emphases. Only the Monção e Melgaço sub-region is permitted to label wines varietally as Alvarinho, reflecting its distinct, riper style; regulation also historically capped minimum and maximum alcohol levels typical of the region's light style.

subRegions.name: Monção e Melgaço
subRegions.notes: The Alvarinho heartland near the Spanish border, producing riper, more structured, often single-varietal wines.

subRegions.name: Lima
subRegions.notes: Dominated by aromatic, floral Loureiro.

subRegions.name: Basto
subRegions.notes: Known for deeply coloured, tannic red wines from Vinhão, mostly consumed locally.

subRegions.name: Ave
subRegions.notes: A central sub-region contributing to blended Vinho Verde whites.

regions.styles: The classic style is a light-bodied, dry white with high acidity, low-to-moderate alcohol, green citrus and stone fruit character, and a light natural or added spritz. Monção e Melgaço Alvarinho wines are richer and more textured. A smaller volume of deeply coloured, high-acid, tannic red wine is made from Vinhão and consumed mainly within the region.
notes: The name 'Vinho Verde' refers to the wine's youthful freshness, not the colour of the grapes or wine.
The traditional light spritz historically came from malolactic fermentation occurring in bottle; today it is often achieved by CO2 addition.
Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço is generally the most prestigious and age-worthy style produced in the region.
High pergola and cross training were traditionally used to combat the region's humidity and rot pressure.

regions.name: Dão
regions.summary: Dão is a mountain-ringed, granite plateau region in north-central Portugal, historically important for elegant, structured red wines built around Touriga Nacional, and increasingly respected for fine whites from Encruzado.
regions.climate: The surrounding mountains, including the Serra da Estrela to the south, shelter Dão from both Atlantic rainfall and the extremes of the wider Iberian interior, giving a moderated continental climate. Many vineyards sit at meaningful elevation, which combined with granite soils produces a notable diurnal temperature range that helps preserve acidity and aromatics in the grapes. This relatively temperate, sheltered setting favours elegance over power.
regions.soils: Predominantly granite, weathering into sandy, well-drained, nutrient-poor soils that naturally restrain vine vigour and contribute to the region's characteristically elegant, structured wines.
regions.classification: Dão was demarcated as a DOC in 1908, making it one of Portugal's oldest official wine regions. For much of the 20th century production was dominated by cooperatives under a restrictive system that limited investment and quality; liberalization from 1990 onward opened the way for independent quintas and a marked rise in quality.

subRegions.name: Serra da Estrela foothills
subRegions.notes: Higher-altitude vineyards contributing freshness and structure.

subRegions.name: Silgueiros
subRegions.notes: One of the traditionally recognized informal sub-zones within the DOC.

subRegions.name: Terras de Azurara
subRegions.notes: A further informal sub-zone contributing to regional blends.

regions.styles: Reds are elegant and aromatic, with firm but refined tannins, red fruit and floral violet notes, and good ageing potential, often likened stylistically to a more rustic cousin of Burgundy. Whites made from Encruzado are increasingly acclaimed for their texture, minerality and capacity to age well in bottle.
notes: Dão's cooperative-dominated system limited quality and investment until liberalization in 1990 opened production to independent growers.
Encruzado is widely regarded as one of Portugal's finest native white grape varieties.
The region's granite soils and elevation are often credited for giving Dão reds an elegance distinct from the bolder wines of the neighbouring Douro.
Surrounding mountain ranges act as a natural barrier, moderating both Atlantic and continental climatic extremes.

regions.name: Alentejo
regions.summary: Alentejo is a vast, warm, plateau region in southern Portugal known for approachable, ripe, full-bodied red wines and a revived ancient tradition of fermenting wine in clay amphorae (talha). It has become a commercially dominant force in Portugal's modern wine industry.
