regions.climate: The climate is Mediterranean-continental, with hot, dry summers and mild winters and abundant sunshine across most of the region, though drought and heat stress are recurring risks. Higher-altitude and more easterly areas, such as Portalegre, are notably cooler and see greater rainfall, producing fresher, more structured wines than the flatter, hotter plains further south and east.
regions.soils: Soils vary considerably by sub-zone, including granite, schist and limestone, generally contributing to the region's full, ripe fruit character, with cooler granite sites in Portalegre giving more freshness and elevation.
regions.classification: The DOC Alentejo sits alongside the broader, more flexible Vinho Regional Alentejano designation, and is further divided into eight recognized sub-regions. Traditional talha wines, fermented and often aged in large clay amphorae, have their own recognized traditional production category (Vinho de Talha, DOP).

subRegions.name: Portalegre
subRegions.notes: The coolest, highest-altitude sub-region, producing the freshest and most distinctive wines.

subRegions.name: Borba
subRegions.notes: Known for approachable, fruit-driven reds on chalky-clay soils.

subRegions.name: Reguengos
subRegions.notes: A warm, productive sub-region central to the region's commercial red wine output.

subRegions.name: Vidigueira
subRegions.notes: A historic sub-region and traditional home of talha winemaking.

regions.styles: Reds are typically ripe, full-bodied and soft-tannined with generous dark fruit, often oak-aged and approachable from an early age, though top examples from Portalegre and elsewhere can age well. Whites are commonly round and fruit-forward; traditional talha wines offer a distinctive, slightly oxidative, textural style.
notes: Ancient talha (clay amphora) winemaking has been revived and given its own recognized DOP category, Vinho de Talha.
Portalegre's higher altitude and granite soils give markedly fresher, more structured wines than the rest of Alentejo.
Large historic agricultural estates (herdades) are characteristic of the region's landscape and wine production scale.
Alentejo has become one of Portugal's most commercially significant wine regions since the 1990s, especially for export.

regions.name: Mosel
regions.summary: The Mosel is one of the world's great Riesling regions, defined by extremely steep, slate-soiled vineyards along the winding Mosel river and its tributaries, the Saar and Ruwer. It produces some of the most delicate, aromatic, ageworthy, and often lower-alcohol white wines in the world.
regions.climate: The climate is cool continental and marginal for ripening, making the river and its steep, often south-facing valley slopes essential: the water reflects sunlight onto the vines and moderates temperature. Vintage variation is significant, with warmer years producing riper, more concentrated wines and cooler years yielding leaner, higher-acid styles. This marginal climate is central to the Mosel's hallmark combination of intense aromatics, high acidity and comparatively low alcohol.
regions.soils: Devonian slate, in blue and red variants, dominates the best sites, retaining and radiating heat while draining excess water on the steep slopes, and is widely credited with the region's distinctive mineral character. Some flatter or lower-lying sites have heavier clay or loam soils, generally producing less refined wine.
regions.classification: The Prädikatswein system classifies wines by the ripeness (must weight) of the grapes at harvest, from Kabinett through Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, with wines ranging from dry to lusciously sweet. The independent VDP classification additionally recognizes top vineyard sites as Erste Lage and Grosse Lage, the latter used for the finest, most age-worthy dry and Prädikat wines.

subRegions.name: Saar
subRegions.notes: A cooler tributary valley producing racy, steely, high-acid Riesling.

subRegions.name: Ruwer
subRegions.notes: The smallest tributary district, known for delicate, aromatic wines.

subRegions.name: Mittelmosel (Bernkastel)
subRegions.notes: The historic heart of the region, home to celebrated sites such as Wehlener Sonnenuhr.

subRegions.name: Terrassenmosel
subRegions.notes: Features some of the steepest, hand-worked terraced vineyards in the region.

regions.styles: Wines are overwhelmingly white and centred on Riesling, spanning a wide sweetness spectrum from bone-dry (trocken) to intensely sweet dessert styles. Hallmarks include high natural acidity, pronounced floral and stone-fruit aromatics that develop petrol-like notes with age, and historically low alcohol, particularly in finer Kabinett and Spätlese wines. The best examples, especially sweeter Prädikat wines, have exceptional ageing potential spanning decades.
notes: The Mosel includes some of the steepest vineyards in the world, such as the Bremmer Calmont, with gradients exceeding 60%.
Individually named slate vineyard sites, such as Wehlener Sonnenuhr and Piesporter Goldtröpfchen, carry particular prestige.
Eiswein is harvested while frozen on the vine, typically at around -7°C, yielding intensely concentrated sweet wine.
On the steepest sites, vines are traditionally trained on individual stakes because terracing or mechanization is impossible.

regions.name: Rheingau
regions.summary: The Rheingau is a small but historically prestigious region along the south-facing bank of the Rhine near Wiesbaden and Rüdesheim, long regarded as a cradle of German Riesling quality and classification, alongside a notable pocket of fine Spätburgunder around Assmannshausen.
regions.climate: The region benefits from a relatively warm, sheltered mesoclimate for Germany, thanks to south-facing slopes along the wide Rhine, which acts as a heat reservoir reflecting light and moderating temperature, combined with protection from cold northerly winds by the Taunus hills. This favourable exposure allows for riper, fuller styles of Riesling than in cooler German regions.
regions.soils: Soils vary from deep loess and loam on the lower slopes to quartzite, slate and phyllite on the steeper upper slopes near Rüdesheim, with marl also present in places; the mix contributes to the region's generally fuller, riper Riesling character compared with the Mosel.
regions.classification: The VDP classification is prominent here, with top sites designated Erste Lage and Grosse Lage; the Rheingau pioneered a precursor system, Erstes Gewächs, in the 1990s that anticipated the national Grosses Gewächs designation for dry wines. The Prädikatswein ripeness scale also applies for traditional fruity and sweet styles.

subRegions.name: Rüdesheim
subRegions.notes: Steep, terraced, quartzite and slate slopes producing powerful, structured Riesling.

subRegions.name: Johannisberg
subRegions.notes: Historic site linked to the legendary origin of Spätlese, home to Schloss Johannisberg.

subRegions.name: Erbach
subRegions.notes: Includes the celebrated Marcobrunn vineyard, known for rich, powerful wines.

subRegions.name: Assmannshausen
subRegions.notes: Specializes in elegant, light-to-medium-bodied Spätburgunder rather than Riesling.

subRegions.name: Hochheim
subRegions.notes: The easternmost district, which gave rise to the old English term 'Hock' for German white wine.

regions.styles: Rheingau Riesling tends to be fuller-bodied and riper than Mosel styles, with dry (trocken) wines now dominant alongside classic fruity and sweet Prädikat wines. Assmannshausen Spätburgunder produces elegant, lighter-bodied red wines with fine perfume, distinctive within Germany's still-limited red wine tradition.
notes: Kloster Eberbach monastery played a central historical role in developing the region's Riesling cultivation and winemaking.
The 1775 legend of a delayed courier at Schloss Johannisberg is often cited as the origin of intentional late-harvest (Spätlese) picking.
The English term 'Hock' for German white wine derives from the village of Hochheim.
The Rheingau led Germany's dry Riesling quality movement through classifications such as Charta and later Erstes Gewächs.

regions.name: Pfalz
regions.summary: The Pfalz is Germany's second-largest wine region, a warm and sheltered area bordering Alsace in the south, known for riper, fuller styles of Riesling as well as extensive plantings of Pinot family varieties (Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder, Weissburgunder).
regions.climate: Sheltered by the Haardt mountains, an extension of the Vosges, from westerly rain, the Pfalz is one of Germany's warmest and driest wine regions, mild enough that almond, fig and lemon trees grow along the Deutsche Weinstrasse. This warmth allows for consistently riper, fuller-bodied wine styles than in Germany's cooler northern regions.
regions.soils: Soils are diverse, including sandstone, limestone, basalt, loess and clay-marl depending on the sub-zone, giving Riesling here a wide range of expression from mineral and structured to opulent and full.
regions.classification: The VDP classification designates top dry-wine sites as Erste Lage and Grosse Lage, with the Prädikatswein ripeness scale also used for traditional styles. The Mittelhaardt, part of the Deutsche Weinstrasse, is considered the qualitative heart of the region.

subRegions.name: Mittelhaardt
subRegions.notes: Home to the celebrated villages of Forst, Deidesheim, Wachenheim and Ruppertsberg, source of the region's finest Riesling.

subRegions.name: Südliche Weinstrasse
subRegions.notes: The warmer southern zone, with a greater focus on red wine and Pinot family varieties.

regions.styles: Pfalz Riesling is typically riper and fuller-bodied, and often drier, than Mosel or Rheingau styles. Pinot family varieties yield full, structured whites, while Dornfelder produces deeply coloured, fruity, everyday red wines. Overall the region shows more weight and less austerity than Germany's cooler regions.
notes: The Pfalz is Germany's warmest and driest major wine region, mild enough to support almond, fig and lemon trees.
Once known largely for bulk wine, the region's reputation shifted dramatically toward quality from the late 20th century, led by Mittelhaardt villages such as Forst and Deidesheim.
It has the largest area under vine for Pinot varieties of any German region.
Basalt soils around Forst, including the Kirchenstück and Jesuitengarten vineyards, are associated with particularly powerful Riesling.

regions.name: Wachau
regions.summary: The Wachau is a small but internationally prestigious stretch of the Danube valley producing some of Austria's finest dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, grown on dramatic terraced vineyards and governed by its own strict private classification system, the Vinea Wachau Codex.
regions.climate: The region sits at a climatic crossroads where cool air funnelling down the Danube from the west meets warmer, drier Pannonian air from the east, producing a wide diurnal temperature range that preserves acidity and aromatic intensity in the grapes. The river also moderates temperature and reflects sunlight onto the steep terraced slopes, aiding ripening on otherwise difficult sites.
regions.soils: The upper terraced slopes near Spitz and Dürnstein are dominated by gneiss and other crystalline primary rock, giving lean, mineral, steely wines, while the lower slopes and valley floor near Krems have wind-blown loess soils, producing richer, spicier, fuller-bodied wines.
regions.classification: Rather than using Austria's national DAC system, Wachau producers largely follow the independent Vinea Wachau Codex, which classifies dry wines by ripeness and body into three tiers: Steinfeder (lightest, capped at a low maximum alcohol), Federspiel (medium-bodied, comparable to a Kabinett-style wine), and Smaragd (the fullest, ripest and most age-worthy, named after the green lizards found basking on the sun-warmed terraces).

subRegions.name: Spitz
subRegions.notes: A cooler, western village zone known for elegant, mineral wines from primary rock soils.

subRegions.name: Weissenkirchen
subRegions.notes: A central village zone with a mix of terrace soils and styles.

subRegions.name: Dürnstein
subRegions.notes: Famed for steep gneiss terraces and structured, age-worthy wines.

subRegions.name: Krems (Stein)
subRegions.notes: The easternmost, loess-influenced zone, producing richer, spicier wines.

regions.styles: Wines are entirely dry and textured, with pronounced acidity and strong mineral character. Grüner Veltliner typically shows white pepper, citrus and stone fruit notes, while Riesling offers apricot, floral and mineral tones. Smaragd wines are full-bodied and built for extended ageing, while Steinfeder wines are light, fresh and meant for early drinking.
notes: The Wachau's dry-farmed, hand-worked terraced vineyards form a UNESCO World Heritage Cultural Landscape.
Vinea Wachau Codex producers voluntarily forgo the national DAC designation and chaptalization to protect their traditional dry, terroir-driven style.
The Smaragd category is named after the green lizards commonly seen basking on the sun-warmed terrace walls.
The contrast between primary-rock and loess soils gives the Wachau two clearly distinguishable stylistic camps within a small area.

regions.name: Burgenland
regions.summary: Burgenland is Austria's easternmost and warmest wine region, bordering Hungary and centred on the shallow Neusiedlersee lake, known for both historically prized botrytis-affected sweet whites and, increasingly, powerful, age-worthy red wines led by Blaufränkisch.
regions.climate: The climate is continental and warmed by the influence of the Pannonian plain, making it Austria's hottest wine region overall. The large, shallow Neusiedlersee lake creates a distinct mesoclimate, with morning mists and humidity around its shores promoting noble rot ideal for sweet wine production, while the flat land east of the lake favours full ripening of red grapes; the hillier Leithaberg area to the west is notably cooler.
regions.soils: Soils vary widely across the region: sandy and gravelly ground near the lake, clay and loess further inland, and limestone and schist on the Leithaberg hills, each contributing distinct styles from the different sub-zones.
regions.classification: Burgenland's DAC system operates at the sub-region level rather than as one blanket designation, with distinct DACs including Mittelburgenland DAC (Blaufränkisch-focused), Leithaberg DAC, Eisenberg DAC and Neusiedlersee DAC, each regulating permitted varieties and stylistic typicity. Botrytized sweet wines around the Neusiedlersee also use the Prädikat sweetness scale, with the traditional Ruster Ausbruch category recognized by its own historic legal status.

subRegions.name: Neusiedlersee
subRegions.notes: Lake-side district famed for Ruster Ausbruch sweet wines and also producing full-bodied reds.

subRegions.name: Leithaberg
subRegions.notes: Limestone and schist hills producing elegant reds and whites.

subRegions.name: Mittelburgenland
subRegions.notes: Known as Austria's Blaufränkisch heartland, sometimes called 'Blaufränkischland.'

subRegions.name: Eisenberg (Südburgenland)
subRegions.notes: Iron-rich soils producing peppery, elegant, structured Blaufränkisch.

regions.styles: Styles range from lusciously sweet, botrytis-affected whites, such as Ruster Ausbruch, to powerful, structured, age-worthy reds built around Blaufränkisch, alongside fresh dry whites. Reds increasingly show dark fruit, black pepper spice and firm, fine tannin, and have gained significant international recognition.
notes: Ruster Ausbruch is historically ranked alongside Tokaji and Sauternes as one of the world's classic sweet wine styles, with its own traditional legal category.
The shallow Neusiedlersee lake and its reed-lined shores create ideal humid conditions for noble rot development.
Blaufränkisch from Mittelburgenland and Eisenberg is widely considered Austria's most serious age-worthy red wine.
Burgenland's DAC system is applied village-by-village or sub-region-by-sub-region rather than as a single regional designation.

regions.name: Tokaj
regions.summary: Tokaj is a historic Hungarian region renowned above all for Tokaji Aszú, one of the world's oldest formally classified sweet wines, made from botrytis-affected grapes grown on volcanic soils in the Tokaj-Hegyalja hills, alongside increasingly acclaimed dry Furmint.
regions.climate: The region has a continental climate with long, warm autumns; morning mists rising from the confluence of the Bodrog and Tisza rivers encourage the development of noble rot, while subsequent sunny, dry afternoons help concentrate and partially raisin the affected berries. The volcanic hills provide varied mesoclimates and shelter across the region's vineyards.
regions.soils: Volcanic rhyolite and andesite bedrock weathers into clay-rich (nyirok) and loess topsoils, which retain water well and contribute a distinctive minerality to both the sweet Aszú wines and the region's dry whites.
regions.classification: Tokaj-Hegyalja's vineyards were formally classified by quality in the 1730s, one of the world's earliest vineyard classification systems, predating Bordeaux's 1855 classification by over a century. Aszú wines were traditionally graded in puttonyos, indicating the proportion of botrytized berry paste added to a base wine, though regulation has since shifted the legal standard toward minimum residual sugar levels rather than the historic puttonyos count alone.

subRegions.name: Mád
subRegions.notes: Widely regarded as home to some of the region's finest vineyard sites.

subRegions.name: Tarcal
subRegions.notes: A historic village with notable classified vineyards.

subRegions.name: Tállya
subRegions.notes: Known for high-elevation sites and mineral-driven wines.

subRegions.name: Bodrogkeresztúr
subRegions.notes: A traditional village contributing to the region's classic Aszú production.

regions.styles: Classic Tokaji Aszú is intensely sweet with high acidity and complex notes of dried apricot, honey and marmalade, capable of ageing for decades. Szamorodni ranges from dry to sweet depending on the proportion of botrytized berries in the harvested lot. Dry Furmint has become increasingly celebrated in its own right as a crisp, mineral, age-worthy white wine.
notes: Tokaj-Hegyalja's 1730s vineyard classification predates Bordeaux's celebrated 1855 classification by more than a century.
Modern puttonyos labeling has been revised to align with minimum residual sugar thresholds rather than the traditional butt-count method alone.
The Tokaj Wine Region Historic Cultural Landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Eszencia is the ultra-rare, extraordinarily sweet, very low-alcohol free-run juice of botrytized berries, sometimes aged for decades.

regions.name: Napa Valley
regions.summary: The most prestigious fine-wine region in the United States, world-renowned for Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends. Though small in total production, it commands the highest grape and wine prices in the country and anchors California's reputation for premium wine.
regions.climate: Mediterranean climate moderated by fog and cooling air drawn in from San Pablo Bay, which creates a marked diurnal temperature swing as morning fog burns off to warm, sunny afternoons. The Mayacamas Mountains to the west and Vaca Mountains to the east create rain-shadow effects and offer elevated sites above the valley fog line. Mesoclimates vary considerably along the valley's roughly 30-mile length, from the cooler, bay-influenced south (Carneros) to the warmer north (Calistoga). This range allows a wide span of ripening styles within a compact area.
regions.soils: Napa's geology is unusually complex for its size, combining volcanic soils on the eastern hillsides (as in Stags Leap District) with marine sedimentary soils on the western side and alluvial fans and gravelly loams across the valley floor. Carneros in the south has cooler, clay-rich soils suited to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay rather than Cabernet.
regions.classification: Napa Valley is an AVA (American Viticultural Area) containing 16 nested sub-AVAs, each recognized for a distinct combination of climate, soil and topography rather than any quality ranking. US AVA rules require a minimum of 75% of grapes to originate from the named AVA, and unlike European appellation systems there are no yield caps or officially mandated styles.

subRegions.name: Stags Leap District
subRegions.notes: Volcanic soils on the eastern hills produce elegant, structured Cabernet Sauvignon with fine tannins.

subRegions.name: Rutherford
subRegions.notes: Alluvial benchland famous for the 'Rutherford dust' tannin character in its Cabernet.

subRegions.name: Oakville
subRegions.notes: Considered a benchmark Cabernet Sauvignon appellation, home to numerous icon wineries.

subRegions.name: Carneros
subRegions.notes: Cool, bay-influenced zone shared with Sonoma, best suited to Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling base wine.

subRegions.name: Howell Mountain
subRegions.notes: High-elevation AVA above the fog line, giving powerful, tannic red wines.

subRegions.name: Calistoga
subRegions.notes: The valley's warmest northern end, producing ripe, bold red wines.

regions.styles: Full-bodied red wines dominate, led by Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends showing ripe black fruit, notable oak spice from extensive new French oak use, firm tannins and strong ageing potential of a decade or more for top examples. Chardonnay is typically full-bodied and oaked with stone and tropical fruit character, while Zinfandel offers jammy, peppery richness. Overall the valley's wines lean toward power, ripeness and relatively high alcohol.
notes: Napa's 1976 'Judgment of Paris' result, where Napa wines outscored top French wines in a blind tasting, was pivotal in establishing California's international reputation.
Phylloxera devastated much of Napa in the late 1980s after the AXR1 rootstock proved non-resistant, forcing large-scale replanting on resistant rootstocks.
Napa Valley produces only a small fraction of California's total wine volume yet accounts for a disproportionate share of its most expensive bottlings.
The valley's extraordinary mesoclimate diversity, driven by fog, elevation and two bordering mountain ranges, is remarkable given its compact size.

regions.name: Sonoma County
regions.summary: A large and climatically diverse California wine county west of Napa, valued for its range of sites from cool coastal zones to warmer inland valleys. It is particularly celebrated for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and old-vine Zinfandel, alongside strong Cabernet Sauvignon from its warmer pockets.
regions.climate: Sonoma's coastline and multiple gaps in the coastal ridge allow direct Pacific fog and wind to penetrate inland, especially along the Russian River corridor, giving many sites a cool, maritime character with significant diurnal swings. Inland and eastern areas such as Alexander Valley and Sonoma Valley are more sheltered by the Mayacamas range and enjoy a warmer, more Mediterranean climate. This produces a wider range of mesoclimates than neighboring Napa within a similarly sized county, enabling both cool- and warm-climate varieties to thrive.
regions.soils: Soils vary widely across the county: Goldridge sandy loam in the Russian River Valley favors Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, volcanic soils appear in Sonoma Valley and Moon Mountain, gravelly alluvial soils in Alexander Valley suit Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel, and ancient seabed and sandstone deposits characterize cooler coastal sites.
regions.classification: Sonoma County AVA contains roughly 18 nested and overlapping sub-AVAs, each defined by distinct climate and soil rather than a quality hierarchy. As with all US AVAs, boundaries reflect geography, not officially mandated quality standards, and labeling requires a minimum of 75% of fruit from the named AVA.

subRegions.name: Russian River Valley
subRegions.notes: Cool, fog-affected AVA regarded as a premier source of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

subRegions.name: Sonoma Coast
subRegions.notes: A broad, cool, often high-elevation coastal zone for elegant Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

subRegions.name: Alexander Valley
subRegions.notes: Warmer inland valley strong for Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel.

subRegions.name: Dry Creek Valley
subRegions.notes: Historic heartland of old-vine Zinfandel.

subRegions.name: Sonoma Valley
subRegions.notes: The county's historic core, with diverse plantings including old-vine Zinfandel.

regions.styles: Pinot Noir ranges from bright, red-fruited wines in cooler coastal sites to riper, darker-fruited examples further inland, generally medium to medium-plus bodied with lively acidity. Chardonnay spans lean, mineral, barrel-fermented styles through to richer, more buttery expressions. Old-vine Zinfandel is robust, jammy and peppery with notably high alcohol, while Alexander Valley Cabernet Sauvignon tends to show riper fruit and softer tannins than Napa's version.
notes: Sonoma has more distinct AVAs than Napa despite comparable overall vineyard area, reflecting its greater climatic diversity.
The Russian River Valley is regarded as one of California's most important Pinot Noir and Chardonnay zones.
Sonoma retains substantial plantings of century-old Zinfandel vines, particularly in Dry Creek and Sonoma Valley.
Multiple gaps in Sonoma's coastal ridge give many of its sites more direct fog and wind exposure than most of Napa.

regions.name: Central Coast (Santa Barbara & Paso Robles)
regions.summary: A long, climatically varied stretch of the California coast south of San Francisco, encompassing the cool, ocean-funneled valleys of Santa Barbara County, noted for Pinot Noir and Syrah, and the warmer, Rhône- and Bordeaux-friendly Paso Robles further north.
regions.climate: Santa Barbara County's defining feature is its rare east-west transverse valleys (Santa Ynez and Santa Maria), which open directly onto the Pacific and funnel cooling fog and wind far inland, creating some of California's coolest vineyard sites. Paso Robles lies further from strong marine influence and instead has a more continental profile, with hot days, cool nights and large diurnal swings driven by elevation rather than direct fog. Together the Central Coast spans from very cool, fog-affected zones near the ocean to warm, dry inland districts.
regions.soils: Soils are highly varied given the region's complex geology. Calcareous and diatomaceous soils are notable in parts of Santa Barbara, such as Sta. Rita Hills, favoring Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, while Paso Robles' west side has extensive limestone-rich soils that contribute structure to its Rhône-variety reds, alongside sandy and alluvial soils elsewhere in the district.
regions.classification: Under the broad Central Coast AVA sit numerous nested sub-AVAs, including Santa Barbara County's Sta. Rita Hills, Santa Ynez Valley and Santa Maria Valley, and San Luis Obispo County's Paso Robles AVA, itself divided into 11 sub-AVAs since 2014 to reflect internal soil and mesoclimate differences. As with all US AVAs, these are geographic rather than quality designations.

subRegions.name: Sta. Rita Hills
subRegions.notes: One of California's coolest AVAs, open to direct Pacific influence, prized for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

subRegions.name: Santa Maria Valley
subRegions.notes: Cool, historic origin point for Santa Barbara Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

subRegions.name: Paso Robles Willow Creek District
subRegions.notes: Limestone-rich sub-AVA known for structured Rhône-style blends.

subRegions.name: Paso Robles Adelaida District
subRegions.notes: Hillside, calcareous-soil sub-AVA producing powerful red wines.

subRegions.name: Edna Valley
subRegions.notes: Cool coastal pocket near San Luis Obispo suited to Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

regions.styles: Santa Barbara's cooler zones produce elegant, aromatic Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with bright acidity, alongside increasingly acclaimed cool-climate Syrah showing peppery, savory character. Paso Robles specializes in bold, full-bodied Rhône-style red blends (Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre) as well as rich Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel with ripe fruit and considerable alcohol. Overall the Central Coast offers an unusually wide stylistic range from lean and mineral to powerful and fruit-forward.
notes: The Santa Ynez and Santa Maria Valleys are rare east-west oriented coastal valleys, unlike California's typically north-south mountain ranges, allowing direct Pacific fog and wind to travel far inland.
Paso Robles experiences some of California's largest diurnal temperature swings, helping Rhône varieties ripen fully while retaining acidity.
The 2004 film Sideways significantly raised the international profile of Santa Barbara Pinot Noir.
Paso Robles was subdivided into 11 sub-AVAs in 2014 in recognition of its considerable internal soil and climate diversity.

regions.name: Willamette Valley
regions.summary: Oregon's leading wine region and one of the New World's most celebrated sources of Pinot Noir, valued for cool-climate elegance, bright acidity and pronounced site expression often compared to red Burgundy.
regions.climate: The valley has a cool, maritime-influenced climate shaped by the Van Duzer Corridor, a gap in the Coast Range that channels cooling Pacific air and afternoon wind into the valley. The Coast Range also provides a rain-shadow effect against the wettest Pacific storms, while the Cascade Mountains lie to the east. The growing season is long and mild, allowing gradual ripening, though rain around harvest remains a recurring risk given the region's northerly, maritime setting.
regions.soils: Three principal soil types define the valley: Jory soils, red, volcanic and well-drained, common in the Dundee Hills; Willakenzie soils, derived from uplifted marine sediment, found in the western hills; and Laurelwood soils, a loess layer over basalt, in the north. These free-draining hillside soils are generally preferred over the valley floor's more fertile alluvial soils, as they encourage vine stress and fruit concentration.
regions.classification: The Willamette Valley AVA contains several nested sub-AVAs recognized chiefly for distinct soils and mesoclimate, including Dundee Hills, Ribbon Ridge, Yamhill-Carlton, McMinnville, Eola-Amity Hills, Van Duzer Corridor and Laurelwood District. Oregon's labeling laws are notably strict, historically requiring higher minimum varietal content for many labeled grapes than the federal 75% standard applied elsewhere in the US.

subRegions.name: Dundee Hills
subRegions.notes: Volcanic Jory soils yield some of the region's most elegant, benchmark Pinot Noir.

subRegions.name: Ribbon Ridge
subRegions.notes: A small AVA on uplifted marine sediment producing concentrated wines.

subRegions.name: Yamhill-Carlton
subRegions.notes: Marine sedimentary soils in a horseshoe-shaped valley give structured Pinot Noir.

subRegions.name: Eola-Amity Hills
subRegions.notes: Wind-swept, volcanic-soil AVA producing cooler, more savory Pinot Noir.

subRegions.name: McMinnville
subRegions.notes: Older marine sediments and basalt on an ancient uplifted seabed.

regions.styles: Pinot Noir is the region's signature, typically medium-bodied with red fruit such as cherry and raspberry, fine tannins, bright acidity and earthy, savory undertones, often drawing comparisons to red Burgundy; top examples can age well beyond a decade. Chardonnay has improved considerably with better clonal selection, showing racy acidity and citrus or orchard fruit. Pinot Gris, typically dry and fresh, is also a commercially significant white style for the valley.
notes: The Willamette Valley sits at roughly the same latitude as Burgundy, though its growing season and soils differ in important ways.
The Van Duzer Corridor, a literal gap in the Coast Range, is a defining cooling influence for the valley's western sub-AVAs.
Oregon has historically enforced some of the strictest varietal labeling laws in the United States.
Serious Pinot Noir plantings only began in the 1960s and 70s, pioneered by figures such as David Lett of The Eyrie Vineyards.

regions.name: Columbia Valley
regions.summary: Washington State's largest AVA and viticultural heartland, a high desert region east of the Cascades producing structured, fruit-forward red and white wines thanks to intense summer sunlight combined with essential irrigation.
regions.climate: The region has a continental, semi-arid to desert climate lying in the rain shadow of the Cascade Mountains, with very low natural rainfall making irrigation from the Columbia and Yakima Rivers essential to viticulture. Its relatively high latitude, around 46-47°N, gives long summer daylight hours that boost sugar accumulation and flavor development, while cold winters pose a genuine risk of vine damage or death in severe years. Large diurnal temperature swings between hot days and cool nights help preserve acidity in the grapes.
regions.soils: Soils are predominantly sandy, loess and loam over basalt bedrock, shaped by the catastrophic Ice Age Missoula Floods, which scoured the landscape and deposited well-draining, mineral-poor material. These sandy soils are notably resistant to phylloxera, allowing many vines in the region to remain ungrafted on their own roots.
regions.classification: Columbia Valley is a very large AVA spanning much of eastern Washington and extending slightly into Oregon, containing numerous nested sub-AVAs defined by soil, elevation and slope aspect, such as Walla Walla Valley, Red Mountain, Yakima Valley and Horse Heaven Hills. Standard US AVA rules apply, with no formal quality hierarchy beyond geographic origin.

subRegions.name: Red Mountain
subRegions.notes: A small, warm, south-facing slope AVA known for powerful, structured Cabernet Sauvignon.

subRegions.name: Walla Walla Valley
subRegions.notes: A historic, soil-diverse AVA prestigious for Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.

subRegions.name: Yakima Valley
subRegions.notes: Washington's oldest AVA, with a broad range of varieties planted.

subRegions.name: Horse Heaven Hills
subRegions.notes: A large, wind-swept AVA strong for Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.

regions.styles: Red wines, especially Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, are typically full-bodied and deeply colored with ripe dark fruit, firm tannin structure and good ageing potential, benefiting from the combination of intense sunlight and cool nights. White wines, particularly Riesling, range from dry to off-dry with vibrant acidity and pure fruit expression. The region is generally known for combining ripeness and structure with retained freshness.
notes: Columbia Valley accounts for the large majority of Washington State's total wine production.
The Ice Age Missoula Floods are directly responsible for shaping the region's distinctive soils and topography.
Because sandy soils largely resist phylloxera, own-rooted vines remain common here, unlike in most of the world's wine regions.
Despite its northerly latitude, irrigation rather than excess rainfall is the region's defining viticultural consideration, owing to its desert climate.

regions.name: Finger Lakes
regions.summary: New York State's leading wine region, centered on a series of long, deep glacial lakes that moderate an otherwise harsh continental climate. It is best known for aromatic, high-quality Riesling alongside other cool-climate varieties.
regions.climate: The region has a cool continental climate significantly moderated by the deep Finger Lakes, particularly Seneca and Cayuga, which retain summer heat and release it during winter, reducing frost risk and extending the growing season near their shores. Vineyard sites further from the lakes face much harsher winter cold, and vine-killing freezes remain the region's central viticultural challenge, favoring cold-hardy varieties and rootstocks. Lake effect also influences local air drainage and humidity around the shoreline vineyards.
regions.soils: Soils combine shale, slate and limestone-derived material with glacial till, generally well-drained on the steep slopes that rise above the lakes. The lakes themselves occupy deep, glacially carved troughs, and the best vineyards sit on the slopes above, benefiting from both drainage and proximity to the moderating water.
regions.classification: The Finger Lakes AVA contains sub-AVAs including Seneca Lake and Cayuga Lake, defined primarily by proximity to specific lakes. Standard federal AVA rules apply, requiring a minimum of 75% of fruit from the named AVA, with no separate quality classification tiers beyond this geographic designation.

subRegions.name: Seneca Lake AVA
subRegions.notes: The deepest of the lakes, giving the strongest moderating effect and the largest concentration of wineries.

subRegions.name: Cayuga Lake AVA
subRegions.notes: New York's first designated lake AVA and a historic wine-growing area.

subRegions.name: Keuka Lake area
subRegions.notes: Steep, terraced vineyard sites with a long winemaking history.

regions.styles: Riesling is the region's signature style, ranging from bone-dry to lusciously sweet, including late-harvest and icewine styles, and characterized by high acidity, green apple and citrus fruit, and often a distinctive mineral note that develops with age. Cabernet Franc shows a cool-climate profile of red fruit and herbaceous notes, and sparkling wine production also has a long history in the region. Overall the wines emphasize freshness and precision over power.
notes: The Finger Lakes are true glacial lakes, some over 600 feet deep, and their thermal mass is the key factor enabling viticulture this far north and inland.
Finger Lakes Riesling has drawn increasing international acclaim, with comparisons sometimes drawn to Germany's cooler regions.
Hybrid grapes such as Vidal Blanc and Seyval Blanc, along with native American varieties, historically dominated the region before the more recent shift toward vinifera.
Dr. Konstantin Frank is widely credited with proving that vinifera vines could succeed in the Finger Lakes, beginning in the 1950s.

regions.name: Okanagan Valley
regions.summary: British Columbia's leading wine region, a long, dramatic, glacially carved valley with one of Canada's warmest and driest climates. It produces a strikingly wide range of styles, from crisp whites to full-bodied reds and internationally acclaimed icewine.
regions.climate: The valley has a continental climate with marked north-south variation across its roughly 150 km length: the northern end near Kelowna is cooler and suited to aromatic whites and Pinot Noir, while the southern end near Osoyoos is near-desert, among Canada's hottest and driest wine-growing areas, capable of fully ripening Bordeaux and Rhône varieties. The large Okanagan Lake moderates temperature extremes and reduces frost risk along much of the valley, though winters away from the lake's influence remain cold, and irrigation is often necessary given the low rainfall.
regions.soils: Soils consist of diverse glacial deposits, including sand, gravel, silt and clay left by retreating glaciers, with well-drained benches above the lake particularly prized for quality plantings. Soil composition varies considerably along the valley's length, contributing to the wide range of styles produced from north to south.
regions.classification: Canada's quality framework for premium wine is the VQA (Vintners Quality Alliance) system, which in British Columbia sets standards for geographic indication, permitted varieties, minimum sugar levels and sensory approval. Okanagan Valley is a designated BC geographical indication under VQA, with growing recognition of sub-appellations reflecting the valley's considerable climatic range.

subRegions.name: Naramata Bench
subRegions.notes: Benchlands above Okanagan Lake noted for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Syrah.

subRegions.name: Golden Mile Bench
subRegions.notes: Warm, well-drained slopes strong for Bordeaux varieties.

subRegions.name: Black Sage Bench / Osoyoos area
subRegions.notes: Hot, near-desert conditions producing full-bodied red wines.

subRegions.name: Kelowna / North Okanagan
subRegions.notes: Cooler northern sites favored for aromatic whites and sparkling wine.

regions.styles: Wine styles span an unusually wide range for a single valley: crisp, aromatic whites such as Riesling, Pinot Gris and Gewürztraminer and elegant Pinot Noir come from cooler northern sites, while full-bodied, ripe reds including Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah come from the hot southern desert sites. The valley is also celebrated for icewine, made from grapes frozen naturally on the vine, yielding intensely sweet, concentrated wines with vibrant acidity.
notes: The Okanagan Valley's southern end is classified as a true, if small, desert, unusual among Canadian wine regions.
Icewine, which requires grapes to freeze naturally to at least -8°C on the vine, is a Canadian specialty in which the Okanagan and Niagara are recognized world leaders.
The valley's considerable north-south length means it functions almost like several distinct climates strung along a single lake.
The region has grown rapidly in international reputation and planted area since the 1990s.

regions.name: Niagara Peninsula
regions.summary: Canada's largest and most established wine region, located in Ontario between Lake Ontario and the Niagara Escarpment. It is internationally recognized for both icewine and increasingly acclaimed cool-climate table wines.
regions.climate: The region has a cool continental climate significantly moderated by Lake Ontario, which tempers winter cold and delays spring frost, and by the Niagara Escarpment, a limestone ridge that creates air drainage and distinct mesoclimates along its slopes and bench lands. This combination of lake effect and escarpment protection allows viticulture at a latitude that would otherwise be too cold, while winters remain reliably cold enough to enable icewine production. The relatively long, cool growing season favors high-acid, aromatic wine styles.
regions.soils: Soils are varied glacial deposits including clay loam, sandy loam and silt over limestone bedrock, with the Niagara Escarpment's limestone particularly influencing sites along the bench above the lake. Drainage and soil variation between the lakeshore plain and the escarpment bench contribute to distinct site character across the region.
regions.classification: The VQA (Vintners Quality Alliance) system governs quality wine in Ontario, with Niagara Peninsula a designated appellation containing ten recognized sub-appellations reflecting distinct mesoclimates, including Niagara-on-the-Lake, Niagara Escarpment and Beamsville Bench. VQA rules set standards for permitted grape varieties, minimum must weights and sensory evaluation, including strict regulations for icewine requiring grapes to be harvested and pressed at or below -8°C.

subRegions.name: Niagara-on-the-Lake
subRegions.notes: A flat, lake-moderated plain and the historic heart of the region's wine industry.

subRegions.name: Beamsville Bench
subRegions.notes: An escarpment bench with good air drainage, noted for Riesling and Chardonnay.

subRegions.name: Twenty Mile Bench
subRegions.notes: An escarpment sub-appellation known for structured whites and reds.

subRegions.name: Short Hills Bench
subRegions.notes: An escarpment bench site with distinct soils and exposure.

regions.styles: Riesling and Chardonnay are benchmark white wines, showing high acidity, orchard and citrus fruit and mineral character. Pinot Noir and Cabernet Franc lead red production, typically medium-bodied with red fruit and, in Cabernet Franc's case, characteristic herbal and savory notes. The region's icewine, made chiefly from Vidal Blanc and Riesling, is intensely sweet and high in acidity, and is among the most internationally celebrated examples of the style.
notes: Niagara Peninsula produces the majority of Canada's wine and is the country's icewine powerhouse.
Canadian icewine, led by Niagara and the Okanagan, is widely regarded as a world benchmark for the style.
The Niagara Escarpment, the same geological feature responsible for Niagara Falls, is central to the region's mesoclimate diversity.
Ontario's VQA rules for icewine, including mandatory harvest and pressing temperatures at or below -8°C, are among the strictest in the world.

regions.name: Barossa Valley
regions.summary: Barossa Valley is Australia's most famous fine wine region, renowned for powerful, full-bodied Shiraz from some of the oldest continuously producing vines in the world. Located north of Adelaide in South Australia, it is a warm, historically important region that helped define Australia's international reputation for bold red wine.
regions.climate: Barossa Valley has a warm, dry Mediterranean-influenced climate with hot summers and mild winters, moderated somewhat by its inland valley location away from direct maritime influence. Rainfall is low and irrigation is common, though many old, deep-rooted vines are dry-grown. Diurnal temperature variation is modest compared to cooler Australian regions, contributing to the ripe, generous fruit character and high natural sugar levels typical of Barossa reds. Occasional heatwaves during ripening can push alcohol levels higher and are a key viticultural risk.
regions.soils: Soils are highly variable across the valley floor and surrounding hills, ranging from ancient sandy loams over clay to ironstone and quartz-rich outcrops. This patchwork contributes to the increasing interest in single-vineyard and sub-district bottlings that express distinct terroir. Well-drained, low-fertility soils in many areas help naturally restrict vigour, concentrating fruit in old, low-yielding vines.
regions.classification: Barossa falls under Australia's Geographical Indications (GI) system rather than a hierarchical quality classification; Barossa Zone contains the Barossa Valley and Eden Valley GIs as separate regions. There is no official quality-tier pyramid, but industry-recognised initiatives such as the Barossa Grounds project and the Old Vine Charter (categorising vines as Old, Survivor, Centenarian and Ancestor Vines by planting date) provide informal, respected markers of heritage and quality.

subRegions.name: Northern Grounds
subRegions.notes: Higher, cooler sites around Kalimna and Moppa producing structured, age-worthy Shiraz.

subRegions.name: Central Grounds
subRegions.notes: Historic core around Tanunda and Rowland Flat with concentrated, richly fruited reds.

subRegions.name: Southern Grounds
subRegions.notes: Cooler, higher-altitude fringe near Lyndoch and Williamstown, often used for more elegant styles.

subRegions.name: Eastern Grounds
subRegions.notes: Foothill sites transitioning toward Eden Valley, giving firmer tannin structure.

regions.styles: Barossa is best known for deeply coloured, full-bodied, high-alcohol Shiraz with ripe blackberry and plum fruit, chocolate and spice notes, and often generous use of new oak, capable of long ageing. Grenache-based blends (including GSM blends with Shiraz and Mataro) range from rich and fruit-forward to increasingly fashionable lighter, perfumed styles from old bush vines. Some fortified wines and old-vine Semillon are also produced, though red table wine dominates production and reputation.
notes: Barossa Valley is home to some of the oldest Shiraz vines in the world, many surviving phylloxera-free since the 1840s, classified under the Barossa Old Vine Charter.
The region was settled largely by Silesian and English immigrants in the 1840s, giving it a distinctive Germanic cultural heritage still visible in town names and Lutheran churches.
Penfolds Grange, Australia's most iconic wine, draws heavily on Barossa fruit.
Barossa Valley and Eden Valley are geographically adjacent but climatically distinct, with Eden Valley's higher elevation producing notably different, cooler-climate wines.
A growing 'old vine, low intervention' movement has shifted some Barossa Grenache production toward lighter, more elegant expressions away from the traditional powerhouse style.

regions.name: Hunter Valley
regions.summary: The Hunter Valley, north of Sydney in New South Wales, is one of Australia's oldest wine regions and is uniquely famous for age-worthy, low-alcohol Semillon alongside earthy, medium-bodied Shiraz. Its warm, humid climate is atypical for fine wine production, making its historic reputation for elegant white wine particularly distinctive.
regions.climate: The Hunter Valley has a warm, humid climate with a maritime influence and a notably high risk of rainfall during harvest due to its subtropical-influenced summer weather patterns. Cloud cover and humidity moderate what would otherwise be excessive heat, allowing grapes such as Semillon to be picked early at low sugar and high acid levels. This combination of early picking and humidity risk is central to the region's unusual, low-alcohol Semillon style and requires careful vineyard management to combat fungal disease.
regions.soils: Soils are varied but generally include sandy alluvial soils on the valley floor near the Hunter River, well suited to Semillon, and red volcanic clay-loam soils on higher ground, particularly favoured for Shiraz. Drainage and moderate fertility across these soil types help manage vigour in a climate with ample summer rainfall.
regions.classification: The Hunter Valley operates under Australia's Geographical Indications (GI) system, registered as a region within New South Wales, with no internal quality-tier hierarchy. Sub-zones such as Pokolbin are recognised informally as premium areas of long-established plantings rather than through a formal appellation structure.

subRegions.name: Pokolbin
subRegions.notes: The historic heart of the Lower Hunter, home to many of the oldest and most respected wineries.

subRegions.name: Broke Fordwich
subRegions.notes: A registered sub-region with sandier soils, known for Semillon and Shiraz.

subRegions.name: Upper Hunter Valley
subRegions.notes: A separate, drier zone further from the coast, more associated with Chardonnay and Verdelho.

regions.styles: Hunter Semillon is famously picked early at around 10-11% potential alcohol, producing a lean, high-acid, citrus-and-grass wine when young that develops remarkable toasty, honeyed complexity with a decade or more of bottle age, all without oak. Hunter Shiraz is medium-bodied by Australian standards, with earthy, savoury, leathery notes alongside red and black fruit, and ages gracefully. Chardonnay in the region tends toward a fuller, sometimes oaked style.
notes: Hunter Valley Semillon is considered one of Australia's most distinctive and age-worthy white wine styles, often mistaken for aged Chardonnay when tasted blind due to its developed complexity.
The Hunter Valley is one of the oldest wine regions in Australia, with vine plantings dating to the early 19th century.
The region's humid climate makes it more prone to vintage variation and disease pressure than most other major Australian regions.
Traditional Hunter Shiraz was historically sometimes labelled 'Hunter Burgundy' before geographical naming reforms.
Despite its fame, the Hunter Valley is a relatively small production region compared to Barossa or Riverina.

regions.name: Margaret River
regions.summary: Margaret River is a maritime-influenced region in Western Australia celebrated for producing some of Australia's most elegant, structured Cabernet Sauvignon and world-class Chardonnay. Despite its relatively small production, it has an outsized reputation for quality, often compared stylistically to Bordeaux and Burgundy.
regions.climate: Margaret River has a distinctly maritime, Mediterranean climate, situated on a narrow peninsula between the Indian and Southern Oceans, which moderates temperatures and provides a long, even ripening season with minimal frost or harvest rain risk. Consistent sea breezes keep afternoon temperatures moderate even in summer, preserving acidity and aromatic freshness. This maritime stability, rare in Australian viticulture, is central to the region's reputation for balance and elegance rather than sheer power.
regions.soils: The region's most distinctive soils are gravelly, well-drained loams derived from ancient granite and gneiss, particularly along the low ridge running through the heart of the region, offering excellent drainage and moderate vigour control ideal for Cabernet Sauvignon. Deeper soils and areas closer to the coast provide slightly different profiles suited to Chardonnay and other varieties.
regions.classification: Margaret River is a registered Geographical Indication under Australia's GI system with no internal formal quality hierarchy, though informal sub-regional distinctions (north, central, and south) are increasingly used by producers to describe stylistic differences tied to climate and soil.

subRegions.name: Wilyabrup
subRegions.notes: A central sub-district with gravelly soils particularly prized for Cabernet Sauvignon.

subRegions.name: Yallingup
subRegions.notes: Northern area known for structured reds and some of the region's founding vineyards.

subRegions.name: Karridale/Southern district
subRegions.notes: Cooler southern area increasingly explored for Chardonnay and aromatic whites.

regions.styles: Margaret River Cabernet Sauvignon (often blended with Merlot and other Bordeaux varieties) is medium to full-bodied with fine, ripe tannins, blackcurrant and cedar notes, and strong ageing potential, frequently likened to a riper, sunnier style of Bordeaux. Chardonnay ranges from taut and flinty to richer barrel-fermented styles with strong varietal fruit and refined acidity, regarded among Australia's best. A classic Semillon-Sauvignon Blanc blend also produces fresh, aromatic, food-friendly white wine.
notes: Margaret River produces around 3-5% of Australia's total wine grape crush but has a disproportionately large share of the country's most highly rated wines.
Commercial viticulture in Margaret River only began in the late 1960s, making it a comparatively young region despite its now-elite reputation.
The region's maritime climate makes it one of the most reliably consistent in Australia from vintage to vintage.
Leeuwin Estate's Art Series Chardonnay was pivotal in establishing the region's reputation for world-class Chardonnay in the 1980s.
The narrow cape between two oceans gives Margaret River one of the most oceanic climates of any major Australian wine region.

regions.name: Yarra Valley
regions.summary: The Yarra Valley, near Melbourne in Victoria, is one of Australia's premier cool-climate regions, prized for elegant Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and increasingly sophisticated Shiraz, as well as high-quality traditional-method sparkling wine. It was a pioneering 19th-century wine region that was revived in the late 20th century to become a leader in cool-climate Australian viticulture.
regions.climate: The Yarra Valley has a cool, temperate climate moderated by elevation and proximity to Port Phillip Bay, with considerable variation between the warmer, lower valley floor and the cooler upper reaches at higher altitude. This range of mesoclimates allows the region to ripen both early varieties like Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in cooler upper sites and later-ripening Shiraz and Cabernet in warmer lower areas. Cool nights preserve acidity and aromatic intensity, a hallmark of the region's elegant style.
regions.soils: Soils vary from grey-brown clay loams over grey clay on the valley floor to red volcanic soils in the upper valley, with the volcanic soils generally favoured for their good drainage and moderate fertility, well suited to Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. This soil diversity, combined with elevation differences, underpins the valley's wide stylistic range.
regions.classification: The Yarra Valley is a registered Geographical Indication under Australia's GI system with no formal internal quality tiers, though the region is informally divided by producers and critics into the cooler Upper Yarra and warmer Lower Yarra based on altitude and temperature.

subRegions.name: Upper Yarra Valley
subRegions.notes: Higher, cooler sites favoured for fine Pinot Noir and sparkling base wine.

subRegions.name: Lower Yarra Valley
subRegions.notes: Warmer valley floor areas better suited to Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon.

regions.styles: Yarra Valley Pinot Noir is elegant and perfumed, with red cherry and spice notes and silky tannins, often considered among Australia's finest examples of the variety. Chardonnay is typically restrained and citrus-driven with careful, often subtle oak use, reflecting a modern, cool-climate Australian style. The region also produces increasingly refined, cool-climate Shiraz with peppery, savoury character, and high-quality traditional-method sparkling wine from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
notes: The Yarra Valley was a significant wine region in the 19th century but was largely abandoned in the early 20th century before being replanted starting in the 1960s and 70s.
It is one of Australia's most climatically diverse regions, allowing both classic Bordeaux and Burgundian varieties to be grown successfully within the same GI.
Domaine Chandon (Green Point) established a major sparkling wine operation in the Yarra Valley, reflecting the region's suitability for traditional-method fizz.
The Yarra Valley is one of the closest major wine regions to a capital city in Australia, making it a significant wine tourism destination for Melbourne.
Its cool climate and elevation variation make vintage conditions more variable here than in Australia's warmer inland regions.

regions.name: Clare & Eden Valleys
regions.summary: Clare Valley and Eden Valley are two elevated South Australian regions renowned above all for producing Australia's finest dry Rieslings, characterised by bone-dry, high-acid, lime-driven styles with exceptional ageing potential. Eden Valley, adjoining the Barossa, also produces highly regarded cool-climate Shiraz, while Clare Valley is known for powerful, structured reds as well.
regions.climate: Both regions owe their character to elevation: Clare Valley sits on a series of high ridges and valleys with a continental climate of warm days moderated by cool nights from altitude, while Eden Valley lies on the higher, cooler eastern edge of the Barossa Ranges. This elevation-driven diurnal temperature swing preserves the natural acidity essential to their Rieslings even in a generally warm, dry Australian setting, while allowing red varieties to reach ripeness with retained freshness. Rainfall is low in both regions, and dry-grown vineyards are common.
regions.soils: Clare Valley features a complex mix of soils including the famous 'terra rossa' red loam over limestone in parts, along with slate and shale in areas like Polish Hill River, which contribute mineral intensity to its Rieslings. Eden Valley has predominantly ancient, shallow, infertile soils over rock, naturally limiting yields and concentrating flavour in both Riesling and Shiraz.
regions.classification: Clare Valley and Eden Valley are each separate, registered Geographical Indications under Australia's GI system, both within the Mount Lofty Ranges Zone (Eden Valley) or Fleurieu/Mount Lofty region grouping for Clare, with no internal formal quality hierarchy. Sub-districts such as Polish Hill River and Watervale within Clare Valley are informally recognised for distinct Riesling character.

subRegions.name: Polish Hill River (Clare)
subRegions.notes: Slate-influenced sub-district producing steely, high-acid Riesling.

subRegions.name: Watervale (Clare)
subRegions.notes: Terra rossa over limestone soils yielding softer, lime-scented Riesling.

subRegions.name: High Eden (Eden Valley)
subRegions.notes: The highest, coolest part of Eden Valley, particularly suited to Riesling.

regions.styles: Clare and Eden Valley Rieslings are bone-dry, tightly structured wines with intense lime and green apple fruit, racy acidity, and a distinctive ability to develop toasty, honeyed complexity with bottle age, considered a benchmark Australian white wine style. Eden Valley Shiraz tends to be more medium-bodied, elegant, and peppery than Barossa Valley Shiraz, reflecting its cooler, higher-altitude sites, while Clare Valley also produces robust, full-bodied Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz.
notes: The Clare Valley Riesling Trail, a former railway line converted to a cycling and walking path, links many of the region's producers and is a popular wine tourism route.
Eden Valley is home to Hill of Grace, one of Australia's most celebrated single-vineyard Shiraz wines, made by Henschke from vines planted in the 1860s.
Australian Riesling, especially from these regions, is typically bottled under screwcap, which is widely credited with preserving its fresh, dry style far better than cork.
Eden Valley lies at higher elevation than the adjacent Barossa Valley, giving it a noticeably cooler climate despite being geographically close.
Jeffrey Grosset, a Clare Valley producer, was highly influential in establishing screwcap closures as standard for premium Australian Riesling.

regions.name: Tasmania
regions.summary: Tasmania is Australia's coolest wine region, an island state south of the mainland whose cool maritime climate makes it the country's premier source of traditional-method sparkling wine base fruit, alongside increasingly acclaimed still Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Its reputation has grown rapidly as producers and even Champagne houses seek out its naturally high-acid, cool-climate fruit.
regions.climate: Tasmania has a cool, maritime climate strongly influenced by its southern latitude and surrounding ocean, with cool summers, a long, slow ripening season, and relatively high rainfall and humidity compared to mainland Australia. This is the coolest major wine-producing area in the country, and site selection (favouring the more sheltered, sunnier northern and eastern parts of the island) is critical to reliably ripening grapes. The climate closely parallels that of Champagne and Burgundy, explaining the island's strength in sparkling wine and Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
regions.soils: Soils vary across Tasmania's dispersed growing areas, including ancient sandstone and mudstone-derived soils, and in some areas, distinctive red volcanic (basalt-derived) soils similar to those found in other cool-climate Pinot Noir regions. Generally well-drained, low-vigour soils help ripen fruit fully in a cool, sometimes humid environment.
regions.classification: Tasmania is a single registered Geographical Indication under Australia's GI system, though it is a large and climatically diverse island; producers and industry bodies informally distinguish sub-regions such as the Tamar Valley, Coal River Valley, Pipers River, and Derwent Valley, but these lack formal legal status as separate GIs in most cases.

subRegions.name: Pipers River / Tamar Valley (North)
subRegions.notes: Historic core in the north, known for sparkling base wine and Pinot Noir.

subRegions.name: Coal River Valley (South)
subRegions.notes: One of the driest, sunniest parts of the island, suited to still Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

subRegions.name: Derwent Valley (South)
subRegions.notes: Cool southern area near Hobart producing aromatic whites and sparkling fruit.

regions.styles: Tasmania's traditional-method sparkling wines, based on Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, are crisp, high-acid, and increasingly regarded as Australia's finest fizz, used both for stand-alone island brands and as a fruit source for major mainland sparkling producers. Still Pinot Noir is light to medium-bodied, perfumed, and high in acid with red fruit character, while Chardonnay tends to be lean, citrus-driven, and elegant. Aromatic whites such as Riesling and Pinot Gris also perform well in the cool climate.
notes: Tasmania supplies a significant portion of premium sparkling wine base fruit used by major producers on the Australian mainland, including some owned by Champagne houses.
House of Arras, based in Tasmania, is considered one of Australia's top traditional-method sparkling wine producers.
Tasmania's total vineyard area is small relative to mainland regions, but its fruit commands some of the highest per-tonne prices in the country.
The island's climate is frequently compared to Champagne and Burgundy, underpinning its suitability for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and sparkling wine.
Vineyard sites are concentrated in the drier, more sheltered eastern and northern parts of the island, as the west coast is too wet and exposed for viticulture.

regions.name: Marlborough
regions.summary: Marlborough, at the northern tip of New Zealand's South Island, is the country's largest and most famous wine region, globally renowned for pioneering a distinctive, intensely aromatic style of Sauvignon Blanc that transformed international perceptions of the variety. It also produces significant quantities of Pinot Noir and sparkling wine.
regions.climate: Marlborough has a cool, dry, sunny maritime climate with high sunshine hours, cool nights, and a long, slow ripening period that preserves natural acidity while allowing full flavour development. Its position at the north of the South Island gives it more sunshine and less rainfall than many other New Zealand regions, while surrounding hills provide some shelter from wind. The large diurnal temperature range between warm sunny days and cool nights is central to the pungent, vivid aromatics that define Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.soils: The Wairau Valley, the historic heart of the region, has free-draining, stony alluvial soils of gravel and silt over a deep gravel base, which restrict vigour and reflect heat, aiding ripening. The more recently developed Awatere Valley to the south has generally thinner, stonier, windier sites producing more herbaceous, minerally wine styles.
regions.classification: New Zealand does not have a formal appellation hierarchy comparable to European systems; wine regions including Marlborough are defined as Geographical Indications (GIs) under New Zealand's registration system, indicating origin without an internal quality-tier structure. Sub-regional names such as Wairau Valley and Awatere Valley are used on labels to indicate distinct stylistic origins within Marlborough.

subRegions.name: Wairau Valley
subRegions.notes: The original, warmer, more fertile heart of Marlborough, giving riper, more tropical Sauvignon Blanc.

subRegions.name: Awatere Valley
subRegions.notes: Cooler, windier, and higher elevation, producing more herbaceous, minerally, structured wines.

subRegions.name: Southern Valleys
subRegions.notes: Smaller, hillier sub-areas with clay soils, often used for Pinot Noir.

regions.styles: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is intensely aromatic with pronounced notes of passionfruit, gooseberry, capsicum, and citrus, high acidity, and a fresh, zesty, unoaked style that is typically consumed young, though it defined a globally recognisable New Zealand wine style. Pinot Noir is medium-bodied with vivid red fruit, and traditional-method sparkling wine is also produced from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Aromatic whites like Pinot Gris and Riesling add to the region's diverse cool-climate white wine output.
notes: Marlborough accounts for the large majority of New Zealand's total vineyard area and wine exports, dominated by Sauvignon Blanc.
The first commercial vines were planted in Marlborough only in 1973, by Montana (now Brancott Estate), making it a remarkably young region for its global fame.
Marlborough's Sauvignon Blanc style, with its pungent thiol-driven aromatics, is widely credited with putting New Zealand wine on the world map in the 1980s and 90s.
The Awatere Valley, developed later than the Wairau Valley, tends to produce a more restrained, savoury, and herbaceous style of Sauvignon Blanc.
Marlborough is also one of New Zealand's most important sources of base wine for premium traditional-method sparkling wine.

regions.name: Central Otago
regions.summary: Central Otago, on New Zealand's South Island, is the world's southernmost significant wine region and the country's premier area for Pinot Noir, prized for its vivid, aromatic, and structured expressions grown in a rare semi-continental climate. Its dramatic mountainous landscape and small, high-quality-focused producers have earned it an outsized international reputation.
regions.climate: Central Otago has New Zealand's only semi-continental climate, set apart from the maritime influence found elsewhere in the country by surrounding mountain ranges, resulting in hot, dry summers, cold winters, and a wide diurnal temperature range. High UV intensity at altitude and long daylight hours during ripening contribute to intense fruit flavour and colour development, while cool nights preserve acidity, a combination well suited to Pinot Noir. Frost risk in spring and autumn is a significant viticultural hazard due to the continental extremes.
regions.soils: Soils are generally free-draining and low in fertility, comprising schist-derived loess, gravel, and sand deposited by ancient glacial and river activity, which naturally restrict vine vigour. This poor, well-drained soil profile, combined with the region's many steep, north-facing slopes for sun exposure, is central to the concentration seen in Central Otago Pinot Noir.
regions.classification: Central Otago is registered as a Geographical Indication under New Zealand's GI system, with no formal internal quality-tier hierarchy, though several distinct sub-regions with differing mesoclimates are widely recognised and used on labels to indicate origin and style.

subRegions.name: Bannockburn
subRegions.notes: Warm, dry sub-region known for rich, powerful Pinot Noir.

subRegions.name: Gibbston
subRegions.notes: Higher, cooler valley producing more elegant, aromatic, lighter-bodied Pinot Noir.

subRegions.name: Bendigo
subRegions.notes: Warm, north-facing sub-region giving concentrated, structured wines.

subRegions.name: Wanaka
subRegions.notes: Small, cool sub-region around Lake Wanaka known for delicate styles.

regions.styles: Central Otago Pinot Noir is typically deeply coloured for the variety, with vivid dark cherry and plum fruit, floral and herbal notes, firm tannic structure, and good ageing potential, generally considered riper and more powerful than Pinot Noir from other New Zealand regions such as Martinborough. Aromatic whites including Pinot Gris and Riesling, produced in styles ranging from dry to lusciously sweet, and increasingly fine Chardonnay round out the region's cool-climate portfolio.
notes: Central Otago is the world's southernmost wine region of significant commercial scale, and one of very few in the world with a semi-continental climate.
The region's modern wine industry only began in earnest in the 1980s and 90s, yet it rapidly established a reputation as New Zealand's leading Pinot Noir area.
Central Otago's mountainous terrain means vineyards are often planted on steep slopes at higher elevations than typical for New Zealand.
The region was previously known for 19th-century gold mining, and some old mining infrastructure remains visible among the vineyards.
Spring frost is one of the most significant vineyard risks in Central Otago due to its continental climate extremes, requiring frost-fighting measures such as wind machines.

regions.name: Hawke's Bay
regions.summary: Hawke's Bay, on the east coast of New Zealand's North Island, is the country's second-largest wine region and its most important area for Bordeaux-style red blends and quality Chardonnay and Syrah, thanks to one of New Zealand's warmest, sunniest climates. It is also New Zealand's oldest wine-producing region, with a winemaking history dating to the 19th century.
regions.climate: Hawke's Bay has a warm, dry maritime climate for New Zealand, benefiting from high sunshine hours and some rain shadow protection from inland ranges, making it one of the country's most reliable regions for ripening later-ripening red varieties. Coastal and inland areas show meaningful climatic variation, with sites closer to the coast moderated by sea breezes and inland areas experiencing greater warmth and diurnal range. This relative warmth, unusual within New Zealand's generally cool, maritime wine landscape, underpins the region's strength in Bordeaux blends and Syrah.
regions.soils: The region's most celebrated soils lie in the Gimblett Gravels and Bridge Pa Triangle, free-draining former riverbed soils of gravel, stone, and sand that retain and radiate heat, helping fully ripen Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and Syrah. Elsewhere, heavier silt and clay soils are found on the Heretaunga Plains, better suited to Chardonnay and other varieties requiring more moisture retention.
regions.classification: Hawke's Bay is a registered Geographical Indication under New Zealand's GI system, without a formal internal quality hierarchy. However, the Gimblett Gravels Winegrowers District has established its own informal, geologically defined boundary and quality association, widely used and respected as a mark of provenance and quality on labels.

subRegions.name: Gimblett Gravels
subRegions.notes: Warm, stony former riverbed area specialising in premium Bordeaux blends and Syrah.

subRegions.name: Bridge Pa Triangle
subRegions.notes: Adjacent gravelly area with similar heat-retaining soils, also strong for red varieties.

subRegions.name: Heretaunga Plains
subRegions.notes: Broader, more fertile coastal plain producing a wide range of styles including Chardonnay.

regions.styles: Hawke's Bay Bordeaux-style red blends (Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot-based) are medium to full-bodied with ripe blackcurrant and plum fruit, firm but ripe tannins, and notable ageing potential, considered among New Zealand's finest reds. Syrah from the region is elegant and peppery, often compared to cooler-climate Northern Rhône styles despite the region's relative warmth. Chardonnay is typically rich and well-structured, and the region also produces good quality Sauvignon Blanc, though in a riper, less overtly aromatic style than Marlborough.
notes: Hawke's Bay is New Zealand's oldest wine region, with vines planted by missionaries as early as the 1850s.

The Gimblett Gravels district's boundary is defined purely by a specific soil type (deep, free-draining shingle), not by traditional geographic or political lines, making it unusual among the world's designated wine areas.
Hawke's Bay Syrah has drawn increasing international acclaim for combining ripeness with a distinctly cool-climate peppery character.
The region is New Zealand's second largest by planted area after Marlborough, but with a much more diverse range of grape varieties.
Napier and Hastings, the region's main towns, are known for Art Deco architecture rebuilt after a major 1931 earthquake, and the wine industry has long been tied to the area's development.

regions.name: Mendoza
regions.summary: Mendoza is Argentina's largest and most important wine region, producing roughly three-quarters of the country's wine and serving as the global heartland of Malbec. High-altitude desert vineyards at the foot of the Andes give the region its distinctive combination of intense sunlight, cool nights, and pure meltwater irrigation.
regions.climate: Mendoza has a continental desert climate with very low rainfall (around 200mm per year), so almost all vineyards depend on irrigation from Andean snowmelt. Altitude is the defining moderating factor: vineyards range from around 600m up to over 1,500m in the Uco Valley, and the resulting high diurnal temperature range preserves acidity and aromatics despite abundant sunshine. The Zonda, a hot foehn wind, can occasionally stress vines during the growing season, while hail is a recurring risk that growers manage with netting.
regions.soils: Soils are predominantly alluvial, composed of sand, silt, clay, and rocky/gravelly deposits washed down from the Andes over millennia, generally poor in organic matter and naturally free-draining. Higher-altitude sites, especially in the Uco Valley, have notable limestone (calcareous) content that is increasingly associated with the region's most structured, mineral Malbecs. The variation in alluvial fan composition from area to area allows for distinct site-driven expressions even within short distances.
regions.classification: Argentina uses a broad Indicación Geográfica (IG) system; within Mendoza this operates at province, department (e.g. Luján de Cuyo, Uco Valley), and increasingly precise sub-district or single-vineyard level as producers push for more granular Geographical Indications. There is no formal quality-pyramid classification akin to French AOC crus, so reputation is built primarily around altitude, sub-region, and producer rather than a legal hierarchy. Luján de Cuyo was Argentina's first officially delimited appellation, established to protect its old-vine Malbec heritage.

subRegions.name: Luján de Cuyo
subRegions.notes: Historic, high-altitude district known for structured, elegant old-vine Malbec and considered Argentina's first appellation.

subRegions.name: Uco Valley (Valle de Uco)
subRegions.notes: The highest and coolest major sub-zone, with limestone-influenced soils producing Mendoza's most aromatic, fine-boned wines.

subRegions.name: Maipú
subRegions.notes: One of the original wine-growing areas near the city of Mendoza, warmer and lower in altitude.

subRegions.name: San Rafael
subRegions.notes: A more southerly, isolated district known for solid-value reds and some sparkling wine production.

regions.styles: Mendoza Malbec ranges from soft, fruit-forward, medium-bodied wines at lower altitudes to deeply concentrated, structured, age-worthy examples from high-altitude Uco Valley sites, typically showing ripe dark plum and violet character with supple tannins. Many premium reds see oak ageing (often a mix of French and American) and can develop well for a decade or more. Bonarda offers a juicy, everyday red alternative, while high-altitude Chardonnay and Torrontés-based whites provide fresh, aromatic options, and some producers make sparkling and rosé from Malbec and Pinot Noir.
notes: Mendoza accounts for roughly three-quarters of Argentina's total wine production.
Vineyard altitude is the single biggest quality lever here, with premium sites now planted above 1,000m and some experimental plots above 1,500m.
Nearly all vineyards rely on irrigation, historically via a centuries-old canal system (acequias) fed by Andean snowmelt.
Malbec, originally a minor Bordeaux blending grape, found its true global identity in Mendoza after phylloxera-era and 20th-century investment.
Hail netting is a common and necessary vineyard sight due to the region's exposure to sudden Andean hailstorms.

regions.name: Salta
regions.summary: Salta, in northern Argentina, is home to some of the highest-altitude commercial vineyards in the world and is the country's benchmark region for aromatic, high-toned Torrontés. Its extreme elevation and intense sunlight produce wines of striking freshness despite the subtropical latitude.
regions.climate: Salta sits at a relatively low latitude for viticulture, but extreme altitude (vineyards commonly planted between 1,700m and over 3,000m in Cafayate/Calchaquí Valley) offsets the subtropical warmth, creating a desert climate with intense UV exposure, very low humidity, and a wide diurnal temperature swing.
