Rainfall is minimal and concentrated in summer, so irrigation from Andean sources is essential. The thin atmosphere and strong sunlight thicken grape skins and boost aromatic compounds, giving Torrontés its intensely perfumed character while nights stay cool enough to retain acidity.
regions.soils: Vineyard soils in the Calchaquí Valley are predominantly sandy, alluvial, and rocky, often pale in colour and low in fertility, which naturally limits vigour and yields. Good drainage from these loose, well-aerated soils suits the region's arid, irrigation-dependent viticulture and helps control disease pressure in the dry climate.
regions.classification: Salta wines fall under Argentina's Indicación Geográfica (IG) system, with Cafayate and the broader Calchaquí Valley recognized as the key geographical designations. There is no separate formal quality-tier classification beyond the IG framework; reputation rests on altitude, sub-district (notably Cafayate), and producer track record rather than a legal hierarchy.

subRegions.name: Cafayate
subRegions.notes: The historic core of Salta viticulture and Argentina's most celebrated source of aromatic Torrontés.

subRegions.name: Calchaquí Valley
subRegions.notes: The broader high-altitude valley system encompassing Cafayate and surrounding extreme-elevation vineyard sites.

regions.styles: Torrontés from Salta is the region's calling card: a dry white with an intensely floral, grapey/muscat-like nose (jasmine, orange blossom) balanced by crisp acidity and a typically bone-dry, sometimes slightly bitter finish that keeps it from tasting cloying. Red wines, chiefly Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon, show deep colour, ripe dark fruit, and firm structure thanks to thick skins from high-altitude sun exposure, often needing food to soften their tannic grip. Overall the region's wines are marked by unusual freshness and aromatic intensity for their warm, low-latitude origin.
notes: Some Salta vineyards, such as those near Molinos and Payogasta, rank among the highest-altitude wine vineyards on earth, exceeding 3,000m.
Torrontés is genetically linked to Muscat of Alexandria and is considered Argentina's signature white grape, with Cafayate its spiritual home.
The extreme UV exposure at altitude thickens grape skins, boosting aromatic and phenolic concentration in both white and red varieties.
Salta's remoteness and tourism appeal (the Cafayate wine route) have made it a boutique, quality-focused rather than high-volume region.

regions.name: Maipo Valley
regions.summary: Maipo Valley, just south of Santiago, is Chile's most historic and internationally renowned fine-wine region, celebrated above all for Cabernet Sauvignon of structure and elegance often compared to Bordeaux. It is home to many of the country's oldest and most prestigious wine estates.
regions.climate: Maipo has a Mediterranean climate with warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters, moderated by cooling influences from the Andes to the east and, in some sub-zones, breezes funneled from the Pacific. Areas closer to the Andes (Alto Maipo) benefit from cool night-time air drainage off the mountains, widening the diurnal range and helping grapes retain freshness and firm tannin structure, while areas nearer the coast or central valley floor are warmer. Rainfall is low and concentrated in winter, so irrigation, historically from Andean meltwater via the Maipo River, is standard practice.
regions.soils: Alto Maipo, closer to the Andean foothills, has notably gravelly, rocky, well-drained alluvial soils that are strongly associated with the region's best Cabernet Sauvignon, echoing the free-draining gravel terroirs prized in Bordeaux. Further from the mountains, soils become more clay- and silt-rich with greater water retention, generally producing softer, less structured wines. This soil gradient from the Andean foothills toward the coast and south is a key organizing principle for quality within the valley.
regions.classification: Chile's overarching system is a geographic Denominación de Origen (DO) framework rather than a hierarchical quality pyramid; Maipo Valley is a recognized DO with informal sub-zones (Alto, Central, Pacific Maipo) used by producers on labels to indicate style and provenance rather than as legally defined quality tiers. Labeling rules require a minimum percentage of the stated grape variety and region for varietal/regional labeling, but there is no cru-style classification of vineyards.

subRegions.name: Alto Maipo
subRegions.notes: The premium, higher-elevation zone nearest the Andes, source of Chile's most structured, age-worthy Cabernet Sauvignon.

subRegions.name: Central Maipo
subRegions.notes: Historic core around Santiago with some of Chile's oldest vineyards and wine estates.

subRegions.name: Pacific Maipo
subRegions.notes: Cooler, coastally-influenced western area better suited to fresher styles and other varieties.

regions.styles: Maipo is best known for medium- to full-bodied Cabernet Sauvignon with characteristic blackcurrant fruit, a distinctive minty/eucalyptus note (from nearby eucalyptus trees influencing the vineyards), firm but ripe tannins, and strong ageing potential in top examples, often oak-aged and built for a decade or more of development. Carménère, Chile's signature grape once mistaken for Merlot, contributes savory, peppery, dark-fruited blends and varietal wines. Overall the region favors structured, classically proportioned reds over the riper, more extracted styles found in some other New World regions.
notes: Maipo is considered the birthplace of Chile's modern fine-wine industry, with several of the country's oldest continuously operating wineries founded here in the 19th century.
The valley's Cabernet Sauvignon is often noted for a signature minty/eucalyptus aromatic streak, linked to eucalyptus trees planted as windbreaks near vineyards.
Carménère was long mistaken for Merlot in Chilean vineyards until DNA analysis in the mid-1990s correctly identified it, and Chile is now its global heartland.
Urban expansion of Santiago has gradually encroached on Central Maipo vineyard land, pushing new premium plantings further into Alto Maipo and beyond.

regions.name: Casablanca Valley
regions.summary: Casablanca Valley is a cool-climate region between Santiago and the Pacific coast that pioneered Chile's move into fresh, aromatic white wines and cool-climate Pinot Noir starting in the 1980s. It remains one of Chile's leading sources of quality Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.climate: Casablanca has a distinctly cool, maritime-influenced climate for Chile, shaped by its proximity to the Pacific Ocean and the cooling Humboldt Current, with persistent morning fog and strong afternoon sea breezes funneling through gaps in the coastal range. This keeps summer temperatures notably lower than in nearby Central Valley regions, slowing ripening and preserving acidity, which suits aromatic whites and cool-climate red varieties. Frost risk is a recognized hazard in the valley, particularly in low-lying spots, requiring frost-protection measures such as wind machines and sprinklers.
regions.soils: Soils are generally clay-loam based over decomposed granite in parts of the valley, with reasonable water-holding capacity that, combined with the region's dry summers, still requires irrigation. The moderate fertility and drainage characteristics support balanced vine growth suited to the aromatic, elegant styles the region is known for.
regions.classification: Casablanca Valley is a recognized Chilean DO (Denominación de Origen) under the country's geographic labeling system, with no internal formal sub-classification; producers may reference proximity to the coast (western, cooler parts versus eastern, slightly warmer parts) informally to signal style. Its establishment as a distinct planting area in the 1980s was itself a landmark in defining Chile's cool-climate potential beyond the traditional Central Valley.
regions.styles: Casablanca is best known for vibrant, aromatic Sauvignon Blanc with citrus and herbaceous character, and for barrel-fermented or partially oaked Chardonnay showing citrus, stone fruit, and a fresher, more restrained profile than warmer-region Chilean Chardonnay. Pinot Noir from the valley tends toward red-fruited, elegant, medium-bodied styles with brighter acidity than Chile's warmer zones, and cool-climate Syrah can show a peppery, savory edge. Overall the valley's wines emphasize freshness, aromatic precision, and moderate alcohol over power and richness.
notes: Casablanca Valley had almost no viticulture before the 1980s; its development marked Chile's first major expansion into a deliberately cool-climate wine region.
The valley lies directly in the path of cooling breezes and fog from the nearby Pacific, funneled through a break in the coastal mountain range.
Frost is a significant risk here precisely because the valley is cooler than most of Chile's traditional wine regions, unusual for a New World fine-wine area at this latitude.
Casablanca helped establish Chile's reputation for quality Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir, complementing the country's traditional strength in Cabernet Sauvignon.

regions.name: Colchagua Valley
regions.summary: Colchagua Valley, part of the larger Rapel Valley, is one of Chile's premier red wine regions, particularly celebrated for rich, full-bodied Cabernet Sauvignon, Carménère, and Bordeaux-style blends. It has become a major wine-tourism destination and a showcase for premium Chilean winemaking investment.
regions.climate: Colchagua has a warm Mediterranean climate, generally warmer than Maipo, with hot, dry summers well suited to ripening thick-skinned red varieties to full maturity. The valley shows a distinct west-to-east climatic gradient: areas closer to the Pacific coast in the west are cooled by ocean influence and morning fog, while inland areas toward the Andean foothills are warmer, giving producers a range of mesoclimates within a single DO. Low rainfall necessitates irrigation across the valley, historically from the Tinguiririca River.
regions.soils: Soils vary considerably across the valley, from alluvial, clay-rich soils on the valley floor with good water retention, to more well-drained, granitic and colluvial soils on hillside sites that are increasingly prized for premium plantings. This diversity allows producers to match variety and site, with hillside, better-drained locations generally reserved for the valley's top red wines.
regions.classification: Colchagua Valley is a recognized DO within the broader Rapel Valley region under Chile's geographic Denominación de Origen system; it has no formal internal quality-tier classification, though producers commonly distinguish coastal (Costa), entre cordilleras, and Andes-facing sub-areas informally to describe style. Its reputation as a premium red-wine zone has been built largely through producer investment and international acclaim rather than legal appellation hierarchy.

subRegions.name: Colchagua Costa
subRegions.notes: Cooler, coastally-influenced western sub-area increasingly planted to fresher reds and some whites.

subRegions.name: Apalta
subRegions.notes: A renowned amphitheater-shaped hillside area with old vines and granitic soils, source of some of Chile's most acclaimed premium reds.

subRegions.name: Marchigüe
subRegions.notes: A western sub-area benefiting from coastal cooling, used for balanced, fresher red wine styles.

regions.styles: Colchagua produces rich, full-bodied, deeply coloured red wines, especially Cabernet Sauvignon and Carménère, with ripe black fruit, notable concentration, smooth tannins, and often generous oak influence, built for both immediate appeal and cellaring. Bordeaux-style blends and premium single-vineyard reds from hillside sites like Apalta represent the valley's flagship, most age-worthy wines. Cooler coastal sub-zones increasingly yield fresher, less overtly ripe reds and some promising whites, broadening the valley's stylistic range beyond its traditional powerful reputation.
notes: Colchagua is part of the larger Rapel Valley, itself divided into Cachapoal Valley to the north and Colchagua Valley to the south.
The Apalta sub-zone, with its horseshoe-shaped hillsides and granitic soils, is home to several of Chile's most internationally acclaimed icon red wines.
Colchagua has developed into one of Chile's leading wine-tourism destinations, with a dedicated wine train and cluster of boutique and icon wineries.
The valley's west-to-east temperature gradient, from Pacific-cooled Colchagua Costa to warmer inland zones, gives producers meaningful stylistic flexibility within one DO.

regions.name: Stellenbosch
regions.summary: Stellenbosch is South Africa's most prestigious and historically significant wine region, renowned for structured, age-worthy Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends as well as the country's signature grape, Pinotage. It is the academic and commercial heart of the South African wine industry, home to Stellenbosch University's viticulture and oenology faculty.
regions.climate: Stellenbosch has a Mediterranean climate with warm, dry summers and cool, wet winters, moderated significantly by proximity to False Bay and cooling southeasterly summer winds known locally as the "Cape Doctor." Mountain ranges surrounding the valley (including the Stellenbosch, Simonsberg, and Helderberg mountains) create numerous distinct mesoclimates and aspects, with cooler, higher-altitude and south-facing sites offering markedly different ripening conditions than warmer valley-floor locations. This combination of maritime cooling and topographic variation allows both powerful reds and increasingly, fresher, elegant styles.
regions.soils: Stellenbosch has notably diverse soils for its size, ranging from decomposed granite on the mountain slopes, prized for red wine quality and good drainage, to sandstone-derived soils and alluvial, sandy soils on the valley floor. This granite-based soil, particularly on hillside sites, is closely associated with the region's most structured, mineral Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux blends.
regions.classification: Stellenbosch falls under South Africa's Wine of Origin (WO) scheme, which certifies origin, vintage, and variety claims and organizes the country geographically into regions, districts, and smaller wards. Stellenbosch is itself a WO district within the Coastal Region, and it contains numerous recognized wards (such as Simonsberg-Stellenbosch and Jonkershoek Valley) reflecting distinct terroirs, though, as with the rest of South Africa, there is no separate legally binding quality-tier hierarchy above origin certification.

subRegions.name: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch
subRegions.notes: A ward on granite-derived soils at the foot of the Simonsberg mountain, known for powerful, structured reds.

subRegions.name: Jonkershoek Valley
subRegions.notes: A cooler, higher-altitude ward with dramatic mountain scenery, suited to elegant, structured reds.

subRegions.name: Bottelary Hills
subRegions.notes: A ward with distinctive shale-influenced soils on rolling hills, contributing to the district's mesoclimate diversity.

subRegions.name: Devon Valley
subRegions.notes: A smaller, cooler ward known for both red and white wine production.

regions.styles: Stellenbosch is best known for full-bodied, structured Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style red blends with dark fruit, firm tannins, and strong ageing potential, alongside Pinotage ranging from rustic, smoky, high-toned styles to more refined, fruit-driven modern examples. Chenin Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc provide fresh, well-regarded white options, with some producers also making barrel-fermented Chardonnay. Overall the district balances New World ripeness and generosity with an increasing move toward freshness and site-specific elegance, particularly from cooler wards and higher-altitude vineyards.
notes: Stellenbosch is home to Stellenbosch University's Department of Viticulture and Oenology, the leading academic center for wine science in South Africa.
Pinotage, a crossing of Pinsage (Cinsault) and Pinot Noir created in 1925 at Stellenbosch University, remains South Africa's signature grape variety.
The cooling southeasterly "Cape Doctor" wind helps moderate summer heat and reduce disease pressure in vineyards.
South Africa's oldest wine estates and some of its most prestigious producers are concentrated in and around Stellenbosch.
Granite-derived mountain soils are strongly linked to the district's most age-worthy, structured red wines, distinguishing hillside from valley-floor sites.

regions.name: Swartland
regions.summary: Swartland, north of Cape Town, has transformed from a region historically known for bulk wine and wheat farming into one of South Africa's most exciting sources of characterful, often naturally-farmed old-vine Chenin Blanc and Rhône-style reds. It is closely associated with a movement of independent winemakers emphasizing minimal intervention and dry-farmed bush vines.
regions.climate: Swartland has a Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers and relatively low rainfall concentrated in winter, making it well suited to dry-farmed, drought-resistant bush vines rather than irrigated trellised vineyards. Cooling influences come from the nearby Atlantic Ocean and, in higher-elevation sites such as the Paardeberg and Kasteelberg hills, from altitude, both of which help offset the region's overall warmth. The dry summer climate also reduces disease pressure, supporting the region's strong tradition of organic and low-intervention viticulture.
regions.soils: Swartland's soils are notably varied, including decomposed granite on hillside sites like the Paardeberg, iron-rich shale, and areas of quartz and sandstone-derived soils known locally as "Malmesbury shale." These generally poor, well-drained soils, combined with dry farming, naturally restrict yields and are credited with contributing to the concentration and mineral character of the region's old-vine wines.
regions.classification: Swartland is recognized as a district under South Africa's Wine of Origin (WO) scheme within the Coastal Region, with several wards (such as Riebeekberg and Malmesbury) delimited within it. As with the rest of South Africa's WO system, there is no formal legal quality-tier hierarchy above origin, variety, and vintage certification, so Swartland's modern reputation for quality has been built primarily through producer-driven innovation rather than appellation status.

subRegions.name: Paardeberg
subRegions.notes: A granite hill area with old bush-vine plantings, closely associated with the region's revival and top-tier producers.

subRegions.name: Riebeekberg
subRegions.notes: A recognized ward known for old-vine plantings and characterful dry-farmed wines.

subRegions.name: Malmesbury
subRegions.notes: An area known for shale-influenced soils contributing structure and minerality to the district's wines.

regions.styles: Swartland's Chenin Blanc, often from old, dry-farmed bush vines, tends toward rich yet textured, dry styles with notes of orchard fruit, waxy lanolin, and a distinctive mineral or savory edge, frequently made with minimal new oak and low intervention. Red wines, led by Rhône-inspired Syrah and Grenache/Mourvèdre/Cinsault blends, show peppery, savory, dark-fruited character with moderate to full body and often a rustic, earthy complexity reflecting old bush-vine fruit. The region overall is associated with a distinctive, less polished, terroir-expressive style that stands apart from more internationally polished Cape wine regions.
notes: Swartland was historically known primarily for wheat farming and bulk/cooperative wine production before a wave of independent winemakers repositioned it as a quality region from the 2000s onward.
The Swartland Independent Producers group, associated figures like Eben Sadie and Adi Badenhorst, and the annual Swartland Revolution festival helped define the region's modern identity.
Many of the district's best vineyards are old, unirrigated bush vines, prized for low yields and concentrated, characterful fruit.
The name Swartland ("black land") is thought to derive from the dark-hued native rhinoceros bush that once covered the area, not the soil colour itself.
The region has become a leading example of low-intervention, minimal-oak winemaking within South Africa.

regions.name: Santorini
regions.summary: Santorini is a small volcanic Greek island in the Cyclades renowned for producing intensely mineral, high-acid white wines from the indigenous Assyrtiko grape, grown on some of Europe's oldest ungrafted vines thanks to the island's phylloxera-free volcanic soils. Its dramatic basket-trained vine-training system (kouloura) is unique to the region and a direct adaptation to its harsh growing conditions.
regions.climate: Santorini has a hot, dry Mediterranean climate with very low annual rainfall, intensified by near-constant strong winds off the Aegean Sea that necessitate the island's distinctive low, basket-shaped vine training to protect grapes from wind and sun. Humidity is unusually supplied by nightly sea mist and morning dew rather than rainfall, which the volcanic soil retains and releases to the vines, allowing dry farming despite the arid conditions. The moderating maritime influence keeps temperatures from becoming extreme, while high sunshine hours and mineral-rich volcanic soils together produce grapes with naturally high acidity despite the warmth.
regions.soils: Santorini's soils are almost entirely volcanic, derived from ancient eruptions of the island's volcano (most dramatically the Late Bronze Age Minoan eruption), consisting of porous pumice, ash, and volcanic rock with very little organic matter or clay. These soils are naturally phylloxera-resistant, meaning many of the island's Assyrtiko vines are ungrafted and extremely old, some reportedly over a century old, and they retain scarce moisture efficiently, which is essential to the island's unirrigated viticulture.
regions.classification: Santorini holds Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status under the EU/Greek wine law framework, one of Greece's most prestigious appellations, which regulates permitted grape varieties (chiefly Assyrtiko, along with Aidani and Athiri) and production methods on the island, including for the traditional sweet wine Vinsanto. There is no internal sub-appellation tiering within the Santorini PDO; quality distinction instead comes from vineyard site, vine age, and producer.
regions.styles: The signature dry white Santorini Assyrtiko is bone-dry, high in acidity, and full-bodied for a white wine, with citrus, green apple, and a distinctive smoky, saline, mineral character derived from its volcanic terroir, capable of both fresh, youthful drinking and notable ageing. The island also produces Nykteri, a traditionally barrel-aged, more powerful style of dry Assyrtiko-based white, and Vinsanto, a rich, luscious sweet wine made from sun-dried Assyrtiko and Aidani grapes, aged in barrel for extended periods and showing dried fruit, raisin, and nutty, oxidative notes. Red wines from Mavrotragano and Mandilaria, though a small proportion of production, are increasingly valued for their structure and character.
notes: The island's kouloura (basket) vine-training method coils each vine into a low, nest-like basket, protecting grapes from wind and intense sun while helping trap humidity for the fruit inside.
Because Santorini's volcanic, sandy soils are naturally resistant to phylloxera, many vines are original, ungrafted, and extremely old, some estimated at well over a century.
The island receives almost no summer rainfall, and vines rely largely on humidity from nightly sea mist absorbed through the porous volcanic soil.
Vinsanto from Santorini is one of Greece's most historic sweet wine styles, traditionally sun-dried and long-aged, unrelated in production method to Italian Vin Santo despite the similar name.
Assyrtiko from Santorini is widely regarded as Greece's finest and most internationally acclaimed white wine, prized for retaining high acidity even when fully ripe in a hot climate.

regions.name: England (Sussex & Kent)
regions.summary: Sussex and Kent, in southeast England, are the heartland of English sparkling wine, built on chalk soils that are a geological continuation of the Champagne basin. A historically cool, marginal climate long limited quality still-wine production, but rising temperatures combined with traditional-method expertise have made English sparkling wine internationally acclaimed.
regions.climate: Sussex and Kent lie near the northern limit of viable viticulture, with a cool maritime climate moderated by the English Channel and North Sea. Growing-season conditions resemble those of Champagne several decades ago, giving high natural acidity and comparatively low alcohol well suited to traditional-method sparkling wine. Spring frost, a short growing season, and unpredictable summer rainfall are the principal viticultural hazards, and vintage variation is significant. South-facing slopes and coastal proximity help maximize sunshine hours and moderate temperature extremes.
regions.soils: The most celebrated vineyards sit on outcrops of the same Cretaceous chalk seam that runs beneath the English Channel and resurfaces in Champagne, particularly across the South Downs of Sussex. Chalk provides excellent drainage and steady water retention, echoing Champagne's terroir. Kent's soils are more varied, including greensand and clay, but are still capable of producing high-quality fruit.
regions.classification: English wine is regulated under a PDO/PGI framework rather than a traditional appellation hierarchy. Wines can carry the protected designation 'English Wine' (PDO) or the broader 'English Regional Wine' (PGI), while Sussex became England's first county-specific wine PDO, recognizing the concentration of chalk-based vineyards there. There is no formal cru or vineyard-ranking system comparable to Champagne's.

subRegions.name: Sussex
subRegions.notes: Home to the greatest concentration of chalk vineyards and England's first county-specific wine PDO.

subRegions.name: Kent
subRegions.notes: England's most historically planted wine county, with more varied soils including greensand.

regions.styles: The overwhelming majority of quality production is traditional-method sparkling wine in brut, rosé, and blanc de blancs styles, marked by high acidity, fine mousse, and citrus, green apple, and red berry notes with bready, autolytic complexity from lees ageing. Still wines are a smaller but growing category, typically light-bodied, aromatic whites from Bacchus with herbaceous, elderflower character, alongside increasingly credible cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Ageing potential for top sparkling cuvées can extend well beyond a decade.
notes: Sussex became England's first wine-specific Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) in 2022.
Chalk vineyards in Sussex sit on the same geological seam as Champagne.
Bacchus has emerged as something of a signature English still white grape, valued for its aromatic character.
Major Champagne houses, including Taittinger and Pommery, have planted vineyards in southern England.
Climate change has been a significant factor in improving ripeness and consistency over recent decades.

regions.name: Valais
regions.summary: Valais, in the upper Rhône valley of southern Switzerland, is the country's largest and most planted wine canton, known for an extraordinary diversity of indigenous and international grape varieties grown on steep, sun-drenched slopes. It is particularly celebrated for the indigenous white grape Petite Arvine and for Fendant (Chasselas).
regions.climate: Valais lies in a deep, dry Alpine valley shielded from Atlantic weather systems by surrounding mountain ranges, giving it one of Switzerland's driest and sunniest climates. Vineyards are planted on steep, terraced, south-facing slopes along the Rhône, often at considerable elevation, allowing excellent sun exposure while cooler nights help preserve acidity. Historic mountain irrigation channels known as bisses are traditionally used given the region's low rainfall. The combination of intense sunshine and diurnal temperature swings supports ripening of both very early and very late-ripening varieties.
regions.soils: Soils vary considerably along the valley, from schist and gneiss on the steep upper slopes to alluvial, gravelly deposits on the valley floor left by the Rhône. Terraced vineyards on rocky, mineral-rich slopes are prized for concentration and structure in wines such as Petite Arvine and Syrah.
regions.classification: Valais operates under Switzerland's AOC system, administered at cantonal level, with Valais AOC governing permitted grape varieties, yields, and minimum sugar levels for the canton's wines. Within this, wines made from Chasselas are traditionally labelled 'Fendant' and red blends of Pinot Noir and Gamay 'Dôle' — long-standing Valais-specific traditional names rather than formal sub-appellations. There is no cru or vineyard-ranking hierarchy comparable to Burgundy.

subRegions.name: Sion area
subRegions.notes: Historic heart of Valais viticulture around the cantonal capital, with some of the steepest terraced vineyards.

subRegions.name: Chamoson
subRegions.notes: Noted for Petite Arvine and other indigenous white varieties.

subRegions.name: Sierre
subRegions.notes: One of the driest and sunniest parts of the valley, historically reliant on bisse irrigation channels.

regions.styles: Valais produces predominantly still wines across a wide stylistic range: crisp, medium-bodied dry whites from Chasselas (Fendant); more aromatic, textured whites from Petite Arvine with citrus and saline notes; and reds ranging from light Pinot Noir and the traditional Dôle blend to fuller-bodied, structured Syrah and rare indigenous reds such as Cornalin. Most wines are made for relatively youthful drinking, though top Petite Arvine, Syrah, and old-vine indigenous bottlings can age well.
notes: Valais is Switzerland's largest wine-producing canton by area under vine.
Historic irrigation channels called 'bisses' remain part of traditional viticulture in the drier parts of the valley.
Petite Arvine is considered one of Valais's signature indigenous white grapes.
Fendant is the traditional local name for wine made from Chasselas.
Switzerland exports very little of its wine, so most Valais production is consumed domestically.

regions.name: Kakheti
regions.summary: Kakheti, in eastern Georgia, is the country's largest and most historic wine region, widely regarded as one of the birthplaces of wine, with archaeological evidence of winemaking stretching back thousands of years. It is closely associated with traditional qvevri (large buried clay vessel) fermentation and with indigenous grapes such as Rkatsiteli and Saperavi.
regions.climate: Kakheti has a warm, semi-continental climate moderated by its position between the Greater and Lesser Caucasus mountain ranges, which shelter it from extreme weather and help create hot summers and cold winters. Much of the region's vineyard area is concentrated in the Alazani River valley, which benefits from fertile soils and a relatively long, warm growing season supporting full ripening of both white and red varieties. Elevation varies across the region, offering some cooling relief on higher vineyard sites.
regions.soils: Soils in the Alazani valley are predominantly alluvial, fertile, and varied, including clay and loam, contributing to the productivity of the region's vineyards. Diversity of soil types across Kakheti's principal sub-zones supports both high-yielding commercial production and, on lower-yielding sites, wines of greater concentration.
regions.classification: Georgia designates a number of protected appellations within Kakheti, most tied to specific villages or districts and, in some cases, to specific styles — for example Kindzmarauli, a naturally semi-sweet red made from Saperavi in a defined area. Traditional qvevri winemaking, in which wine ferments and ages in buried clay vessels, is recognized separately as an element of intangible cultural heritage and is often indicated on labels as a distinct production method.

subRegions.name: Telavi district
subRegions.notes: One of Kakheti's two principal sub-zones, associated with a range of appellations including Tsinandali.

subRegions.name: Kvareli district
subRegions.notes: The other principal sub-zone, home to appellations such as Kindzmarauli.

subRegions.name: Tsinandali
subRegions.notes: Well-known appellation for dry white blends of Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane.

subRegions.name: Kindzmarauli
subRegions.notes: Protected appellation for a naturally semi-sweet red wine made from Saperavi.

regions.styles: Kakheti produces both modern, European-style still wines — crisp or textured dry whites and medium- to full-bodied reds — and traditional qvevri-made wines, including amber ('orange') wines made from white grapes fermented on their skins in buried clay vessels, which show pronounced tannin, texture, and dried-fruit or nutty character. Saperavi, a teinturier grape, produces deeply coloured, high-acid, tannic red wines capable of ageing. Naturally semi-sweet reds, notably Kindzmarauli, are also traditional to the area.
notes: Georgia is widely cited as one of the oldest wine-producing countries in the world, with archaeological evidence of grape wine production dating back thousands of years.
Traditional qvevri winemaking was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013.
Saperavi is a teinturier grape, meaning its flesh as well as its skin is pigmented, giving very deep-coloured wines.
Kakheti accounts for the large majority of Georgia's total vineyard area.
Amber ('orange') wine, made by fermenting white grapes on their skins, is a Georgian tradition that has influenced natural-wine movements worldwide.

regions.name: Bekaa Valley
regions.summary: The Bekaa Valley is Lebanon's principal wine-producing region and one of the Eastern Mediterranean's most historic winemaking areas, with a viticultural heritage tracing back to Phoenician and Roman times. It is best known for full-bodied red blends, often based on Bordeaux and Rhône varieties, grown at high altitude.
regions.climate: The Bekaa Valley sits at high elevation between the Mount Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges, giving it a semi-arid, continental-influenced climate with hot, dry summers moderated by altitude, and cold winters. This elevation provides significant diurnal temperature variation, helping preserve acidity despite intense summer sunshine. Rainfall is low and concentrated in winter, and the generally dry summer conditions limit disease pressure, though water availability can be a constraint.
regions.soils: The valley floor and lower slopes feature a mix of gravel, limestone, and clay soils, with limestone-influenced sites in particular contributing structure and freshness to the wines. Well-drained soils on the valley's margins are often favoured for quality red-wine production.
regions.classification: Lebanon does not have a long-established, government-enforced appellation hierarchy comparable to French AOC or Italian DOC/DOCG systems. A national Indication Géographique Protégée (IGP) framework has more recently been introduced for Lebanese wine, including a designation covering the Bekaa Valley, but quality signalling in the Lebanese wine trade has historically relied, and largely still relies, on individual producer reputation rather than a formal tiered classification.

subRegions.name: Kefraya
subRegions.notes: Village area in the western Bekaa associated with well-known wine estates.

subRegions.name: Ksara
subRegions.notes: Area southwest of Zahlé, home to one of Lebanon's oldest commercial wineries.

regions.styles: Bekaa Valley wines are dominated by full-bodied, structured reds, often Bordeaux- or Rhône-style blends built around Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Cinsault, and Grenache, showing ripe dark fruit, high alcohol, and firm tannins, with real ageing potential in top examples. White wines, from both international varieties and indigenous grapes like Obaideh, tend to be fuller-bodied and less aromatically pronounced than cooler-climate equivalents. Rosé production is also significant, generally in a fuller, more structured style than typical Provençal rosé.
notes: The Bekaa Valley has a winemaking history that some trace back to the Phoenicians, and it was an important wine-producing area in Roman times, home to the temple of Bacchus at Baalbek.
Cinsault has historically been an important grape in Lebanon, associated with French influence during the French Mandate period.
Chateau Ksara, founded by Jesuit monks in the nineteenth century, is often cited as Lebanon's oldest commercial winery.
High elevation is critical to quality here, moderating what would otherwise be a very hot, Mediterranean-adjacent climate.
Lebanese wine production has continued through periods of regional conflict, with Bekaa vineyards at times located close to areas of instability.

regions.name: Judean Hills
regions.summary: The Judean Hills, surrounding Jerusalem, is one of Israel's most acclaimed quality wine regions, known for high-elevation vineyards producing some of the country's most highly regarded red and white wines. It has become a focal point of Israel's modern quality-wine revival since the late twentieth century.
regions.climate: The Judean Hills benefit from relatively high elevation, with many vineyards planted several hundred metres above sea level, moderating the otherwise hot Mediterranean climate typical of the region. Cooler nights and a greater diurnal temperature range compared to lower-lying Israeli wine areas help preserve acidity and aromatic freshness. Rainfall is concentrated in the winter months, typical of a Mediterranean climate, with warm, dry summers.
regions.soils: Soils are predominantly limestone and terra rossa, similar in character to other prominent limestone-based quality regions of the eastern Mediterranean, offering good drainage and often associated with structured, mineral-inflected wines.
regions.classification: Israel's formal appellation system is relatively limited compared to European models; the Judean Hills is recognized as one of Israel's principal named winegrowing regions, but there is no strict tiered quality hierarchy within it, and quality signalling relies more on producer reputation than on a formal cru or appellation ranking. For many wines, kosher certification status is also indicated on the label, though it is independent of quality level.

subRegions.name: Jerusalem Hills
subRegions.notes: High-elevation vineyards close to Jerusalem, among the coolest sites in the region.

subRegions.name: Ella Valley
subRegions.notes: Lower-elevation area in the Judean foothills known for several boutique wineries.

regions.styles: The Judean Hills produces predominantly still wines, led by structured, age-worthy red blends built around Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and Syrah, often labelled as Bordeaux-style blends, alongside increasingly well-regarded barrel-fermented Chardonnay and aromatic Sauvignon Blanc. Reds tend toward medium to full body with ripe dark fruit and firm tannins, while whites show fresher acidity than warmer, lower-altitude Israeli regions. Many of the country's flagship, internationally exported wines originate here.
notes: The Judean Hills is one of Israel's officially recognized major wine regions, alongside areas such as the Upper Galilee and the Golan Heights.
Elevation is the key quality factor here, distinguishing the region from Israel's warmer coastal and lowland vineyard areas.
Many Judean Hills wineries are small, boutique operations that emerged as part of Israel's quality-wine boom from the 1990s onward.
A significant share of Israeli wine production, including in this region, is certified kosher, though kosher status and quality level are independent of one another.
Terra rossa and limestone soils here are geologically related to soils found in other eastern Mediterranean wine regions.

regions.name: Ningxia
regions.summary: Ningxia, an autonomous region in north-central China, has emerged since the early 2000s as the country's most internationally acclaimed fine-wine region, producing structured Bordeaux-style reds that have won significant international recognition. It lies along the Yellow River at the foot of the Helan Mountains.
regions.climate: Ningxia has a semi-arid, continental climate on the Yellow River plain at the base of the Helan Mountains, which shield vineyards from the harshest winds of the Gobi Desert to the west. Summers are hot and sunny with a high diurnal temperature range, aiding ripening and colour development, while winters are severe enough that vines must be buried in soil to protect them from freezing. Rainfall is low, so irrigation drawing on Yellow River water is essential to viticulture here.
regions.soils: Vineyard soils are generally sandy, gravelly, and alluvial in character, deposited by the Yellow River and the Helan Mountains' alluvial fans, providing good drainage. These well-drained soils, combined with the region's aridity, help limit vine vigour and disease pressure.
regions.classification: China does not yet have a formal, legally enforced appellation hierarchy on the European model. Ningxia has, however, developed its own regional quality initiatives for wineries and vineyards as part of an effort to build a recognizable regional identity, though this remains less standardized and less internationally codified than systems such as AOC or DOC. In practice, quality signalling relies heavily on individual winery reputation and results at international competitions.

subRegions.name: Helan Mountain East Foothills (Helanshan Donglu)
subRegions.notes: The core sub-zone along the eastern foot of the Helan Mountains, home to the great majority of Ningxia's quality wineries.

subRegions.name: Qingtongxia
subRegions.notes: A recognized wine-producing area within the broader Ningxia region, home to a cluster of newer vineyards and wineries.

regions.styles: Ningxia is known predominantly for still red wines in a Bordeaux-inspired style, based on Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, typically full-bodied with ripe dark fruit, firm tannins, and, in top examples, genuine ageing potential. A smaller but growing amount of white wine, notably Chardonnay, and some sparkling wine is also produced. The need to bury vines each winter to protect them from extreme cold is a distinctive and labour-intensive feature of viticulture here.
notes: Ningxia wines have won top international awards, including at competitions such as the Decanter World Wine Awards, helping establish the region's reputation from the 2010s onward.
Vines must be buried under soil each winter to survive the region's severe cold, then uncovered again in spring — a labour-intensive practice sometimes called 'hilling up'.
Chinese national and regional authorities have actively promoted the wine industry in Ningxia as a strategic development priority.
A number of prominent international wine consultants have worked with Ningxia producers to help establish quality benchmarks.
Marselan, a Cabernet Sauvignon x Grenache crossing, has become increasingly popular in Ningxia and more broadly in China.

regions.name: Yamanashi
regions.summary: Yamanashi, near Mount Fuji west of Tokyo, is Japan's historic heartland of wine production and the country's most important region for the indigenous pink-skinned grape Koshu. It is home to many of Japan's oldest and most established wineries.
regions.climate: Yamanashi has a temperate climate within the Kofu Basin, surrounded by mountains including Mount Fuji, which provide some rain-shadow protection compared with more exposed coastal areas of Japan. Nonetheless, Japan's broader climatic challenge of high humidity and significant growing-season rainfall, including the summer rainy season and typhoon risk in early autumn, remains a factor, historically addressed through training systems that maximize airflow and reduce disease pressure.
regions.soils: Soils in the Kofu Basin are largely alluvial and volcanic in origin, well-drained on the basin's gently sloping fan-shaped terrain, suited to the traditional pergola-style training used for Koshu and table grapes alike.
regions.classification: Japan's wine labelling standards include a Geographical Indication (GI) system, under which 'Yamanashi' was designated as one of Japan's wine GIs, setting requirements around grape sourcing and production within the region. This sits within Japan's broader national labelling rules, introduced to clarify the distinction between wine made from Japanese-grown grapes and wine made domestically from imported bulk wine or must, historically a significant source of consumer confusion.

subRegions.name: Kofu Basin
subRegions.notes: The historic core of Yamanashi viticulture, surrounding the city of Kofu.

subRegions.name: Katsunuma
subRegions.notes: Long-established sub-district within Yamanashi particularly associated with Koshu.

regions.styles: Yamanashi's signature wine is Koshu, a pale-skinned, aromatically subtle white grape typically vinified as a light-bodied, delicate, dry white with citrus and light floral notes and gentle acidity, though styles range from lean and crisp to skin-contact and lees-aged versions with more texture. Muscat Bailey A, a hybrid grape, produces light, fruity, often slightly sweet reds and rosés with a distinctive candied, strawberry-like character. International varieties are increasingly used for more structured, Western-style reds and whites as producers pursue higher quality tiers.
notes: Koshu is believed to have arrived in Japan via ancient trade routes many centuries ago and is Yamanashi's signature indigenous grape.
Muscat Bailey A was bred in Japan in the twentieth century specifically to suit the country's humid growing conditions.
'Yamanashi' is one of Japan's registered wine Geographical Indications, part of a national system intended to protect and define regional wine identity.
Katsunuma, within Yamanashi, has one of the longest continuous histories of grape growing in Japan.

High humidity and rainfall during the growing season are the central viticultural challenge across Japan, including in Yamanashi, driving widespread use of vertical trellising and canopy management to aid airflow.

regions.name: Canelones (Southern Uruguay)
regions.summary: Canelones, in southern Uruguay near Montevideo, is the country's largest and most important wine region, central to Uruguay's identity as a leading producer of Tannat. Its maritime-influenced climate distinguishes Uruguayan wine from its larger South American neighbours.
regions.climate: Canelones and the surrounding southern Uruguayan wine zone have a temperate, humid climate strongly influenced by proximity to the Atlantic Ocean and the Río de la Plata estuary, giving cooler, more variable conditions than the drier, more continental climates typical of Argentina and much of Chile. This maritime influence brings higher humidity and more consistent rainfall through the year, raising disease pressure and requiring careful canopy management, but also moderating summer heat and helping preserve acidity in the grapes.
regions.soils: Soils are variable but often include clay and clay-loam over rocky subsoils, with reasonable water retention suited to the region's rainier climate; producers favour well-drained sites to help manage the higher humidity.
regions.classification: Uruguay's wine regulatory system includes a Vinos de Calidad Preferente (VCP) designation for quality wines meeting defined production standards, alongside broader table-wine categories, but does not have a detailed geographic cru or appellation hierarchy comparable to European systems. Canelones itself is recognized administratively as Uruguay's principal wine-producing department rather than through a tiered formal appellation structure.

subRegions.name: Canelón Chico
subRegions.notes: Historic concentration of long-established wineries and old Tannat vines within Canelones.

subRegions.name: Atlántida area
subRegions.notes: Coastal-influenced sub-zone within southern Uruguay's wine region.

regions.styles: Uruguay's, and Canelones's, signature wine is Tannat, traditionally a robust, deeply coloured, high-tannin red, though modern winemaking has produced softer, more approachable styles alongside the fuller, structured, age-worthy traditional expression. Bordeaux varieties such as Merlot and Cabernet Franc are also widely planted, used both varietally and in blends with Tannat. Aromatic whites, including a growing planting of Albariño, have become an increasingly important part of the region's modern identity, generally fresh and citrus-driven.
notes: Tannat, originally from southwest France, is so closely associated with Uruguay that it is often considered the country's national grape.
Uruguay's wine regions benefit from a more maritime, Atlantic-influenced climate than the drier growing regions of neighbouring Argentina.
Basque and other European immigrants brought Tannat to Uruguay in the nineteenth century.
Albariño has grown rapidly in popularity in Uruguay in recent decades as producers look for cool-climate white alternatives.
Many of Uruguay's wineries remain small, family-owned operations concentrated around Canelones, near the capital Montevideo.

regions.name: Serra Gaúcha
regions.summary: Serra Gaúcha, in the southern state of Rio Grande do Sul, is Brazil's largest and most historically important wine region, shaped by Italian immigrant winemaking traditions dating to the late nineteenth century. It produces the majority of Brazil's wine, including both still wines and increasingly well-regarded traditional-method sparkling wines.
regions.climate: Serra Gaúcha has a humid subtropical climate moderated by elevation, with vineyards generally planted on hillsides several hundred metres above sea level in a mountainous, forested landscape. High humidity and abundant, non-seasonal rainfall are the region's central viticultural challenge, raising disease pressure and requiring careful site selection, canopy management, and well-adapted grape varieties. Harvest-time rain is a persistent risk that growers must plan around.
regions.soils: Soils are predominantly basaltic in origin, derived from the volcanic rock underlying much of the region, generally reddish, well-drained, and moderately fertile on the hillside sites favoured for quality vineyards.
regions.classification: Brazil operates a Geographical Indication system modeled loosely on European frameworks. Within Serra Gaúcha, Vale dos Vinhedos was Brazil's first area to achieve Denominação de Origem (DO) status, the country's highest formal quality tier, having earlier held the lower Indicação de Procedência (IP) designation; other parts of Serra Gaúcha and Rio Grande do Sul hold IP status. These designations regulate permitted grape varieties, geographic boundaries, and production standards for wines labelled with the relevant name.

subRegions.name: Vale dos Vinhedos
subRegions.notes: Brazil's first Denominação de Origem, known for its basaltic soils and strong Italian immigrant winemaking heritage.

subRegions.name: Pinto Bandeira
subRegions.notes: Higher-elevation sub-zone within Serra Gaúcha holding its own Indicação de Procedência, noted especially for sparkling wine.

subRegions.name: Monte Belo do Sul
subRegions.notes: Another recognized sub-zone within the broader Serra Gaúcha wine area.

regions.styles: Serra Gaúcha produces a wide range of still wines, historically dominated by hybrid and native American grape varieties for everyday wine but increasingly focused on vinifera varieties such as Merlot, Tannat, and Cabernet Sauvignon for medium-bodied, fruit-forward reds. The region has also built a strong reputation for traditional-method and Charmat-method sparkling wines, particularly from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, considered by some critics to be Brazil's most internationally competitive wine category. Sweeter Muscat-based sparkling wines (Moscatel) are also a significant, historically popular style domestically.
notes: Vale dos Vinhedos, within Serra Gaúcha, was Brazil's first wine region to achieve Denominação de Origem status.
Italian immigrants, arriving from the late nineteenth century onward, founded the modern wine industry of Serra Gaúcha, and their heritage remains culturally central to the region.
Brazilian sparkling wine, especially from Serra Gaúcha, has won growing international recognition in recent years.
Basaltic soils, associated with ancient volcanic activity, are a defining geological feature of the region's best vineyard sites.

High rainfall and humidity mean disease-resistant hybrid grapes have historically played a larger role here than in most fine-wine regions, though quality vinifera plantings have expanded significantly.

regions.name: Istria & Dalmatia
regions.summary: Istria, in Croatia's northern Adriatic, and Dalmatia, along the country's long southern coastline, together represent Croatia's most important quality wine regions, each with distinct indigenous grape traditions — Istria for aromatic Malvazija Istarska whites and Dalmatia for powerful reds and coastal whites, including the grape genetically identical to Zinfandel/Primitivo.
regions.climate: Both regions have a Mediterranean climate, with Istria's more northerly position and the influence of the Adriatic and nearby mountains giving somewhat milder summer heat than Dalmatia, whose coastal and island vineyards, especially along the southern Dalmatian coast, experience some of the hottest, sunniest conditions in Croatia. Coastal breezes and, in Dalmatia, considerable elevation on some island and peninsula vineyards help moderate heat and preserve freshness, while Istria's inland areas are somewhat cooler and more continental in influence than its coast.
regions.soils: Istria is known particularly for red 'terra rossa' soils in its western coastal areas, associated with its best Malvazija Istarska vineyards, alongside areas of flysch (grey marl and sandstone) further inland. Dalmatia's vineyards, especially on its islands and steep coastal slopes, are often planted on limestone and karst terrain, frequently worked by hand on narrow, stony terraces.
regions.classification: Croatia's wine law follows an EU-aligned PDO/PGI system, with numerous small, geographically defined subregions recognized as protected designations of origin within both Istria and Dalmatia, each specifying permitted grape varieties and production rules for wines labelled with that name. Dalmatia in particular contains a large number of small, historically rooted appellations, often tied to a single island or peninsula, reflecting the fragmented, small-scale nature of much of the region's viticulture.

subRegions.name: Istria (peninsula)
subRegions.notes: Northern Adriatic peninsula best known for aromatic Malvazija Istarska whites and structured Teran reds.

subRegions.name: Pelješac peninsula
subRegions.notes: Dalmatian sub-region especially associated with high-quality Plavac Mali reds, including the noted Dingač and Postup sites.

subRegions.name: Korčula island
subRegions.notes: Dalmatian island known for the indigenous white grapes Pošip and Grk.

subRegions.name: Hvar island
subRegions.notes: Sun-drenched Dalmatian island with a long viticultural history.

regions.styles: Istria produces predominantly still whites led by Malvazija Istarska, typically medium-bodied and aromatic, with notes of stone fruit, herbs, and acacia, ranging from fresh and unoaked to richer, skin-contact or oak-aged versions, alongside age-worthy Teran reds with high acidity and dark fruit character. Dalmatia is best known for full-bodied, high-alcohol reds from Plavac Mali, especially from top sites like Dingač, showing ripe dark fruit, firm tannin, and real ageing potential, alongside fresh, saline coastal whites such as Pošip and Grk.
notes: Plavac Mali is a natural crossing of Crljenak Kaštelanski (the grape genetically identical to Zinfandel/Primitivo) and Dobričić, making it a close genetic relative of Zinfandel.
Dingač, on the Pelješac peninsula, is one of Croatia's most celebrated and historic single-vineyard sites for Plavac Mali, on extremely steep terraced slopes.
Istria's Malvazija Istarska is genetically distinct from other Mediterranean Malvasia varieties despite the shared name.
Many Dalmatian vineyards, especially on steep island and coastal terraces, must still be worked largely by hand due to the terrain.
Croatia has a very high number of small, EU-recognized PDO wine subregions relative to its overall vineyard area, reflecting a long history of localized, small-scale winemaking.

regions.name: Alto Adige & Trentino
regions.summary: Italy's northernmost wine region, spanning the alpine Alto Adige (Südtirol) and Trentino to its south, renowned for aromatic, high-precision white wines and increasingly for fine Pinot Nero and traditional-method sparkling wine. Alto Adige's bilingual, Austrian-influenced culture and high-altitude vineyards make it one of Italy's most distinctive terroirs.
regions.climate: Alpine to continental, with vineyards ranging from valley floor to over 900 meters, giving pronounced diurnal temperature swings that preserve aromatics and acidity. The Adige river valley channels the afternoon 'Ora' wind through Alto Adige, cooling vineyards despite intense mountain sunshine. Trentino, further south, is slightly milder. Elevation and exposure are the key determinants of style, with warmer valley sites suited to reds and higher slopes reserved for aromatic whites.
regions.soils: Alto Adige's slopes around Bolzano are notably volcanic (porphyry), well suited to red varieties like Lagrein, while limestone and dolomitic soils dominate higher sites favoring whites. Trentino's valley floor has alluvial and glacial soils, with more calcareous composition on the hillsides, and the flat gravelly Campo Rotaliano plain is the historic home of Teroldego.
regions.classification: Alto Adige DOC (Südtirol) covers the large majority of production, almost always varietally labeled; Trento DOC is reserved for traditional-method sparkling wine made from Chardonnay and Pinot Nero; Teroldego Rotaliano DOC protects Trentino's signature red. Labels frequently carry German synonyms alongside Italian names, reflecting the region's Austro-Hungarian history.

subRegions.name: Bolzano/Bozen area
subRegions.notes: Volcanic porphyry slopes especially suited to Lagrein and Schiava.

subRegions.name: Valle Isarco
subRegions.notes: Cool, steep valley producing intensely aromatic, high-acid whites.

subRegions.name: Trento
subRegions.notes: Home of Trento DOC, Italy's pioneering traditional-method sparkling wine zone.

subRegions.name: Campo Rotaliano
subRegions.notes: Flat gravel plain that is the near-exclusive home of Teroldego.

regions.styles: Whites dominate and are typically dry, aromatic and high in acidity, from intensely perfumed Gewürztraminer to richer, more structured Pinot Grigio than is typical elsewhere in Italy. Schiava yields light, pale, easy-drinking reds, while Lagrein and Teroldego are deeper-colored, more tannic and fruit-driven. Trento DOC produces high-quality traditional-method sparkling wine with fine mousse and toasty, autolytic character comparable in ambition to Champagne.
notes: Gewürztraminer is widely believed to take its name from the Alto Adige village of Tramin (Termeno).
Trento DOC, pioneered by Giulio Ferrari in the early 20th century, predates Franciacorta as Italy's original fine traditional-method sparkling wine zone.
Alto Adige is bilingual, and many wine names appear in both Italian and German (e.g. Lago di Caldaro/Kalterersee).
Cooperative wineries (cantine sociali) produce a large share of Alto Adige's output and are respected for consistent quality.
Teroldego Rotaliano is grown almost exclusively on the flat, gravelly Campo Rotaliano plain in Trentino.

regions.name: Friuli-Venezia Giulia
regions.summary: A northeastern region bordering Slovenia and Austria, widely regarded as Italy's finest zone for single-varietal white wine, prized for precision and minerality. Its hillside Collio and Colli Orientali districts are also the birthplace of Italy's modern skin-contact 'orange wine' movement.
regions.climate: A continental climate tempered by Adriatic influence from the south and shielded from the coldest northern air by the Julian Prealps and Alps. The cold, dry Bora wind and marked diurnal temperature swings on the hillsides help preserve acidity and aromatic freshness, particularly important for the region's white-wine focus. Hillside sites with good sun exposure and drainage are prized over the flatter, warmer plains.
regions.soils: The hillside Collio and Colli Orientali zones sit on ponca, a marl-and-sandstone flysch soil prized for giving structured, mineral whites; the large Grave plain has alluvial gravel and clay, historically suited to higher-volume production; pockets of red ferretto soil and limestone karst (in Carso) add further variation.
regions.classification: Production is organized around numerous zonal DOCs, including Collio DOC and Colli Orientali del Friuli DOC for premium hillside wine, and the larger Friuli Grave, Friuli Isonzo and Friuli Aquileia DOCs; Ramandolo DOCG and Picolit DOCG protect two rare sweet whites. Varietal labeling is the norm throughout the region.

subRegions.name: Collio
subRegions.notes: Premier hillside zone on the Slovenian border for structured, ageworthy whites.

subRegions.name: Colli Orientali del Friuli
subRegions.notes: Hillside zone for whites and native reds Refosco and Schioppettino, home of Ramandolo and Picolit.

subRegions.name: Friuli Grave
subRegions.notes: Large flat plain producing high-volume, everyday Pinot Grigio.

subRegions.name: Carso
subRegions.notes: Limestone karst near Trieste, known for Vitovska and Terrano.

regions.styles: Dry white wines dominate, ranging from clean, crisp, high-volume Pinot Grigio on the Grave plain to concentrated, textured Friulano and Ribolla Gialla from Collio and Colli Orientali, some made with extended skin contact into amber 'orange wine' styles. Native reds Refosco and Schioppettino are peppery, high-acid and food-friendly. Ramandolo and Picolit are rare, often botrytis-influenced sweet whites with real ageing potential.
notes: Friuli, especially around Collio and Oslavia, is considered the birthplace of Italy's modern extended skin-contact 'orange wine' movement, led by producers such as Gravner and Radikon.
Friulano was formerly labeled Tocai Friulano until a 2007 EU ruling forced the name change to avoid confusion with Hungarian Tokaji.
Schioppettino was once effectively banned from commercial production under Italian law until local growers won its reinstatement in the 1970s.
Ramandolo and Picolit are two of Italy's few DOCGs dedicated to sweet white wine.
The ponca/flysch soil of Collio continues geologically into Slovenia's Brda district just across the border, reflecting a terroir split by a modern frontier.

regions.name: Campania
regions.summary: A southern region around Naples cultivating some of Italy's oldest indigenous grape varieties on volcanic soils, producing structured, ageworthy reds from Aglianico (Taurasi) and distinctive mineral whites (Fiano di Avellino, Greco di Tufo). Campania's history as part of ancient Magna Graecia underlies many of its native varieties.
regions.climate: Mediterranean along the coast, but significantly tempered by elevation in the inland Irpinia hills, where vineyards up to 600-700 meters see cooler nights and a longer growing season than the warm coastal plains. Volcanic terrain around Vesuvius and the Campi Flegrei adds further variation, with some sandy volcanic sites historically escaping phylloxera.
regions.soils: Volcanic soils define the region: ash, pumice and tuff from Vesuvius and the Campi Flegrei give wines a saline, mineral edge, while the Irpinia hills around Taurasi combine volcanic material with limestone and clay, contributing to Aglianico's firm structure.
regions.classification: Three DOCGs anchor Campania's quality reputation: Taurasi DOCG for Aglianico-based reds with extended ageing requirements, and Fiano di Avellino DOCG and Greco di Tufo DOCG for dry whites, all centered on Irpinia. Numerous DOCs (Irpinia, Sannio, Campi Flegrei, Vesuvio, Ischia) and the broad IGT Campania cover other native varieties such as Falanghina and Piedirosso.

subRegions.name: Irpinia
subRegions.notes: Hilly interior around Avellino, home to all three of Campania's DOCGs.

subRegions.name: Taurasi zone
subRegions.notes: Aglianico's grand cru area, often called the 'Barolo of the South.'

subRegions.name: Campi Flegrei
subRegions.notes: Volcanic coastal area near Naples with rare, ungrafted old vines.

subRegions.name: Vesuvio
subRegions.notes: Volcanic slopes of Mount Vesuvius, source of Lacryma Christi wines.

regions.styles: Taurasi is a powerful, tannic, high-acid red with dark fruit, tar and spice notes and serious ageing potential, frequently compared to Barolo. Fiano di Avellino gives medium-bodied dry whites with honeyed, hazelnut character and real ageing capacity, while Greco di Tufo offers steelier, more citrus-driven mineral whites. Falanghina produces fresher, more immediate aromatic whites, and Piedirosso yields lighter, fruit-forward reds.
notes: Taurasi DOCG requires extended ageing, including time in wood, and is often nicknamed the 'Barolo of the South.'
Some sandy volcanic sites around Vesuvius and Campi Flegrei escaped the phylloxera louse, preserving rare pre-phylloxera, ungrafted vines.
Greco and Aglianico are both believed to have ancient Greek origins, reflecting Campania's history as part of Magna Graecia.
Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio ('tears of Christ') is a traditional wine name tied to vineyards on the volcano's slopes.
Fiano di Avellino, Greco di Tufo and Taurasi were among the first southern Italian wines to reach DOCG status, establishing Campania's fine-wine credentials.

regions.name: Abruzzo
regions.summary: A central-eastern Adriatic region and one of Italy's largest wine producers by volume, best known internationally for Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, a deeply colored, fruit-forward red, alongside crisp Trebbiano-based whites and the distinctively dark Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo rosato.
regions.climate: Mediterranean along the Adriatic coast, becoming cooler and more continental inland toward the Apennines and the Gran Sasso massif, which dominates the region's western border. Vineyard altitude ranges from near sea level to several hundred meters, and higher sites help preserve acidity in an otherwise warm growing environment.
regions.soils: Predominantly clay and limestone in the hills, with sandy and alluvial soils near the coast and river valleys. Historically fertile soils encouraged high yields, though quality-focused producers now target better-drained hillside sites.
regions.classification: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC is the large-volume backbone of the region, with Colline Teramane DOCG as its stricter sub-zone requiring lower yields and longer ageing. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo DOC covers the main white, while Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo DOC protects the region's notably deep-colored rosato made from Montepulciano. Single-variety DOCs for Pecorino and Passerina recognize revived native whites.

subRegions.name: Colline Teramane
subRegions.notes: DOCG hillside zone near Teramo for premium, longer-aged Montepulciano.

subRegions.name: Terre di Casauria
subRegions.notes: Interior zone recognized for quality-focused Montepulciano.

subRegions.name: Terre Aquilane/Colline Aquilane
subRegions.notes: Higher-altitude interior zone with cooler ripening conditions.

regions.styles: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo ranges from everyday, deeply colored, soft-tannin fruity reds to more structured, sometimes oak-aged wines from top Colline Teramane producers. Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is an unusually dark, full-bodied, food-friendly rosato, darker than most Italian rosati. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo whites are typically light and neutral, though a few producers make richer, ageworthy versions, while Pecorino and Passerina offer more aromatic, higher-acid modern whites.
notes: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo (the grape and wine) is unrelated to the Tuscan town of Montepulciano or the Sangiovese-based Vino Nobile di Montepulciano.
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo takes its name from 'cerasa' (cherry in local dialect), referencing its deep cherry-red hue.
Abruzzo is consistently among Italy's highest-volume wine regions, historically better known for bulk production than fine wine.
Pecorino and Passerina are native white varieties that were nearly extinct before being revived by growers from the 1990s onward.
DNA analysis has shown Trebbiano Abruzzese to be genetically distinct from the more widely planted Trebbiano Toscano, despite the similar name.

regions.name: Marche
regions.summary: A central Adriatic region best known for Verdicchio, one of Italy's most respected and ageworthy white grape varieties, alongside increasingly recognized reds Conero and Rosso Piceno made primarily from Montepulciano and Sangiovese.
regions.climate: Mediterranean along the coast, moderated by the Adriatic Sea, with the Apennine mountains to the west lending a cooler, more continental influence inland. Hillside vineyards benefit from good sun exposure and drainage, and diurnal temperature swings at higher elevations help preserve the acidity important to Verdicchio's ageing potential.
regions.soils: Predominantly calcareous clay and limestone in the hills, which suit Verdicchio's structure and mineral character. Monte Conero's slopes, used for Conero DOCG reds, also show notable limestone influence, contributing to firmer tannic structure.
regions.classification: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC and Verdicchio di Matelica DOC (each with a Riserva DOCG tier) are the flagship whites. Conero DOCG covers the top Montepulciano-based reds from Monte Conero, sitting above the broader Rosso Conero DOC, while Rosso Piceno DOC covers Sangiovese/Montepulciano blends across the wider southern zone.

subRegions.name: Castelli di Jesi
subRegions.notes: Larger, more varied Verdicchio zone including the historic Classico core.

subRegions.name: Matelica
subRegions.notes: Higher-altitude, more continental Verdicchio zone inland, giving more structured wines.

subRegions.name: Monte Conero
subRegions.notes: Coastal hill zone for Conero DOCG, Montepulciano-based reds.

subRegions.name: Piceno
subRegions.notes: Broad southern zone for the lighter Rosso Piceno DOC.

regions.styles: Verdicchio ranges from light, crisp, almond- and citrus-driven everyday wines to concentrated, ageworthy Riserva bottlings that develop honeyed, savory complexity with bottle age. Conero and Rosso Conero reds are medium-to-full-bodied, dark-fruited and firmly tannic, while Rosso Piceno is generally lighter and more approachable. Lacrima di Morro d'Alba offers a distinctive, intensely perfumed red with violet and blackberry aromatics.
notes: Verdicchio is one of the few Italian white varieties widely acknowledged to have serious ageing potential.
The traditional amphora-shaped bottle historically used for Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi became a recognizable marketing symbol for the wine.
Conero DOCG requires wines to be nearly or entirely 100% Montepulciano, marking it as a distinct, higher tier above Rosso Conero DOC.
Lacrima di Morro d'Alba is a rare, highly aromatic native red grape grown almost exclusively in a small zone near Morro d'Alba.
Matelica's more inland, higher-altitude, continental site gives its Verdicchio a reputation for being more structured and austere than the coastal-influenced Castelli di Jesi style.

regions.name: Umbria
regions.summary: Italy's only landlocked central region, historically known for white Orvieto but now equally recognized for Montefalco Sagrantino, one of Italy's most powerfully tannic red wines.
regions.climate: Continental-Mediterranean, moderated by Lake Trasimeno and hilly terrain. The landlocked, inland position gives warm summers and cooler winters than coastal regions, with meaningful diurnal temperature variation at typical vineyard elevations supporting balanced ripening.
regions.soils: Volcanic tuff soils around Orvieto give the region's whites their characteristic minerality and historically enabled cave-cellar ageing beneath the town; clay and limestone are common around Montefalco, contributing to Sagrantino's dense structure and tannic grip.
regions.classification: Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG is the flagship, made from 100% Sagrantino with mandatory extended ageing given the grape's extreme tannin. Torgiano Rosso Riserva DOCG is a smaller, historic Sangiovese-based DOCG. Orvieto DOC (which extends into neighboring Lazio) covers the well-known white in both dry (secco) and off-dry/sweet (amabile) styles, while Montefalco Rosso DOC is a Sangiovese-based blend that may include a small amount of Sagrantino.

subRegions.name: Montefalco
subRegions.notes: Hilltop town at the heart of Sagrantino production.

subRegions.name: Orvieto
subRegions.notes: Historic volcanic-tuff zone for the region's best-known white wine.

subRegions.name: Torgiano
subRegions.notes: Small historic DOCG zone closely associated with the Lungarotti winery.

subRegions.name: Colli del Trasimeno
subRegions.notes: Lakeside zone benefiting from Lake Trasimeno's moderating influence.

regions.styles: Montefalco Sagrantino is a deeply colored, extremely tannic, full-bodied red with dark and dried fruit and spice notes, made in both dry and traditional sweet passito styles with serious ageing potential. Orvieto whites are typically light, crisp and fresh in the dry style, with a historic sweet, botrytis-influenced version also made. Montefalco Rosso and Torgiano Rosso offer more approachable, medium-bodied, Sangiovese-driven reds.
notes: Sagrantino is regarded as one of the most tannic red grape varieties in the world, historically used mainly for sweet passito wine before dry versions became prominent.
Grechetto is Orvieto's key supporting white grape, adding body and structure to blends otherwise based on Trebbiano.
Orvieto's underground volcanic tuff caves were historically used both for quarrying building material and for wine cellar storage.
Torgiano Rosso Riserva DOCG, though small in production, was one of Italy's earlier DOCGs, closely tied to the pioneering Lungarotti winery.
Umbria is Italy's only region with no coastline, a fact tied directly to its continental climate character.

regions.name: Puglia
regions.summary: The 'heel' of Italy and one of its highest-volume wine regions, historically known for bulk and blending wine but increasingly recognized for characterful, sun-ripened reds from Primitivo and Negroamaro, and for its long rosato tradition.
regions.climate: A hot, dry Mediterranean climate, among the warmest and sunniest in Italy, with the Adriatic and Ionian seas flanking the long peninsula and providing moderating breezes. The generally flat terrain offers little elevation relief, so heat and drought stress are significant factors, favoring drought-tolerant, traditionally bush-trained old vines.
regions.soils: Predominantly red clay over limestone bedrock, across generally fertile, flat-to-gently-undulating land that historically enabled high yields. Limestone contributes minerality and drainage on sites where growers farm for quality over quantity.
regions.classification: Primitivo di Manduria DOC anchors Primitivo production, including a traditional sweet Dolce Naturale version and a smaller Riserva DOCG. Salice Salentino DOC covers Negroamaro-based reds and rosati, while Castel del Monte DOC in the north includes Riserva DOCG tiers for Bombino Nero rosato and Nero di Troia. The broad IGP Puglia/Salento covers large-volume, often varietally labeled wine.

subRegions.name: Salento peninsula
subRegions.notes: Negroamaro and Primitivo heartland, including Salice Salentino.

subRegions.name: Manduria
subRegions.notes: Historic zone for Primitivo di Manduria, including its sweet Dolce Naturale style.

subRegions.name: Gioia del Colle
subRegions.notes: Primitivo DOC zone also known for Sangiovese.

subRegions.name: Castel del Monte
subRegions.notes: Northern zone for Nero di Troia and Bombino Nero rosato.

regions.styles: Primitivo produces rich, ripe, high-alcohol, dark-fruited reds, genetically identical to California Zinfandel, from everyday fruity styles to more concentrated, sometimes oak-aged examples and a traditional sweet Dolce Naturale version. Negroamaro gives deeply colored, robust, earthy reds and underpins Puglia's well-regarded rosato tradition. Nero di Troia offers firmer tannin and greater ageing potential. Overall styles skew warm-climate, full-bodied and fruit-forward.
notes: DNA profiling has shown Primitivo to be genetically identical to California's Zinfandel and Croatia's Crljenak Kaštelanski, all descending from the same Croatian-origin variety.
Puglia is consistently one of Italy's top wine regions by volume, historically supplying blending wine to boost color and alcohol in other regions' wines.
Traditional bush-trained (alberello) old vines remain common, well suited to the region's hot, dry, windy climate.
Puglia has a long-standing reputation for high-quality, food-friendly rosato, particularly from Negroamaro in the Salento area.
Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale is a traditional sweet red made from late-harvested, partially raisined grapes.

regions.name: Sardinia
regions.summary: A large Mediterranean island region with a wine culture historically shaped by Spanish Aragonese and Catalan rule, known for Cannonau (Grenache) reds, Vermentino whites, and the distinctive oxidative dessert wine Vernaccia di Oristano.
regions.climate: A warm Mediterranean island climate, influenced by sea exposure on nearly all sides and by the persistent Mistral-like wind known locally as the Maestrale, which helps ventilate vineyards and reduce disease pressure despite abundant sunshine. Inland hill and mountain sites provide cooler, higher-altitude alternatives to the hot coastal plains.
regions.soils: Varied across the island: granite and schist dominate much of the interior and the northeastern Gallura zone prized for Vermentino, while limestone, clay and alluvial soils are found elsewhere, generally free-draining and suited to low-vigor, drought-tolerant traditional varieties.
regions.classification: Vermentino di Gallura DOCG is Sardinia's only DOCG, requiring the grape to be grown in the granite-soil Gallura zone in the northeast. Cannonau di Sardegna DOC covers the island-wide red with permitted sub-zone designations, Carignano del Sulcis DOC protects old-vine Carignano in the southwest, and Vernaccia di Oristano DOC covers the traditional oxidative wine of the Oristano area.

subRegions.name: Gallura
subRegions.notes: Northeastern granite-soil zone and Sardinia's only DOCG, for Vermentino.

subRegions.name: Sulcis
subRegions.notes: Southwestern zone of old, ungrafted, sandy-soil Carignano bush vines.

subRegions.name: Oristano
subRegions.notes: West-central home of the oxidative Vernaccia di Oristano.

subRegions.name: Mandrolisai/Ogliastra
subRegions.notes: Interior and eastern zones focused on Cannonau.
