regions.styles: Vermentino di Gallura is a dry, aromatic, medium-bodied white with citrus and herbal notes, generally showing more structure and richness than Vermentino grown elsewhere in Italy. Cannonau produces warm, full-bodied, fruit-forward reds with relatively high alcohol, occasionally in sweet or fortified styles. Carignano del Sulcis reds are concentrated and dark-fruited, benefiting from old, ungrafted vines. Vernaccia di Oristano is a distinctive oxidative white, dry to sweet, aged under flor-like conditions somewhat reminiscent of Sherry.
notes: Sulcis's Carignano vines are largely ungrafted (own-rooted), as the sandy soils there naturally resist phylloxera, preserving some of Europe's oldest surviving pre-phylloxera vineyards.
Cannonau is genetically the same variety as Grenache/Garnacha, though some ampelographers have debated whether Sardinia could be an alternate point of origin.
Vernaccia di Oristano is unrelated to the Tuscan white grape Vernaccia di San Gimignano despite the shared name.
Vermentino di Gallura is Sardinia's sole DOCG, reflecting the particular esteem for Vermentino grown on Gallura's granite soils.
Sardinia is one of the world's recognized 'Blue Zones' for longevity, and locals often anecdotally link this to traditional, moderate Cannonau consumption.

regions.name: Emilia-Romagna
regions.summary: A northern-central region split between Emilia, the heartland of Italy's famous lightly sparkling Lambrusco, and Romagna, known for Sangiovese-based reds and the Albana white grape. Its cuisine, including Parmigiano-Reggiano and balsamic vinegar, is closely tied to Lambrusco's traditional role as a food wine.
regions.climate: Emilia's Po Valley plain, home to the main Lambrusco zones around Modena, Reggio Emilia and Parma, has a continental climate with hot summers, cold winters and frequent morning river fog. Romagna, further southeast toward the Apennine foothills and the Adriatic, enjoys a milder, more Mediterranean-influenced climate better suited to ripening Sangiovese.
regions.soils: Emilia's plains have fertile, alluvial clay and silt soils deposited by the Po river, historically favoring the high yields typical of much Lambrusco production. Romagna's hillier terrain has more clay-limestone and sandstone soils, giving Sangiovese di Romagna greater structure on higher, better-drained sites.
regions.classification: Several Lambrusco DOCs recognize genuinely distinct grape sub-varieties and zones, including Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC, Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro DOC, Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce DOC and Lambrusco Reggiano DOC. Romagna Sangiovese DOC covers the region's red backbone, and Albana di Romagna DOCG, Italy's first white wine DOCG (1987), covers both dry and sweet versions of the Albana grape.

subRegions.name: Sorbara
subRegions.notes: Lightest, most fragrant, palest style of Lambrusco.

subRegions.name: Grasparossa di Castelvetro
subRegions.notes: Fuller-bodied, deeper-colored, more tannic Lambrusco.

subRegions.name: Salamino di Santa Croce
subRegions.notes: Fruity, structured Lambrusco sub-zone.

subRegions.name: Romagna hills
subRegions.notes: Home to Sangiovese di Romagna and Albana di Romagna.

regions.styles: Lambrusco is a lightly sparkling (frizzante, occasionally fully spumante) red ranging from dry (secco) to off-dry or sweet (amabile), typically low-to-moderate in alcohol with high acidity and fresh red-fruit character, meant for early drinking; style varies meaningfully by sub-zone, from Sorbara's pale delicacy to Grasparossa's depth and structure. Sangiovese di Romagna is a still, medium-bodied, food-friendly red with cherry fruit and firm acidity, from everyday to more serious Riserva bottlings. Albana di Romagna makes full-bodied dry whites and a rarer sweet passito version.
notes: Albana di Romagna became Italy's first white wine to receive DOCG status in 1987, a decision that was widely debated at the time given the grape's modest reputation.

Lambrusco suffered a serious reputation problem internationally in the late 20th century due to mass-produced, sweetened export versions; quality dry Lambrusco from top sub-zones is taken far more seriously today.
The distinct Lambrusco DOCs (Sorbara, Grasparossa, Salamino) reflect genuinely different Lambrusco grape sub-varieties, not just different zones of a single grape.
Emilia-Romagna is home to Parmigiano-Reggiano and traditional balsamic vinegar, and Lambrusco's acidity and light fizz have long made it a natural pairing for the region's rich cuisine.
Pignoletto, a native white grape mainly from the Bologna hills, has its own DOCG (Colli Bolognesi Classico Pignoletto) for the higher-quality version.

regions.name: Rueda
regions.summary: Rueda is a DO on the high plateau of Castilla y León and Spain's leading white wine region, built almost entirely around the aromatic Verdejo grape. It shifted from a historic fortified-wine tradition to become synonymous with fresh, dry, herbaceous whites from the late 20th century onward.
regions.climate: Continental, with hot, dry summers and cold winters typical of Spain's northern plateau (Meseta). Vineyards sit at high altitude (roughly 700-800m), which brings a wide diurnal temperature range that preserves acidity and aromatics in the grapes. Rainfall is low and irrigation is often needed, but the altitude and cool nights are essential to keeping Verdejo fresh rather than flabby.
regions.soils: Poor, stony and sandy soils with gravel and some limestone subsoil predominate, giving low natural fertility and excellent drainage. These conditions naturally restrict vigor and yields, concentrating flavor in the Verdejo grape.
regions.classification: Wines labeled simply "Rueda" require a minimum of 50% Verdejo; "Rueda Verdejo" requires at least 85% Verdejo, and varietal Sauvignon Blanc bottlings similarly require a minimum 85% of that grape. Oak-aged whites may be labeled "Fermentado en Barrica" or similar to indicate barrel fermentation or ageing.
regions.styles: The dominant style is a dry, unoaked white with pronounced aromatics of citrus, green apple, fennel and a characteristic bitter-almond note, finishing crisp and fresh. Barrel-fermented and lees-aged versions add texture and richness while retaining Verdejo's herbal signature. A small amount of traditional oxidative, sherry-like fortified wine is still made but is now a historical curiosity rather than the region's focus.
notes: Rueda's Verdejo is a distinct grape from the unrelated Verdejo/Verdelho grown elsewhere and from Argentine or Uruguayan plantings labeled similarly.
Before its white-wine revival, Rueda was known for oxidative, flor-aged fortified wines similar in style to Sherry.
Sauvignon Blanc was introduced in the 1970s by Marqués de Riscal and remains an important secondary variety, sometimes blended with Verdejo.
Old, ungrafted bush vines of Verdejo still survive in parts of the region thanks to the sandy soils' natural resistance to phylloxera.

regions.name: Toro
regions.summary: Toro is a DO in Castilla y León along the Duero river, renowned for powerful, deeply colored red wines from Tinta de Toro, a local clone of Tempranillo. Its extreme continental climate and old, often ungrafted vines produce some of Spain's most concentrated and high-alcohol reds.
regions.climate: Extreme continental, with very hot, dry summers and cold winters; altitude (roughly 600-750m) provides some moderation but the climate remains harsher and hotter than neighboring Ribera del Duero. Drought stress is common and rainfall is low, pushing sugar and tannin ripeness to high levels and often resulting in wines of considerable alcoholic strength.
regions.soils: Sandy soils dominate much of the region, which historically protected vines from phylloxera and allowed many pre-phylloxera, ungrafted plantings to survive. Areas of clay and limestone also occur, adding structure and water retention in an otherwise arid landscape.
regions.classification: Under DO Toro rules, red wines must contain a high minimum proportion (commonly cited as at least 75%) of Tinta de Toro, with Garnacha as the main permitted blending partner; small amounts of white Malvasía and Verdejo are also produced within the DO.

subRegions.name: Zone around Toro town
subRegions.notes: The historic core of the appellation, with the highest concentration of old vineyards.

subRegions.name: San Román de Hornija area
subRegions.notes: A cooler, more northerly pocket of the DO along the Duero.

regions.styles: Reds are typically full-bodied, deeply colored and high in alcohol (often 14-15% or more), with ripe black fruit, firm tannins and considerable ageing potential. Historically rustic and powerful, modern winemaking has tempered extraction in many bottlings while retaining the grape's natural intensity.
notes: Sandy soils meant Toro largely escaped the phylloxera epidemic, leaving some of Spain's oldest surviving, ungrafted vineyards.
Tinta de Toro is considered a distinct local clone of Tempranillo, generally smaller-berried with thicker skins, giving darker color and higher tannin than Tempranillo elsewhere.
Toro wines have a documented history of export dating back centuries, including shipment to the Americas during the colonial era.
The region gained modern international attention in the 1990s-2000s as investment poured in to exploit its old-vine potential.

regions.name: Bierzo
regions.summary: Bierzo is a DO in the northwest of Castilla y León, in a mountain-sheltered basin that acts as a climatic transition zone between humid Atlantic Galicia and the dry continental Meseta. It has become one of Spain's most acclaimed regions for terroir-driven reds from the Mencía grape, largely thanks to a quality revival led by outside investment in the early 2000s.
regions.climate: A transitional climate shaped by surrounding mountains, which shelter the basin from the harshest Atlantic weather while still allowing meaningful maritime influence and moderate rainfall compared to the drier Meseta. Summers are warm but rarely extreme, and diurnal temperature swings on higher slopes help preserve freshness in the grapes.
regions.soils: Soils vary considerably across the region, from fertile clay and alluvial deposits on the valley floor to poor, slate and schist-based soils on the higher hillsides. The best, most sought-after old-vine Mencía typically comes from these steep slate slopes, which give lower yields and more mineral, structured wines.
regions.classification: DO Bierzo governs production; there has been growing momentum, inspired by models like Priorat and Burgundy, toward recognizing individual villages and single vineyards (viñedos singulares) with particularly distinguished old-vine slate sites, though this remains less formalized than in some other Spanish regions.

subRegions.name: Corullón
subRegions.notes: A village associated with some of Bierzo's most prized steep, slate-soil old vineyards.

subRegions.name: Valtuille de Abajo
subRegions.notes: Another noted village source for high-quality old-vine Mencía.

regions.styles: Reds range from fresh, fruit-forward, easy-drinking styles to more serious, age-worthy wines from old, high-altitude vines, showing red and black fruit, floral aromatics, fine tannin and mineral, savory depth. Godello-based whites are increasingly important, offering fresh, textured, mineral wines with ageing potential.
notes: Bierzo's modern reputation was built largely by Álvaro Palacios and his nephew Ricardo Pérez Palacios (Descendientes de J. Palacios), who arrived in the late 1990s/early 2000s to champion old-vine, slate-soil Mencía.
Many of the best vineyards are old bush vines (vaso-trained), farmed by hand on steep terraces that make mechanization difficult.
Godello, once nearly extinct, has been revived in Bierzo (and neighboring Valdeorras) as a serious quality white grape.
Bierzo's climate is notably wetter than most of Castilla y León, giving it more in common with Galicia than with the arid Duero valley regions.

regions.name: Navarra
regions.summary: Navarra is a DO in northern Spain immediately east of Rioja, historically celebrated for dry rosado (rosé) made from Garnacha and now known for a broader range of reds blending Tempranillo with international varieties. Its diverse subzones span a climatic gradient from Atlantic-influenced north to Mediterranean-influenced south.
regions.climate: Navarra spans a transition from cooler, wetter Atlantic conditions in the north to a warmer, drier Mediterranean/continental climate in the south, giving considerable stylistic diversity across its subzones. This range allows both freshness in cooler northern sites and full ripeness in the warmer south.
regions.soils: Soils vary by subzone, including alluvial river terraces, clay-limestone slopes and iron-rich clay soils, contributing to the range of styles produced across the region.
regions.classification: DO Navarra is divided into five official subzones reflecting its climatic diversity, and the appellation permits a relatively liberal mix of traditional Spanish and international varieties compared to neighboring Rioja.

subRegions.name: Baja Montaña
subRegions.notes: Cooler, hilly northeastern subzone traditionally strong in Garnacha.

subRegions.name: Valdizarbe
subRegions.notes: Central subzone along the Camino de Santiago route.

subRegions.name: Tierra Estella
subRegions.notes: Western subzone with varied elevation and soils.

subRegions.name: Ribera Alta
subRegions.notes: Central subzone with a more moderate climate.

subRegions.name: Ribera Baja
subRegions.notes: Warmest, driest southern subzone, suited to fuller-bodied reds and sweet Moscatel.

regions.styles: Navarra is historically famous for pale, dry, fruity rosado from Garnacha, still an important category. Reds range from lighter Tempranillo-Garnacha blends to fuller, oak-aged wines incorporating Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and the southern subzones also produce sweet, aromatic Moscatel dessert wines.
notes: Navarra is often credited as one of Spain's pioneering regions for high-quality dry rosado.
The regional research institute EVENA drove significant viticultural modernization and clonal research from the 1980s onward.
Unlike neighboring Rioja, Navarra's regulations have long allowed greater use of international varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Chardonnay.
The Chivite family is one of the region's most historically important producers, with winemaking roots dating back centuries.

regions.name: Jumilla
regions.summary: Jumilla is a DO in southeastern Spain (mostly in Murcia) built on the Monastrell (Mourvèdre) grape, grown on high, sandy plateaus that famously escaped the worst of phylloxera. It has moved from a bulk-wine reputation toward increasingly serious, good-value reds.
regions.climate: Hot, semi-arid and Mediterranean-continental, with high altitude on the plateau providing some relief from extreme heat and helping preserve acidity. Rainfall is scarce and summers are intense, conditions to which drought-tolerant Monastrell is particularly well suited.
regions.soils: Predominantly sandy soils over limestone, low in fertility and organic matter. The sandy composition famously provided natural resistance to the phylloxera louse, allowing many vines to remain ungrafted.
regions.classification: DO Jumilla regulations set minimum proportions of Monastrell for red wines, with higher-tier or varietal designations requiring greater percentages of the grape; the appellation also permits international varieties as blending components.
regions.styles: Reds are typically full-bodied and high in alcohol, with ripe, jammy dark fruit and (traditionally) rustic, firm tannins; modern producers increasingly favor more balanced, fresher styles with careful oak use. Old, dry-farmed bush-vine Monastrell can yield remarkably concentrated, characterful wine at accessible prices.
notes: Jumilla contains one of the world's largest concentrations of pre-phylloxera, ungrafted old vines, thanks to its sandy soils.
Monastrell here is the same grape as Mourvèdre in France and Monastrell/Mataro elsewhere, thriving in Jumilla's heat and drought.
The region was historically known mainly for cheap, high-alcohol bulk wine before a quality-focused shift beginning in the 1990s-2000s.
Low rainfall and poor soils naturally restrict yields, concentrating flavor even without deliberate crop-thinning.

regions.name: Montsant
regions.summary: Montsant is a Catalan DO that forms a ring around the more famous DOQ Priorat, sharing much of its grape mix and hilly terrain while generally offering more approachable prices. It produces predominantly Garnacha- and Cariñena-based reds, often seen as a strong-value alternative to its illustrious neighbor.
regions.climate: Mediterranean climate moderated by hilly terrain and some continental influence inland; elevation and exposure vary considerably across the DO, giving a range of ripening conditions from warmer lower slopes to cooler, higher sites nearer Priorat.
regions.soils: Soils are more varied than in Priorat's famously uniform llicorella slate, ranging from clay and limestone in lower areas to slate-influenced soils in the hillier zones bordering Priorat, contributing to a broader range of wine styles.
regions.classification: Montsant was elevated to full DO status in 2001, having previously been a subzone of DO Tarragona; it geographically surrounds DOQ Priorat and its regulations allow both traditional Catalan varieties and international blending partners.
regions.styles: Reds range from medium-bodied, fruit-driven wines to fuller, more structured bottlings from old-vine Garnacha and Cariñena, generally less powerful and tannic than typical Priorat but sharing similar dark-fruited, mineral character. Some rosado and white wine is also produced.
notes: Montsant literally encircles DOQ Priorat, and the two regions share considerable overlap in grape varieties and winemaking philosophy.
Old-vine Garnacha and Cariñena are particularly prized, often sourced from low-yielding, dry-farmed hillside vineyards.
Montsant is frequently marketed as a more affordable entry point into the same style of wine that made Priorat famous.
Unlike Priorat, Montsant does not use Spain's top DOQ/DOCa classification tier.

regions.name: Somontano
regions.summary: Somontano is a DO in Aragón, its name meaning "under the mountain," referring to its position in the foothills of the Pyrenees. A relatively young appellation, it built its reputation on modern winemaking and an unusually wide range of both native and international grape varieties.
regions.climate: Continental climate moderated by proximity to the Pyrenees, which brings cooling mountain air and helps preserve acidity relative to Spain's hotter southern regions. Rainfall is moderate for Spain, and the mountain backdrop provides a meaningful diurnal temperature range that benefits aromatic ripening.
regions.soils: Predominantly alluvial and clay-limestone soils, generally fertile by Spanish standards, requiring careful vineyard management to control vigor and yields.
regions.classification: DO Somontano was established in 1984, relatively recently by Spanish standards, and its regulations have from the outset encouraged experimentation with both traditional Aragonese grapes and international varieties, distinguishing it from more tradition-bound neighboring DOs.
regions.styles: The region produces fresh, aromatic whites (from Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer and native varieties) alongside medium- to full-bodied reds in a generally modern, fruit-forward international style, as well as varietal bottlings of the local Moristel grape.
notes: Moristel is a native red grape found almost exclusively in Somontano, valued for fresh, light-to-medium-bodied reds.
Somontano was a pioneer among Spanish DOs in embracing international varieties like Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from its founding.
Significant investment in modern winery technology since the DO's creation helped establish its reputation relatively quickly compared to more historic Spanish regions.
Proximity to the Pyrenees gives Somontano cooler nights than much of inland Aragón, aiding aromatic freshness.

regions.name: Madeira
regions.summary: Madeira is a volcanic Atlantic island producing one of the world's most distinctive fortified wines, deliberately heated and oxidized in a process that mimics the effects of historical long sea voyages through tropical heat. The result is an exceptionally long-lived wine, virtually indestructible once bottled and even after opening.
regions.climate: Subtropical Atlantic climate, warm and humid year-round, with steep volcanic terrain forcing vines onto terraces (poios) at varying altitudes. Higher-altitude vineyards provide cooler conditions better suited to grapes like Sercial, while lower, warmer sites favor Tinta Negra and sweeter styles.
regions.soils: Volcanic basalt soils dominate the island, well-drained and mineral-rich, farmed on dramatic hand-built stone terraces due to the steepness of the landscape.
regions.classification: Wines are classified by ageing and, when made from a single "noble" grape at a minimum 85% proportion, may be labeled varietally (Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey), each traditionally associated with a sweetness level from dry to very sweet. Quality tiers include 3-year, 5-year (Reserve), 10-year (Special Reserve or Old Reserve), Colheita (single-vintage, aged a minimum of five years) and Vintage/Frasqueira (single-vintage, cask-aged a minimum of twenty years).
regions.styles: Styles range from bone-dry, tangy Sercial to lusciously sweet Malmsey, with Verdelho and Bual occupying the medium-dry to medium-sweet range in between. All styles share a deliberately oxidative character with high acidity and flavors of caramel, dried fruit, nuts and citrus peel, and the wines have essentially unlimited ageing potential.
notes: Basic Madeira is heated in tanks (estufagem), while premium wines are aged slowly and naturally in warm attic lodges over years (canteiro), a gentler process that yields greater complexity.
Once opened, Madeira can last for weeks or months without spoiling due to its oxidative, already-heated nature.
Tinta Negra is the most widely planted grape and forms the base of most everyday Madeira, while the four "noble" varieties are reserved for the finest, longest-aged wines.
The heating process originated from the historical observation that wine shipped through tropical heat on long sea voyages improved rather than spoiled.

regions.name: Bairrada
regions.summary: Bairrada is a DOC on Portugal's Atlantic coast, historically defined by the tannic, high-acid Baga grape and by a long tradition of sparkling wine production. Its cool, maritime climate and clay-heavy soils give the region a distinct identity among Portugal's coastal appellations.
regions.climate: Cool, maritime Atlantic climate with high humidity and significant rainfall, which can create disease pressure, especially given Baga's thin, late-ripening character. The moderate temperatures favor high natural acidity in both grapes and finished wines.
regions.soils: Clay-rich soils ("bairro" meaning clay, the likely source of the region's name) predominate, retaining moisture that helps the late-ripening Baga reach maturity, though they can also contribute to rot risk in wet vintages.
regions.classification: DOC Bairrada regulations have historically centered on Baga as the defining red variety for quality reds, while permitting Touriga Nacional and other varieties as blending partners; a separate long-standing tradition covers traditional-method sparkling wine (espumante) production.
regions.styles: Traditional reds from Baga are notably tannic and high in acid, requiring time or specific techniques (such as destemming) to soften into elegant, age-worthy wines with red fruit and earthy, savory notes; modern producers increasingly favor gentler extraction for more approachable styles. Bairrada is also one of Portugal's most important regions for traditional-method sparkling wine, and its whites (from Maria Gomes/Fernão Pires and Bical) are fresh and aromatic.
notes: Baga is thick-skinned and late-ripening, traditionally fermented with stems and skins in shallow stone lagares, producing intensely tannic, structured wines.
Bairrada has one of Portugal's longest continuous traditions of sparkling wine production, predating much of the rest of the country.
The clay soils that give the region its name retain water well, an asset in dry years but a liability for rot in wet ones.
Touriga Nacional plays a growing role in modern Bairrada blends, softening Baga's naturally high tannin and acidity.

regions.name: Setúbal
regions.summary: Setúbal is a small DOC on the Setúbal Peninsula south of Lisbon, dedicated to sweet, intensely aromatic fortified wine made from Moscatel. Moscatel de Setúbal is distinguished by an unusual production method involving extended skin maceration after fortification, giving it exceptional aromatic intensity.
regions.climate: Maritime climate with strong Atlantic influence, tempered by the Arrábida mountain range, which shelters vineyards on its limestone slopes while the surrounding ocean moderates summer heat. This combination allows the aromatic Moscatel grape to ripen fully while retaining balancing acidity.
regions.soils: Limestone slopes of the Serra da Arrábida provide the region's best sites, while sandier, clay-influenced soils on the lower-lying peninsula are also planted, generally to less prestigious sites.
regions.classification: DOC Setúbal covers fortified wine made predominantly from Moscatel de Setúbal (Muscat of Alexandria) and the rarer, more prized pink-skinned mutation Moscatel Roxo; wines are typically categorized by age (such as aged or "old"/"very old" designations) reflecting extended cask maturation.
regions.styles: Wines are sweet, richly aromatic and grapey when young, developing notes of orange marmalade, honey, dried fruit and, with extended ageing, rancio and nutty complexity; high acidity keeps the wines balanced despite their sweetness, and they have strong ageing potential in old wood.
notes: Unusually among fortified wines, Moscatel de Setúbal undergoes extended maceration on its skins after fortification, sometimes for several months, to maximize aromatic extraction.
Moscatel Roxo is a rare pink-skinned mutation of Muscat of Alexandria, more limited in plantings and generally considered more prestigious than standard Moscatel de Setúbal.
José Maria da Fonseca is historically one of the most important producers associated with the style.
The neighboring Palmela DOC, on the same peninsula, is known instead for dry red wines from the Castelão grape.

regions.name: Jura
regions.summary: A small, cool-climate region in eastern France near the Swiss border, Jura is celebrated for two singular oxidative styles: nutty, sherry-like Vin Jaune and raisiny, sweet Vin de Paille. Its isolation preserved a set of indigenous grapes found almost nowhere else, making it a magnet for sommeliers and natural-wine enthusiasts.
regions.climate: Jura has a cool, semi-continental climate moderated by its position in the foothills of the Jura mountains, with cold winters and warm but short summers. Vineyards sit on east-facing slopes at moderate elevation to maximize sun exposure and drainage. Morning mists off the nearby rivers and forests promote noble rot for Vin de Paille-style drying, while overall coolness preserves the high acidity essential to the region's whites.
regions.soils: Grey and blue marls (marne) dominate, particularly around Château-Chalon, providing water retention and minerality that suit Savagnin. Limestone outcrops and scree appear on higher slopes, favoring Chardonnay and red varieties, while clay-limestone mixes support Poulsard and Trousseau.
regions.classification: Jura wines fall under a handful of AOCs: Arbois (the largest and most varied), Côtes du Jura (broad regional appellation), L'Étoile (whites and Vin Jaune only), and Château-Chalon (exclusively Vin Jaune from Savagnin). Vin Jaune must be aged a minimum of six years and three months in barrel under a flor-like veil (sous voile) without topping up, and is bottled in the distinctive 620ml clavelin.

subRegions.name: Château-Chalon
subRegions.notes: Prestigious appellation producing only Vin Jaune from Savagnin.

subRegions.name: Arbois
subRegions.notes: Largest and most stylistically diverse Jura appellation, home to all wine types including Vin de Paille.

subRegions.name: Côtes du Jura
subRegions.notes: Broad regional appellation covering the length of the vineyard area.

subRegions.name: L'Étoile
subRegions.notes: Small zone known for whites and Vin Jaune from limestone-rich soils.

regions.styles: Signature Vin Jaune is deep gold, intensely nutty and oxidative with flavors of walnut, curry spice, and dried fruit, and can age for decades. Vin de Paille is a rich, sweet dessert wine made from grapes dried on straw mats. Non-oxidative whites from Chardonnay and Savagnin are fresh and mineral, while reds and rosés from Poulsard and Trousseau are typically pale, light-bodied, and floral; Crémant du Jura provides a fresher sparkling counterpoint.
notes: Vin Jaune develops under a film of flor-like yeast (voile) similar to Sherry, but without fortification.
The clavelin, a squat 620ml bottle, is unique to Vin Jaune and reflects the volume remaining after years of evaporative aging (the 'angels' share').
Poulsard (Ploussard) has such thin, lightly pigmented skins that its wines are often nearly rosé in color.
Jura's isolation kept indigenous varieties like Savagnin and Trousseau from being replaced by international grapes.
The region has become a leading center of France's natural wine movement.

regions.name: Savoie
regions.summary: Tucked into the French Alps near the Swiss border, Savoie produces predominantly light, crisp, high-altitude whites from little-known indigenous grapes like Jacquère and Altesse. It is a small but distinctive region historically tied to the ski resort trade.
regions.climate: Savoie has a cool alpine climate shaped by high elevation, steep valley slopes, and proximity to lakes and rivers that moderate temperature. Vineyards are planted on well-exposed south-facing slopes to capture maximum sunshine during the short growing season, while mountain air preserves freshness and acidity. Frost and hail are ever-present risks given the terrain.
regions.soils: Soils are largely glacial in origin, consisting of moraine deposits, scree, and alluvial fans mixed with limestone, giving good drainage on the steep slopes. Limestone-rich sites, as at the Roussette de Savoie crus, contribute to more structured, ageworthy whites.
regions.classification: The regional AOC Savoie (Vin de Savoie) allows the appellation name to be followed by one of around fifteen recognized cru or village names (e.g., Apremont, Abymes, Chignin) when stricter local rules are met. AOC Roussette de Savoie is reserved for Altesse-based whites, with four crus permitted to add their name, and AOC Seyssel covers both still and sparkling wines from a specific zone.

subRegions.name: Apremont
subRegions.notes: Well-known cru for light, floral Jacquère whites from scree-derived soils.

subRegions.name: Abymes
subRegions.notes: Neighboring cru to Apremont, similarly known for fresh Jacquère.

subRegions.name: Chignin-Bergeron
subRegions.notes: Produces richer, more aromatic whites from Roussanne (locally called Bergeron).

subRegions.name: Roussette de Savoie crus
subRegions.notes: Marestel, Monterminod, Frangy and Monthoux are named crus for Altesse-based whites.

regions.styles: Most Savoie wines are light-bodied, high-acid, delicately aromatic whites, often with a faint natural spritz, made for early drinking alongside alpine cuisine like fondue and raclette. Chignin-Bergeron offers a richer, more perfumed style from Roussanne. Reds and rosés from Mondeuse and Gamay are light, peppery, and fresh, and small amounts of traditional-method sparkling wine are also produced.
notes: Jacquère is the most widely planted grape and is almost exclusively found in Savoie.
Mondeuse produces deeply colored, peppery reds and is genetically linked to several other French varieties.
Much of Savoie's production is consumed locally by tourists in nearby ski resorts.
Altesse is also known locally as Roussette and is thought to have originated near Cyprus, though this is debated.
The region's steep, small parcels make mechanization difficult, keeping much of the harvest manual.

regions.name: South West France
regions.summary: A patchwork of appellations inland and south of Bordeaux, South West France is best known for two robust, tannic reds: Cahors' dark 'black wine' built on Malbec, and Madiran's powerful Tannat-based wines. The area also produces distinctive sweet and dry whites from Petit and Gros Manseng.
regions.climate: The region has a warmer, more continental climate than Bordeaux, as Atlantic maritime influence diminishes further inland and southward toward the Pyrenean foothills. Cahors sits along the Lot river valley with a mix of river-moderated and drier plateau sites, while Madiran benefits from the Pyrenees' rain shadow and autumn winds that aid ripening. Hail and spring frost are notable risks across the area.
regions.soils: In Cahors, the best sites lie on limestone causse plateaus and ancient gravel terraces along the Lot river, giving structure and concentration to Malbec. Madiran's soils are a mix of clay-limestone and gravelly terraces, which help temper Tannat's naturally high tannin.
regions.classification: Cahors AOC requires a minimum of 70% Malbec (locally called Côt or Auxerrois), blended with Merlot and/or Tannat. Madiran AOC requires a minimum proportion of Tannat blended with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, and/or Fer Servadou. Neighboring Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh AOC covers both dry and late-harvest sweet whites from Manseng and other varieties within the same zone as Madiran, and Jurançon AOC further south is dedicated to Manseng-based dry and sweet whites.

subRegions.name: Cahors
subRegions.notes: Historic 'black wine' region on the Lot river, dominated by Malbec.

subRegions.name: Madiran
subRegions.notes: Powerful, tannic reds built on Tannat, softened via micro-oxygenation, a technique pioneered here.

subRegions.name: Jurançon
subRegions.notes: Produces both dry and richly sweet Manseng-based whites near the Pyrenees.

subRegions.name: Gaillac
subRegions.notes: Diverse appellation making reds, whites, and sparkling wines from local and international varieties.

regions.styles: Cahors reds are deeply colored, full-bodied, and structured, with dark fruit, earth, and firm tannins that soften with age, historically earning the nickname 'black wine.' Madiran reds are similarly powerful and tannic, built for aging, though modern winemaking has softened their once-rustic edge. Jurançon and Pacherenc whites range from crisp and dry to intensely sweet, showing honeyed, tropical, and citrus notes from late-harvested Manseng grapes.
notes: Micro-oxygenation, now used worldwide to soften tannins, was developed in Madiran to tame Tannat.
Cahors is considered Malbec's ancestral home, predating its rise to fame in Argentina.
Jurançon's sweet wines are made from late-harvested Petit Manseng, a thick-skinned grape resistant to rot.
Cahors' 'black wine' nickname dates back centuries and reflects the wine's historically intense color and structure.
The South West is one of France's most varietally diverse regions, home to numerous grapes found almost nowhere else.

regions.name: Corsica
regions.summary: A mountainous Mediterranean island with strong Italian historical ties, Corsica grows largely indigenous varieties, especially Nielluccio (a Sangiovese clone) and Sciacarello for reds and rosés, and Vermentino for aromatic whites. Rosé is a particularly important category on the island.
regions.climate: Corsica has a warm Mediterranean climate softened by altitude and near-constant sea breezes, with vineyards often planted on granite hillsides for cooling and drainage. Strong winds, including influence from the mistral, help keep vineyards dry and disease pressure low despite high summer heat. Coastal sites benefit from maritime moderation while inland and higher-elevation vineyards retain more freshness.
regions.soils: Granite predominates in the west and south, giving perfumed, elegant wines, while schist and limestone are more common in the north around Cap Corse and Patrimonio, adding structure and minerality.
regions.classification: Corsica's main appellation is AOC Corse (or Vin de Corse), which can be followed by a specific sub-zone name such as Calvi or Figari. Two prestigious standalone appellations, Patrimonio and Ajaccio, have their own defined boundaries and rules. Muscat du Cap Corse AOC is reserved for a sweet fortified Vin Doux Naturel made from Muscat.

subRegions.name: Patrimonio
subRegions.notes: Considered Corsica's finest appellation, known for structured Nielluccio-based reds on limestone-clay soils.

subRegions.name: Ajaccio
subRegions.notes: Centered on Sciacarello, giving perfumed, spicy, medium-bodied reds and rosés on granite.

subRegions.name: Cap Corse
subRegions.notes: Northern peninsula known for Muscat du Cap Attributed VDN and coastal whites.

subRegions.name: Calvi
subRegions.notes: Sub-zone in the northwest producing fresh whites, reds, and rosés.

regions.styles: Whites from Vermentino are fresh, aromatic, and citrusy with a saline edge from coastal influence. Rosés, a major category, are typically pale, dry, and fragrant. Reds range from the lighter, herbal, spicy wines of Sciacarello to the firmer, more tannic, cherry-fruited wines of Nielluccio, often carrying a wild, herbal 'maquis' scrubland character. Muscat du Cap Corse is a lusciously sweet, aromatic fortified wine.
notes: Nielluccio is genetically identical or very closely related to Sangiovese, reflecting centuries of Genoese/Tuscan influence.
The scrubland vegetation known as 'maquis' is said to lend a distinctive herbal aroma to Corsican wines.
Rosé accounts for a large share of Corsica's total production, more than in many mainland French regions.
Corsica has a long history of Greek and Italian settlement that shaped its unique grape varieties.
Muscat du Cap Corse is one of France's lesser-known Vins Doux Naturels.

regions.name: Nahe
regions.summary: A relatively small German wine region along the Nahe river, a tributary of the Rhine, Nahe is prized among Riesling specialists for its unusually varied geology, which produces an exceptionally wide stylistic range within a compact area. Long overshadowed by its larger neighbors, it has increasingly gained recognition for quality.
regions.climate: The Nahe enjoys a mild, sheltered continental climate, protected from cold winds by the Hunsrück hills to the north and warmed by the river valley. Numerous side valleys create a mosaic of mesoclimates, and southern and southwestern exposures allow good ripening despite the region's northern latitude. This climatic patchwork, combined with its geological diversity, gives the wines notable site-to-site variation.
regions.soils: Nahe is often called a 'geological garden' for its unusual diversity within a small area, including volcanic porphyry, slate, sandstone, quartzite, and loess, sometimes changing within a single vineyard. This variety directly shapes the differing weight and mineral character of wines from neighboring sites.
regions.classification: Nahe follows the German Prädikatswein system (Kabinett through Trockenbeerenauslese) based on grape ripeness at harvest, alongside dry (trocken) and off-dry (halbtrocken) Qualitätswein. Top estates belonging to the VDP growers' association classify their best vineyard sites as Erste Lage and Grosse Lage, with Grosses Gewächs denoting dry wines from the highest-rated sites.

subRegions.name: Schlossböckelheim
subRegions.notes: Home to the renowned Kupfergrube vineyard on volcanic and porphyry soils.

subRegions.name: Niederhausen
subRegions.notes: Includes the celebrated Hermannshöhle Grosse Lage, one of the Nahe's most prestigious sites.

subRegions.name: Bad Kreuznach
subRegions.notes: Larger town area with a range of vineyard soils producing elegant Rieslings.

subRegions.name: Traisen
subRegions.notes: Small but highly regarded area including the steep Bastei vineyard.

regions.styles: Nahe Riesling spans the full spectrum from bone-dry and mineral to lusciously sweet late-harvest styles, generally combining the elegance of the Mosel with more body and ripeness akin to the Rheingau. Wines are prized for their aromatic purity and the way soil differences express themselves clearly from vineyard to vineyard. Other varieties like Weissburgunder and Silvaner produce fuller-bodied dry whites.
notes: The Nahe's geological diversity, spanning volcanic, slate, and sandstone soils, is unusually concentrated for such a small region.
Hermannshöhle in Niederhausen is considered one of Germany's greatest Grosse Lage vineyards.
The region was historically undervalued relative to the Mosel and Rheingau despite comparable quality potential.
The Nahe river joins the Rhine at Bingen, marking the region's northern edge.
Production is relatively small, keeping many top Nahe wines less internationally known than their quality would suggest.

regions.name: Rheinhessen
regions.summary: Germany's largest wine region by area, Rheinhessen was long associated with mass-market Liebfraumilch but has undergone a dramatic quality revival led by a new generation of winemakers, particularly around the steep Roter Hang slope and the Rheinterrasse villages.
regions.climate: Rheinhessen has a warm, dry climate, sitting in the rain shadow of the Hunsrück and Taunus hills, making it one of Germany's driest wine regions. The Rhine river moderates temperatures along its banks, particularly in the Rheinterrasse villages, while the interior's rolling hills offer varied exposures. Overall warmth and low rainfall allow reliable ripening across a broad range of grape varieties.
regions.soils: Loess and loam cover much of the rolling landscape, supporting high-yielding, fruit-forward wines, while the famous Roter Hang ('red slope') features red sandstone and clay that yield more structured, mineral Riesling. Limestone appears in parts of the Wonnegau district, favoring Silvaner and Pinot varieties.
regions.classification: Rheinhessen wines range from simple Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein (including much of the historic Liebfraumilch production) to increasingly serious dry wines. VDP member estates classify top sites as Erste Lage and Grosse Lage, with dry Grosses Gewächs wines from the best vineyards, particularly along the Roter Hang, now recognized among Germany's finest.

subRegions.name: Rheinterrasse
subRegions.notes: Prestigious strip along the Rhine including Nierstein and Nackenheim, home to the Roter Hang.

subRegions.name: Roter Hang
subRegions.notes: Steep red sandstone slope renowned for structured, age-worthy dry Riesling.

subRegions.name: Wonnegau
subRegions.notes: Southern district with limestone soils increasingly known for quality Silvaner and Pinot Noir.

regions.styles: Historic Rheinhessen wines were simple, semi-sweet, and inexpensive, typified by Liebfraumilch, but the modern region produces a growing share of dry, mineral, ageworthy Riesling from top sites, especially the Roter Hang. Silvaner and Pinot varieties are increasingly used for fuller-bodied, food-friendly dry whites, and Spätburgunder reds have improved markedly in quality.
notes: Liebfraumilch, the sweetish blended wine that shaped (and damaged) Germany's global reputation, originated in Rheinhessen.
The Roter Hang gets its name and reddish color from iron-rich sandstone and clay soils.
Rheinhessen is Germany's largest wine-growing area by planted hectares.
A younger generation of growers, sometimes called the 'Message in a Bottle' group, has driven the region's dry-wine quality revolution since the 2000s.
Nierstein and Nackenheim on the Rheinterrasse are considered the region's most prestigious villages.

regions.name: Baden
regions.summary: Stretching nearly 400 kilometers along the Rhine opposite Alsace, Baden is Germany's southernmost and warmest major wine region, known especially for dry, full-bodied Pinot family wines, above all Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir).
regions.climate: Baden has the warmest overall climate of Germany's wine regions, benefiting from a southerly latitude and, in areas like the Kaiserstuhl, near-Mediterranean warmth sheltered by the Black Forest and Vosges mountains. This warmth allows red varieties, particularly Pinot Noir, to ripen more fully and consistently than elsewhere in Germany. The region's long, narrow shape means considerable variation in mesoclimate from north to south.
regions.soils: The extinct volcanic Kaiserstuhl features dark volcanic soils and deep loess, retaining heat and supporting rich, structured wines. Limestone and loess are common elsewhere in the region, particularly in the Markgräflerland, favoring lighter, fresher styles such as Gutedel.
regions.classification: Baden follows the German Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein system but is overwhelmingly a dry (trocken) wine region in practice. VDP member estates classify top vineyards as Erste Lage and Grosse Lage, with Grosses Gewächs denoting the finest dry wines, especially Spätburgunder from Kaiserstuhl and Ortenau.

subRegions.name: Kaiserstuhl
subRegions.notes: Extinct volcano with warm volcanic soils, Baden's most celebrated area for Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder.

subRegions.name: Ortenau
subRegions.notes: Known for granite-influenced Spätburgunder and Riesling near Baden-Baden.

subRegions.name: Markgräflerland
subRegions.notes: Southernmost district famous for light, easy-drinking Gutedel.

subRegions.name: Kraichgau
subRegions.notes: Northern district with varied soils producing a broad range of styles.

regions.styles: Baden is best known for full-bodied, dry, structured Spätburgunder among Germany's most serious red wines, alongside rich dry Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder. Gutedel from the Markgräflerland offers light, neutral, easy-drinking whites, while the overall regional style favors dry, food-friendly wines over the sweeter Prädikat styles common elsewhere in Germany.
notes: Baden is the warmest of Germany's thirteen wine regions, enabling reliable red-wine ripening.
The Kaiserstuhl's volcanic soils and heat-retentive character make it Germany's premier zone for serious Spätburgunder.
Gutedel (Chasselas) is a Markgräflerland specialty rarely seen elsewhere in Germany.
Much of Baden's production historically ran through large, quality-focused cooperatives (Winzergenossenschaften).
Baden's roughly 400km north-south span makes it one of the most climatically stretched wine regions in Europe.

regions.name: Franken
regions.summary: Centered on the Main river in northern Bavaria, Franken is known for dry, earthy Silvaner considered by many the grape's finest expression worldwide, traditionally bottled in the distinctive squat Bocksbeutel flask.
regions.climate: Franken has a more continental, marginal climate than most other German wine regions, with colder winters and greater frost risk, situated further from moderating maritime or river-delta influences. The Main river and its tributary valleys provide some mesoclimatic moderation and reflect heat onto south-facing slopes. This more extreme climate makes ripening less reliable, favoring hardier varieties and adding to the wines' characteristic firm, austere structure.
regions.soils: Shell-limestone (Muschelkalk) dominates around Würzburg, giving racy, mineral wines, while red sandstone (Buntsandstein) appears further east and loess is found in flatter areas, together shaping Franken's distinctively earthy, mineral wine character.
regions.classification: Franken follows the standard German Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein system but produces predominantly dry (trocken) wines. VDP estates classify top sites as Erste Lage and Grosse Lage, and traditional Franken wine, especially from the best sites, is sold in the protected Bocksbeutel, a flattened, rounded bottle unique to the region (and a few neighboring areas).

subRegions.name: Maindreieck
subRegions.notes: Central district around Würzburg, home to the famous Stein vineyard and the bulk of top estates.

subRegions.name: Mainviereck
subRegions.notes: Western district with sandstone soils near the Spessart forest.

subRegions.name: Steigerwald
subRegions.notes: Eastern district known for gypsum-keuper soils and structured Silvaner.

regions.styles: Franken wines are predominantly dry, full-bodied, and earthy, with Silvaner showing a distinctive combination of ripe stone fruit, herbal notes, and firm mineral structure. Riesling and Müller-Thurgau are also grown but play a smaller role than in other German regions, and sweet Prädikat styles are comparatively rare here.
notes: The Bocksbeutel, a flattened round bottle, is legally protected and closely associated with Franken (also used in a few nearby areas of Baden).
Franken's Silvaner is widely regarded as the grape's most serious and ageworthy expression globally.
The Würzburger Stein vineyard is one of Germany's most historically famous single sites.
Franken's continental climate makes it one of Germany's more frost-prone and marginal wine regions.
Unlike much of Germany, Franken wines are overwhelmingly dry rather than off-dry or sweet.

regions.name: Kamptal & Kremstal
regions.summary: Neighboring regions along the Danube and its Kamp tributary in Lower Austria, Kamptal and Kremstal sit alongside the Wachau at the heart of Austria's premium dry white wine production, built primarily on Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.
regions.climate: Both regions have a continental climate warmed by hot Pannonian air from the east and cooled by forested hills and the Danube and Kamp rivers, creating a wide diurnal temperature range that preserves acidity while allowing full ripeness. Elevated terraced vineyards on steep slopes benefit from strong sun exposure, while river proximity moderates extremes. This interplay of warmth and cooling influence produces wines with both ripeness and freshness.
regions.soils: Loess predominates on lower and mid-slope sites, giving fuller, spicier wines, while higher terraces feature primary rock such as gneiss and granite, and Kremstal's Kremser Sandstein (a local sandstone) contributes distinctive minerality to its wines.
regions.classification: Both regions use Austria's DAC (Districtus Austriae Controllatus) system, with Kamptal DAC and Kremstal DAC each reserved for typical dry, varietal wines, chiefly Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, at Klassik and Reserve quality tiers reflecting increasing ripeness and concentration. Wines outside DAC rules are labeled simply as Niederösterreich or Landwein.

subRegions.name: Heiligenstein (Kamptal)
subRegions.notes: Renowned, geologically unusual site on ancient sandstone and volcanic soil, prized for powerful Riesling.

subRegions.name: Langenlois
subRegions.notes: Largest wine town in Kamptal and a hub for leading producers.

subRegions.name: Kremser Sandstein / Wachtberg (Kremstal)
subRegions.notes: Distinctive sandstone terrain giving Kremstal wines their mineral character.

regions.styles: Grüner Veltliner from both regions is dry, full-bodied, and peppery, with white pepper, citrus, and stone fruit notes, ranging from everyday Klassik wines to concentrated, ageworthy Reserve bottlings. Riesling is racy, mineral, and precise, often more powerful than Wachau's lighter Federspiel-style wines. Increasing amounts of quality Pinot Noir and Zweigelt reds are also produced.
notes: Kamptal and Kremstal DAC were both established in 2007, formalizing dry regional wine styles.
The Heiligenstein vineyard in Kamptal has unusual desert-like sandstone and volcanic soils found almost nowhere else in Austria.
Unlike the Wachau's Steinfeder/Federspiel/Smaragd system, Kamptal and Kremstal use the DAC Klassik/Reserve tiers.
Langenlois, in Kamptal, is considered Austria's largest wine-growing town.
Both regions border the world-famous Wachau but are generally less expensive despite comparable quality.

regions.name: Styria (Steiermark)
regions.summary: Austria's southernmost wine region, bordering Slovenia, Styria is known for crisp, aromatic dry whites, especially Sauvignon Blanc, and for Schilcher, a tart, pale rosé made uniquely from the local Blauer Wildbacher grape.
regions.climate: Styria has a cooler, wetter, more Alpine- and Mediterranean-influenced climate than eastern Austria, with hilly terrain and higher rainfall creating conditions closer to those of nearby Slovenia. Steep, often dramatically terraced south-facing slopes are essential for adequate ripening and drainage. The cooler overall climate favors aromatic freshness and high acidity over power.
regions.soils: Volcanic basalt soils are prominent in Vulkanland Steiermark, adding richness and minerality, while Südsteiermark features marl and sandstone that contribute to its wines' elegance and precision.
regions.classification: Styria is divided into three DAC zones: Südsteiermark, Vulkanland Steiermark, and Weststeiermark, each defining its own typical varietal wines under the DAC system, generally dry and site-expressive. Weststeiermark DAC is unique in centering on Schilcher rosé from Blauer Wildbacher.

subRegions.name: Südsteiermark
subRegions.notes: Home to Austria's steepest vineyards, celebrated for elegant Sauvignon Blanc and Morillon.

subRegions.name: Vulkanland Steiermark
subRegions.notes: Volcanic-soil district known for richer whites and Traminer.

subRegions.name: Weststeiermark
subRegions.notes: Small western district uniquely dedicated to Schilcher rosé.

regions.styles: Styrian whites are crisp, dry, and intensely aromatic, with Sauvignon Blanc showing pronounced herbaceous and citrus character and minimal residual sugar in keeping with regional tradition. Morillon (Chardonnay) and Welschriesling add texture and citrus-driven freshness respectively, while Schilcher is a tart, high-acid, pale pink wine with distinctive berry and rhubarb notes, unlike any other Austrian rosé style.
notes: Südsteiermark contains some of Austria's steepest vineyard slopes, often exceeding 50% gradient.
Blauer Wildbacher, used almost exclusively for Schilcher, is native to and found almost only in Weststeiermark.
Styria's three DAC zones (Südsteiermark, Vulkanland Steiermark, Weststeiermark) were formalized in 2016 and 2018.
Styrian Sauvignon Blanc is widely regarded as Austria's finest expression of the variety.
Styria has a notably higher rainfall and cooler, greener landscape than Austria's other wine regions, closer in feel to Slovenia.

regions.name: Texas Hill Country
regions.summary: Texas Hill Country, centered on Fredericksburg west of Austin, is the geographic and cultural heart of the Texas wine industry and one of the largest AVAs in the US by area. It has become known for warm-climate Mediterranean and Iberian varieties, particularly Tempranillo and Rhône blends, that suit its hot, variable conditions.
regions.climate: The climate is hot and semi-arid, tempered somewhat by elevation on the Edwards Plateau (roughly 1,200-1,800 feet). Spring frost is the region's single biggest viticultural hazard, as late freezes regularly damage buds after an early budbreak, and hail is also a recurring threat. Rainfall is limited and unevenly distributed, and the long, hot growing season favors heat-loving Spanish and Rhône varieties over delicate cool-climate grapes. Because of frost losses in the Hill Country itself, much fruit used by wineries here is trucked in from the higher, more frost-reliable Texas High Plains AVA.
regions.soils: Soils are dominated by limestone and caliche over granite and clay in places, generally shallow and well-drained. The limestone base echoes soils found in parts of Spain and the southern Rhône, reinforcing the suitability of Tempranillo and GSM-style blends.
regions.classification: Texas Hill Country is an AVA (established 1991) covering a vast, sparsely-planted area across multiple counties; a nested sub-AVA, Bell Mountain, sits within it. Labeling follows standard US AVA rules (minimum 85% of grapes from the named area), but because Pierce's disease and spring frost limit reliable local supply, many Hill Country wineries legally source significant fruit from the High Plains AVA further north and label accordingly.

subRegions.name: Fredericksburg
subRegions.notes: The tourism and winery hub of the region, with the highest concentration of tasting rooms.

subRegions.name: Bell Mountain AVA
subRegions.notes: A small nested AVA within Texas Hill Country, one of the first in Texas to be recognized.

regions.styles: Rhône and Iberian-inspired blends dominate: medium-to-full-bodied reds with ripe dark fruit, warm spice, and moderate tannins, generally made for early-to-medium term drinking rather than long aging. Viognier and other aromatic whites are full-bodied and floral, and rosé is widely produced and popular with the region's large wine-tourism audience.
notes: Texas Hill Country AVA is one of the largest AVAs in the US by land area, though only a small fraction is actually planted to vine.
Spring frost and Pierce's disease are the two biggest threats, pushing many wineries to source fruit from the Texas High Plains AVA near Lubbock.
Fredericksburg has become a major wine-tourism destination, drawing comparisons to Napa in visitor volume relative to production.
The industry has grown rapidly since the 2000s, though Texas wine remains a small fraction of total US production.

regions.name: Virginia
regions.summary: Virginia is a historic East Coast wine region — Thomas Jefferson famously failed to grow European vinifera at Monticello — now recognized for elegant, food-friendly wines built around Viognier, its signature white grape, and Bordeaux-style reds led by Cabernet Franc. Humid, variable weather makes it a genuinely challenging place to grow grapes well.
regions.climate: Virginia has a humid subtropical-to-continental climate with high humidity and rainfall, especially around harvest, that brings significant fungal disease pressure and demands careful canopy management. The Blue Ridge Mountains and proximity to the Atlantic and Chesapeake Bay moderate temperatures, and hillside sites with good air drainage are favored to reduce frost and humidity risk. Late-season hurricanes and tropical storms pose an additional harvest-time threat.
regions.soils: Soils vary considerably across the state, from clay loams to granite- and schist-derived soils in the Blue Ridge foothills and Piedmont. Well-drained hillside and slope sites are strongly preferred over low-lying ground to help manage the region's abundant rainfall.
regions.classification: Virginia wines fall under the standard US AVA system, with several AVAs recognized across the state, including Monticello and Middleburg in the Piedmont/Blue Ridge foothills. There is no additional state quality hierarchy; producers may also use the broader 'Virginia' appellation, which requires a minimum percentage of in-state fruit.

subRegions.name: Monticello AVA
subRegions.notes: Centered on Charlottesville and Jefferson's historic Monticello estate; strong for Cabernet Franc and Viognier.

subRegions.name: Middleburg Virginia AVA
subRegions.notes: A cooler, hillier Piedmont zone in Loudoun County, one of the fastest-growing wine districts in the state.

subRegions.name: Shenandoah Valley AVA (Virginia)
subRegions.notes: A cooler inland valley distinct from California's Shenandoah Valley, with a growing number of vineyards.

subRegions.name: Eastern Shore AVA
subRegions.notes: A small maritime-influenced AVA on the Chesapeake Bay peninsula.

regions.styles: Cabernet Franc is widely regarded as Virginia's best red variety, typically medium-bodied with red fruit, herbal lift, and moderate tannins; it anchors many Bordeaux-style blends. Viognier, the state's signature white, is aromatic and full-bodied with stone-fruit character. Petit Manseng, valued for its thick skin and acid retention in humid conditions, is increasingly used for both dry and off-dry/late-harvest styles. Overall, wines favor moderate alcohol and freshness over sheer ripeness.
notes: Thomas Jefferson attempted repeatedly and unsuccessfully to grow European vinifera at Monticello in the late 18th century, a story central to Virginia wine lore.
Viognier is often called Virginia's signature or 'state' grape, and the state hosts significant plantings relative to its global scarcity.
Humidity and rain around harvest are the defining viticultural challenge, requiring meticulous canopy and disease management.
The modern Virginia wine industry largely dates from the 1970s-80s and has grown into one of the more dynamic East Coast wine regions.

regions.name: Lodi
regions.summary: Lodi, in California's Central Valley north of Stockton, is one of the state's largest and most historic wine regions, long a source of bulk and blending wine but increasingly celebrated for its old-vine Zinfandel and broad, diverse plantings.
regions.climate: Lodi has a warm Mediterranean climate, but cooling breezes funneled inland from San Francisco Bay through the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta moderate summer heat and preserve acidity, giving the region a meaningful diurnal temperature swing despite its Central Valley location. This combination of warmth and breeze-driven cooling makes it well suited to Zinfandel and Rhône varieties.
regions.soils: Much of Lodi sits on sandy loam alluvial soils, with more clay in some sub-zones. The sandy soils are notably resistant to phylloxera, which is a major reason the region retains some of California's oldest own-rooted vines.
regions.classification: Lodi AVA was established in 1986 and further divided in 2006 into seven nested sub-AVAs reflecting local soil and climate variation. The region also runs Lodi Rules, one of the first third-party-certified sustainable winegrowing programs in the US, widely used as a marketing and quality signal.

subRegions.name: Mokelumne River AVA
subRegions.notes: The historic core of Lodi, with sandy soils and the highest concentration of old-vine Zinfandel.

subRegions.name: Clements Hills AVA
subRegions.notes: Slightly elevated, with more varied soils supporting Cabernet Sauvignon and other varieties.

subRegions.name: Borden Ranch AVA
subRegions.notes: Warmer, granitic-soil sub-zone in the northeast of the appellation.

subRegions.name: Sloughhouse AVA
subRegions.notes: One of the warmest and highest-elevation sub-AVAs, planted to a range of red varieties.

regions.styles: Zinfandel is Lodi's calling card: full-bodied, jammy, and dark-fruited, often with relatively high alcohol, and old-vine bottlings can show real depth and complexity. The region also produces large volumes of value-priced varietal wine, alongside a growing number of boutique, quality-focused producers making robust, fruit-forward Rhône-style blends.
notes: Lodi is home to some of the oldest continuously producing, own-rooted Zinfandel vines in the US, some over a century old.
Sandy soils across much of the region spared many old vineyards from the phylloxera epidemic that devastated other California regions.
Historically Lodi supplied enormous volumes of bulk wine and grape concentrate to larger California brands.
Lodi Rules, launched in the region, was one of the first third-party sustainability certification programs in American wine.

regions.name: Sierra Foothills
regions.summary: The Sierra Foothills, in the Sierra Nevada east of Sacramento, is a historic Gold Rush-era wine region, often called Gold Country, known for old-vine Zinfandel planted by 19th-century Italian immigrant miners and for its warm, elevated, granite-soil sites well suited to Rhône and Italian varieties.
regions.climate: The Mediterranean climate is moderated by elevation, with vineyards ranging from roughly 500 to over 3,000 feet, producing significant diurnal temperature swings that help retain acidity despite warm summer days. Rainfall is low and largely confined to winter, and higher-elevation sites stay noticeably cooler than the Central Valley floor below.
regions.soils: Decomposed granite and volcanic soils predominate, generally low in fertility and well-drained, which stresses vines and helps concentrate fruit. Historic gold-mining activity has also left tailings and disturbed ground in some vineyard areas.
regions.classification: The broad Sierra Foothills AVA contains several nested sub-AVAs distinguished mainly by elevation and county, including California Shenandoah Valley, Fiddletown, Fair Play, and El Dorado. There is no formal quality-tier system beyond AVA and varietal labeling; the region remains dominated by small, family-owned wineries.

subRegions.name: California Shenandoah Valley AVA (Amador County)
subRegions.notes: The historic heart of Sierra Foothills Zinfandel, distinct from Virginia's Shenandoah Valley.

subRegions.name: Fiddletown AVA
subRegions.notes: A small, high-elevation Amador County zone known for old-vine Zinfandel.

subRegions.name: El Dorado AVA
subRegions.notes: Higher-elevation sub-region producing fresher, more structured wines.

subRegions.name: Fair Play AVA
subRegions.notes: One of the highest-elevation sub-AVAs in the region, favoring cooler-climate expressions.

regions.styles: Zinfandel is typically robust, spicy, and dark-fruited, often with relatively high alcohol, while Barbera and Rhône varieties are increasingly planted to add freshness and balance. Wines across the region tend toward a rustic, full-bodied, food-friendly character rather than polish, reflecting its heritage as a smaller-scale, family-farmed region.
notes: Many of the region's oldest vines were planted by Italian immigrant miners during and after the California Gold Rush of the 1850s.
Amador County's Shenandoah Valley AVA is the historic core of Sierra Foothills Zinfandel and should not be confused with Virginia's Shenandoah Valley.
Elevation, not latitude, is the main moderating factor here, with some vineyards among the highest in California.
Production is small relative to Napa or Sonoma, and the region remains dominated by family-owned, low-volume wineries.

regions.name: Long Island
regions.summary: Long Island, New York, is a young maritime wine region on the eastern forks of Long Island, established in the 1970s and best known for Bordeaux-style reds, particularly Merlot and Cabernet Franc, grown in a climate moderated by surrounding Atlantic waters.
regions.climate: The maritime climate, moderated by the Atlantic Ocean, Long Island Sound, and Peconic Bay, gives a longer growing season and reduced frost risk compared with inland New York. Humidity brings meaningful fungal disease pressure, and the region faces occasional risk from hurricanes and nor'easters around harvest.
regions.soils: Soils are sandy, well-drained loams over glacial outwash gravel, deposited during the last ice age. Good natural drainage suits Bordeaux varieties, which struggle in wetter, heavier ground.
regions.classification: Long Island wines are covered by two federally recognized AVAs, North Fork of Long Island and The Hamptons, Long Island, both nested within the broader Long Island AVA. The region is one of the youngest in the US, with the first vinifera vines planted in 1973.

subRegions.name: North Fork of Long Island AVA
subRegions.notes: Warmer, drier, and home to the great majority of vineyards and wineries; the region's Bordeaux-variety heartland.

subRegions.name: The Hamptons, Long Island AVA
subRegions.notes: Cooler and more maritime South Fork zone, with fewer, smaller vineyards.

regions.styles: Merlot is often considered the flagship variety, producing medium-bodied, softly-tannic reds with red fruit and herbal notes; it frequently anchors Bordeaux-style blends alongside Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon. Whites, especially Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, are crisp and food-friendly, and rosé is widely produced given the region's warm, maritime summers.
notes: The first vinifera vines were planted only in 1973 by Alex and Louisa Hargrave, making Long Island one of the youngest fine-wine regions in the US.
The maritime climate has drawn frequent comparisons to Bordeaux, particularly for its suitability to Merlot and Cabernet Franc.
Proximity to New York City drives significant wine tourism and supports premium pricing despite the region's small size.
Hurricanes and nor'easters at harvest time are a recurring and serious risk for growers.

regions.name: Elqui Valley
regions.summary: Elqui Valley, in Chile's arid Norte Chico region on the edge of the Atacama Desert, is one of the world's most extreme and northerly fine-wine valleys. Long famous as Chile's premier Pisco-producing valley, it has more recently gained recognition for intensely flavored, high-elevation Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.climate: The climate is desert-like with extremely high sunlight and UV intensity, but coastal sites are cooled by fog and breezes off the cold Humboldt Current, while inland sites toward the Andes benefit from high elevation and wide diurnal temperature swings. Rainfall is minimal, so irrigation drawing on Andean snowmelt is essential for viticulture.
regions.soils: Vineyards occupy a narrow river valley with alluvial soils near the river and decomposed granite on surrounding hillsides, generally poor and well-drained, encouraging low yields and concentrated fruit.
regions.classification: Elqui falls under Chile's Denominación de Origen (DO) system as part of the Coquimbo region; wines labeled Elqui Valley must meet the national minimum of 75% of grapes from the named area. Much of the valley's grape production still goes toward Pisco, a distilled grape spirit, rather than table wine.

subRegions.name: Coastal Elqui
subRegions.notes: Cooler, fog-influenced sites near the Pacific, favored for Sauvignon Blanc.

subRegions.name: Upper/Andean Elqui
subRegions.notes: Higher-elevation inland sites with intense sunlight, producing structured, peppery Syrah.

regions.styles: Syrah from Elqui is notably peppery and dark-fruited with firm structure and fresh acidity, a product of high elevation and wide diurnal swings offsetting the desert heat. Sauvignon Blanc from coastal sites is zesty and mineral. Much of the valley's Moscatel still goes into Pisco rather than still wine.
notes: Elqui is one of the northernmost and most extreme wine-growing valleys in the world, bordering the Atacama Desert.
The valley is internationally famous for Pisco, a grape brandy, arguably even more than for table wine.
Elqui's clear, dark skies (a major astro-tourism draw, with several observatories) reflect the same intense solar exposure that shapes its viticulture.
Irrigation from Andean snowmelt rivers is essential, as natural rainfall is minimal.

regions.name: Limarí Valley
regions.summary: Limarí Valley, just south of Elqui in Chile's Norte Chico, has emerged since the 1990s-2000s as one of the country's premier cool-climate regions, producing mineral, high-acid Chardonnay and increasingly Pinot Noir despite its desert latitude, thanks to persistent coastal fog and unusually limestone-rich soils.
regions.climate: Although technically semi-arid, Limarí's coastal and near-coastal vineyards are strongly cooled by the camanchaca, a dense morning fog driven by the cold Humboldt Current, which typically burns off to sunny, mild afternoons. This gives the region a surprisingly cool mesoclimate for its latitude. Rainfall is very low, and vines rely on irrigation from Andean snowmelt.
regions.soils: Limarí is notable for soils with significant calcium carbonate (limestone-like) content, unusual in Chile, which is credited with contributing fresh acidity and a mineral quality to the region's white wines. Further inland, alluvial terraces predominate.
regions.classification: Limarí is a recognized DO within Chile's Coquimbo region under the national Denominación de Origen system. Producers increasingly emphasize the valley name on labels specifically to signal its cool-climate credentials, distinguishing it from warmer central Chilean regions.

subRegions.name: Coastal Limarí
subRegions.notes: The coolest, most fog-affected sites, planted mainly to Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.

subRegions.name: Interior Limarí
subRegions.notes: Warmer sites further from the coast, more suited to Syrah.

regions.styles: Chardonnay is the region's signature wine: taut, citrus-driven, and mineral, with racy acidity uncommon in Chile. Syrah shows a distinctly cool-climate profile with white pepper and violet notes, differing markedly from the riper Syrah of warmer Chilean valleys. Pinot Noir plantings in the coolest coastal sites are a more recent and promising development.
notes: Limarí's limestone-influenced soils are unusual for Chile and are widely cited as a key reason for the region's mineral character.
The camanchaca coastal fog, not latitude, is the main reason Limarí can ripen fresh, cool-climate varieties despite bordering the Atacama Desert.
Serious investment in fine wine here is relatively recent, dating mainly from the 1990s onward.
The region's Syrah is often cited as stylistically closer to cool-climate Northern Rhône examples than typical New World Syrah.

regions.name: Bío Bío & Itata Valleys
regions.summary: Bío Bío and Itata, in Chile's cooler, wetter south, are the country's oldest wine-growing valleys, planted since Spanish colonial times, and have become central to Chile's old-vine and natural-wine movement thanks to their heritage dry-farmed bush-vine País and Muscat, alongside promising cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
regions.climate: Both valleys sit further south than Chile's central wine regions and have a cooler, wetter, more maritime-influenced climate, with meaningfully higher rainfall than the arid valleys further north. This higher natural rainfall makes dry-farming viable, unlike in Chile's irrigation-dependent central and northern regions, and the cooler growing season supports fresher, lighter wine styles.
regions.soils: Itata in particular has old, ungrafted bush vines planted on granitic and metamorphic soils on unirrigated (secano) hillsides, farmed without modern trellising or irrigation. Bío Bío has broadly similar sandy and granitic soil components, generally poor and well-drained.
regions.classification: Both Itata and Bío Bío are recognized DOs under Chile's national Denominación de Origen system, situated within Chile's southern wine regions. There is growing use of producer associations and heritage/old-vine labeling to highlight the valleys' historic dry-farmed plantings, though this sits alongside, rather than replacing, standard DO and varietal labeling.

subRegions.name: Itata Valley
subRegions.notes: The older of the two, home to Chile's oldest surviving vineyards and dry-farmed bush-vine País and Muscat.

subRegions.name: Bío Bío Valley
subRegions.notes: Cooler and further south, with more recent plantings of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

regions.styles: Traditional País and Muscat, historically made in simple, rustic styles for everyday drinking, are increasingly vinified with more careful, low-intervention winemaking to produce fresher, more precise wines that have become emblematic of Chile's natural-wine scene. Newer plantings of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in Bío Bío show real cool-climate elegance and freshness, distinct from Chile's warmer central regions.
notes: Itata is considered the birthplace of Chilean viticulture, with vines planted by Spanish missionaries as early as the 16th century.
The region holds some of the oldest surviving own-rooted, dry-farmed bush vines in the world, some well over a century old.
Since the 2010s, Itata and Bío Bío have become central to Chile's old-vine and natural/artisanal wine renaissance, reframing grapes once used mainly for cheap bulk wine.
Higher rainfall than central Chile allows genuine dry-farming here, unlike most other Chilean wine regions.

regions.name: San Juan
regions.summary: San Juan, just north of Mendoza, is Argentina's second-largest wine region, a hot, high-altitude desert zone historically associated with bulk wine, spirits, and raisins but increasingly producing full-bodied quality Syrah, Bonarda, and Malbec, especially from its cooler Pedernal Valley.
regions.climate: The climate is hot, dry, and desert-like in the Andean foothills, with extremely low rainfall meaning vines depend entirely on irrigation from Andean rivers. Sunlight and UV intensity are very high, and higher-elevation sites such as Pedernal Valley see a meaningful diurnal temperature swing that moderates the daytime heat and helps preserve freshness.
regions.soils: Soils are alluvial, sandy, and stony, deposited by the San Juan and Jáchal rivers flowing from the Andes. They are generally poor in organic matter and very well-drained, requiring irrigation to support viticulture.
regions.classification: San Juan wines fall under Argentina's Indicación Geográfica (IG) system, with several IGs recognized within the province, including Tulum Valley and Pedernal Valley, reflecting distinct elevations and mesoclimates. There is no formal quality-pyramid beyond geographic indication and varietal/vintage labeling.

subRegions.name: Tulum Valley
subRegions.notes: The largest and historically most important zone, lower and warmer, long associated with bulk wine production.

subRegions.name: Pedernal Valley
subRegions.notes: A higher-elevation zone (over 1,300m) that has emerged since the 2000s as San Juan's leading quality area for Syrah and Malbec.

subRegions.name: Zonda Valley
subRegions.notes: A smaller, distinctive site known for particular wind and altitude effects.

regions.styles: Wines are typically full-bodied, ripe, and high in alcohol, with Syrah and Bonarda showing dark fruit and spice; Malbec from the warmer Tulum floor tends to be riper and fuller than high-altitude Mendoza examples, while Pedernal Valley fruit shows more elegance and structure thanks to its altitude. Alongside premium wine, San Juan remains a major producer of bulk wine, grape concentrate, and raisins.
notes: San Juan is Argentina's second-largest wine-producing province by volume, after Mendoza.
Pedernal Valley has developed rapidly since the 2000s into a recognized high-altitude quality zone for Syrah and Malbec.
The province has historically been more associated with bulk wine, brandy, and raisin production than fine wine, though this is changing.
As in Mendoza, irrigation from Andean snowmelt rivers is essential given the region's extreme aridity.

regions.name: Patagonia (Río Negro)
regions.summary: Río Negro, in Argentine Patagonia, is the country's southernmost major fine-wine region and is prized for elegant, aromatic Pinot Noir and fresher-styled Malbec, made possible by a cool, high-latitude desert climate along the Río Negro river rather than the high altitude that defines Mendoza and Salta.
regions.climate: Río Negro's coolness comes from its high southern latitude rather than elevation, giving it a long, cool ripening season unusual for Argentina. Persistent, strong Patagonian winds are a defining feature, naturally reducing disease pressure but also requiring windbreaks and careful site management. Rainfall is very low, so vines rely on irrigation from the Río Negro and Río Colorado.
