regions.soils: Vineyards sit on alluvial terraces along the river, with a mix of sand, clay, and calcareous pebbly deposits known locally as rodados patagónicos. Soils are generally low in fertility and well-drained.
regions.classification: Wines fall under Argentina's Indicación Geográfica (IG) system, with Río Negro recognized as an IG containing zones such as Alto Valle and Valle Medio. 'Patagonia' functions largely as a promotional geographic term embracing both Río Negro and the neighboring Neuquén province, rather than a strict formal classification tier.

subRegions.name: Alto Valle del Río Negro
subRegions.notes: The historic core of the region around General Roca, with the highest concentration of established vineyards.

subRegions.name: Valle Medio
subRegions.notes: A newer zone further downstream along the Río Negro.

regions.styles: Pinot Noir is the region's most celebrated wine: perfumed and red-fruited with fresh acidity, considered among Argentina's best expressions of the variety. Malbec here is fresher and more restrained and floral than the riper styles typical of Mendoza. Old plantings of Semillón and Torrontés also produce distinctive whites, and overall the region's wines favor freshness and aromatic lift over sheer power.
notes: Río Negro is Argentina's coolest major fine-wine region due to high latitude rather than high altitude, contrasting with Mendoza and Salta.
Near-constant strong winds are a defining viticultural feature, reducing disease pressure but demanding windbreaks and robust trellising.
The region has old vineyard plantings dating to early 20th-century irrigation projects, including the historic Humberto Canale winery founded in 1909.
Río Negro, together with neighboring Neuquén, is increasingly regarded as Argentina's leading zone for cool-climate Pinot Noir.

regions.name: McLaren Vale
regions.summary: McLaren Vale, south of Adelaide in South Australia, is a warm coastal region best known for full-bodied Shiraz and old-vine Grenache, alongside a growing reputation for Mediterranean varieties. It sits among Australia's most historic wine regions and has become a leader in organic and sustainable viticulture.
regions.climate: Mediterranean climate warmed by its inland position but tempered by the cooling influence of the nearby Gulf St Vincent and afternoon sea breezes, giving reliably warm, dry growing seasons with low disease pressure. Rainfall is concentrated in winter, so irrigation supplements many vineyards, and the sea breeze creates useful diurnal variation that helps retain acidity and aroma. Little frost or vintage variation risk makes ripening reliable most years, favouring rich, ripe styles.
regions.soils: The Vale is unusually diverse for its size, with more than 150 recognised soil types ranging from sandy loams over clay to ancient ironstone-rich and calcareous soils. Pockets of deep sand, such as around Blewitt Springs, allowed own-rooted, phylloxera-free old Grenache vines to survive, while heavier clay-based soils elsewhere favour Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.classification: Like all Australian wine regions, McLaren Vale is defined as a Geographical Indication (GI) under the label integrity program, a geographic delimitation with no quality-tier hierarchy; wines labelled with the GI must be at least 85% sourced from within it. Within the region, informal sub-district names such as Blewitt Springs, Seaview and McLaren Flat are used by producers to signal distinctive terroir but carry no legal classification status.

subRegions.name: Blewitt Springs
subRegions.notes: Deep sandy soils that preserved ungrafted, dry-grown old-vine Grenache.

subRegions.name: Seaview
subRegions.notes: Elevated, ironstone-influenced site prized for structured Shiraz.

subRegions.name: McLaren Flat
subRegions.notes: Lower, warmer valley floor known for ripe, full-bodied reds.

regions.styles: The signature style is a rich, generous Shiraz with dark berry fruit, chocolate and mocha notes and soft, ripe tannins, often oak-aged and capable of ageing for a decade or more. Old-vine Grenache ranges from pale, perfumed and juicy to more concentrated, savoury examples, and GSM (Grenache-Shiraz-Mourvèdre) blends are a regional specialty. A newer wave of Mediterranean white varieties like Fiano and Vermentino produces fresh, textural whites suited to the warm climate.
notes: McLaren Vale is a national leader in certified organic and biodynamic viticulture.
Old, ungrafted Grenache bush vines here are among the oldest in the world, some planted before 1900.
The region has notable geological diversity within a small overall area.
GSM blends (Grenache-Shiraz-Mourvèdre) are strongly associated with McLaren Vale producers.

regions.name: Adelaide Hills
regions.summary: Adelaide Hills is a cool-climate region in the Mount Lofty Ranges east of Adelaide, prized for aromatic whites, elegant Pinot Noir and high-quality sparkling wine base. Its altitude sets it apart from the warmer regions surrounding it and it has become a hub for boutique and experimental winemaking.
regions.climate: Elevation of roughly 400-700 metres makes this one of the coolest regions in South Australia despite its northerly latitude, with cool nights, significant diurnal temperature swings and a longer, slower ripening season than the Adelaide Plains below. Rainfall is higher than surrounding lowland regions, and spring frost is a real risk in the higher sub-zones. These conditions favour aromatic, high-acid whites and delicate red styles.
regions.soils: Soils vary across the Hills, including ironstone gravels, sandy loams and pockets of ancient, weathered clay, generally free-draining and of low to moderate fertility. This variability contributes to the range of styles produced, from steely whites on cooler, higher sites to riper reds on lower, warmer slopes.
regions.classification: A South Australian GI region within the larger Mount Lofty Ranges zone, delimited geographically with no internal quality hierarchy. Growers and producers commonly refer to sub-districts such as Piccadilly Valley and Lenswood, which are recognised as registered GIs in their own right and can appear on labels.

subRegions.name: Piccadilly Valley
subRegions.notes: The highest, coolest sub-zone, renowned for Chardonnay and sparkling wine base.

subRegions.name: Lenswood
subRegions.notes: Steep, cool sites known for structured Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir.

subRegions.name: Basket Range
subRegions.notes: A warmer pocket associated with a thriving natural and low-intervention wine scene.

regions.styles: Sauvignon Blanc here is more restrained and textural than Marlborough's pungent style, while Chardonnay is typically taut and citrus-driven with careful oak use. Pinot Noir is light to medium-bodied and perfumed, and the region's cooler pockets supply high-quality base wine for traditional-method sparkling. Warmer sites, particularly around Basket Range, also produce cool-climate Shiraz with peppery, savoury character.
notes: Adelaide Hills was one of Australia's first regions to champion cool-climate viticulture from the 1970s onward.
Its Sauvignon Blanc has been central to several of Australia's best-known white wine brands.
Basket Range has become a well-known centre for natural and minimal-intervention winemaking.
Piccadilly Valley grapes are a key component in premium South Australian sparkling wines.

regions.name: Coonawarra
regions.summary: Coonawarra, in South Australia's Limestone Coast, is famous for its narrow strip of terra rossa soil and for producing some of Australia's most distinguished Cabernet Sauvignon. Its cool, flat terrain and iconic red-over-white soil profile have made it a benchmark region for structured, age-worthy reds.
regions.climate: A cool, maritime-moderated climate driven by proximity to the Southern Ocean, with flat, low-lying terrain and one of the longest, coolest ripening seasons in mainland Australia. The moderating sea influence produces reliable diurnal variation without extreme heat spikes, allowing slow, even ripening that preserves natural acidity and firm tannin structure. Frost is an occasional risk given the flat topography and cool nights.
regions.soils: The defining feature is a narrow band, roughly 15 kilometres long, of terra rossa (red clay-loam) sitting over free-draining limestone bedrock. This combination provides excellent drainage while allowing vine roots access to reliable subsoil moisture, and is widely credited with the distinctive quality of Coonawarra Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.classification: Coonawarra is a South Australian GI, notable for having been the subject of a lengthy 1990s legal dispute over where its boundary should fall, ultimately settled by defining the region tightly around the terra rossa strip rather than the broader district. There is no internal sub-zone classification; the GI boundary itself functions as the quality marker.
regions.styles: Coonawarra Cabernet Sauvignon is the regional benchmark: medium to full-bodied, with blackcurrant fruit, characteristic mint or eucalyptus notes, firm tannins and excellent ageing potential. Shiraz from the region shows similar elegance and structure, and the two varieties are sometimes blended. Whites, mainly Chardonnay, play a minor role compared to the region's reputation for structured reds.
notes: Coonawarra's terra rossa-over-limestone strip was the subject of a formal legal dispute in the 1990s over which land could use the name.
Wynns Coonawarra Estate is one of Australia's most historically significant producers, dating to the 1890s.
The mint/eucalyptus character often noted in Coonawarra Cabernet is associated with cool ripening and surrounding eucalyptus trees.
Coonawarra is sometimes nicknamed Australia's 'other Bordeaux' for its Cabernet focus.

regions.name: Rutherglen
regions.summary: Rutherglen, in north-east Victoria, is Australia's foremost fortified wine region, famous for luscious fortified Muscat and Topaque made using solera-like blending across old oxidative stocks. It also produces powerful dry reds from Durif, a variety rarely found elsewhere in the world.
regions.climate: A warm to hot continental climate with low rainfall, hot dry summers and cold winters, historically well suited to producing very ripe, sometimes semi-raisined fruit for fortification. The heat and dryness limit disease pressure and allow grapes to reach the high sugar levels needed for rich fortified styles, while irrigation supports the vines through dry summers.
regions.soils: Sandy loam and alluvial soils dominate, generally fertile and free-draining, well suited to the vigorous old bush-vine plantings, particularly of Muscat and Muscadelle, that underpin the region's fortified wine tradition.
regions.classification: Rutherglen is a Victorian GI, but it is best known for a unique, style-based classification specific to its fortified wines: Rutherglen Muscat and Topaque are graded into four ascending quality tiers — Rutherglen, Classic, Grand and Rare — reflecting increasing average age, concentration and complexity from long-term barrel maturation and solera-style blending, rather than a fixed vintage or vineyard hierarchy.
regions.styles: Rutherglen Muscat is deeply sweet, dark and raisined, with notes of dried fruit, toffee, coffee and nuts built up through years of oxidative barrel ageing; Topaque (made from Muscadelle) shows a similar richness with more citrus-peel and tea-leaf character. Dry reds from Durif are deeply coloured, full-bodied and firmly tannic, distinct from the softer character of Shiraz grown in the same district.
notes: Rutherglen's four-tier Muscat/Topaque classification (Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare) is unique among the world's fortified wine regions.
Durif, also known as Petite Sirah, found an especially successful home in Rutherglen despite being little planted elsewhere.
Old fortified wine stocks are blended using a solera-like fractional system to maintain consistent house styles over decades.
The region was a major wine hub in the 19th century before phylloxera devastated its vineyards.

regions.name: Great Southern
regions.summary: Great Southern, in the far south of Western Australia, is a large, sparsely planted, cool-climate region best known for aromatic Riesling, peppery Shiraz and structured Cabernet Sauvignon. Its isolation and size make it one of Australia's most distinctive fine-wine areas despite relatively small production.
regions.climate: A cool climate shaped by both maritime influence from the Southern Ocean and a degree of continental variation across its large geographic spread, with a long, slow ripening season. Conditions vary meaningfully between its coastal and inland sub-zones, giving the region a wide range of mesoclimates within one GI. Rainfall and temperature differences across the area mean grape variety suitability shifts noticeably from one sub-region to the next.
regions.soils: Soils are generally ancient, low-fertility gravelly loams over granite or laterite base rock, providing good drainage and naturally restraining vine vigour, which supports concentrated, aromatic fruit.
regions.classification: Great Southern is a Western Australian GI, itself divided into five recognised sub-regions (Denmark, Frankland River, Mount Barker, Porongurup and Albany), each a registered GI in its own right; there is no quality tier above the geographical delimitation.

subRegions.name: Mount Barker
subRegions.notes: The historic heart of the region, known for Riesling and peppery Shiraz.

subRegions.name: Frankland River
subRegions.notes: Warmer and drier, producing structured Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz.

subRegions.name: Porongurup
subRegions.notes: Elevated granite slopes yielding some of the region's most aromatic, age-worthy Riesling.

subRegions.name: Denmark
subRegions.notes: Cooler and wetter, suited to Pinot Noir and aromatic whites.

subRegions.name: Albany
subRegions.notes: Coastal and maritime-influenced, a smaller planted area.

regions.styles: Riesling is dry, aromatic and high in acid, with lime and floral notes and strong ageing potential, especially from Porongurup and Mount Barker. Shiraz shows a distinctly cool-climate, peppery, medium-bodied character, while Cabernet Sauvignon from Frankland River is firmly structured with blackcurrant fruit. Cooler pockets such as Denmark also produce increasingly well-regarded Pinot Noir.
notes: Great Southern is one of Australia's largest wine regions by area but among its most sparsely planted.
Its isolation from other Western Australian wine regions helped it develop a distinct identity, especially for Riesling.
Porongurup's granite-based soils are particularly prized for fine, mineral Riesling.
The region's Shiraz is often compared stylistically to cool-climate Rhône examples for its pepper and spice notes.

regions.name: Nelson
regions.summary: Nelson is a small, sunny wine region at the north-western tip of New Zealand's South Island, producing aromatic whites and increasingly well-regarded Pinot Noir. Though it sits near Marlborough, it has developed its own distinct identity, shaped by a strong community of small, artisan producers.
regions.climate: A maritime climate with high sunshine hours, moderate rainfall and protection from wind by surrounding hills, giving reliable, even ripening. The region is split between two distinct sub-areas whose differing terrain — flat plains versus rolling hills — creates meaningfully different growing conditions within a small overall area. Coastal influence keeps summers from becoming excessively hot.
regions.soils: The Waimea Plains have deep, free-draining gravelly and alluvial soils, while the Moutere Hills feature older, heavier clay-based soils with iron content, generally lower in vigour and associated with more concentrated fruit.
regions.classification: Nelson is a registered wine region under New Zealand's Geographical Indications (GI) framework, with no formal internal quality tiers; the Waimea Plains and Moutere Hills are recognised informally as distinct terroirs rather than legally defined sub-appellations.

subRegions.name: Waimea Plains
subRegions.notes: Flat, gravelly alluvial land producing riper, fruit-forward styles.

subRegions.name: Moutere Hills
subRegions.notes: Older clay-based hill soils giving more structured, concentrated wines.

regions.styles: Sauvignon Blanc from Nelson tends to be softer and less overtly pungent than Marlborough's, often with riper stone-fruit notes. Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris are increasingly important, showing supple fruit and good varietal definition, while Chardonnay and Riesling round out a versatile, largely white-and-Pinot-focused portfolio.
notes: Nelson is one of New Zealand's sunniest wine regions, favouring reliable ripening.
It has a strong reputation for small-scale, artisan and organic producers relative to its size.
The region is geologically distinct from neighbouring Marlborough despite similar latitude.
Nelson's wine history dates back to some of New Zealand's earliest 19th-century plantings.

regions.name: Martinborough (Wairarapa)
regions.summary: Martinborough is New Zealand's most celebrated Pinot Noir district, located in the Wairarapa at the southern tip of the North Island. Free-draining ancient river terraces and a small group of pioneering producers established its reputation for structured, ageworthy Pinot Noir from the 1980s onward.
regions.climate: A cool, dry climate with strong winds, low rainfall and free-draining terraces that together produce naturally low yields and concentrated fruit; irrigation is often required given the low rainfall. Its inland position gives greater diurnal temperature range than coastal regions at similar latitude, helping retain acidity while achieving full ripeness. The wind also reduces disease pressure, supporting low-intervention viticulture.
regions.soils: The region sits on ancient, free-draining gravel and alluvial river terraces, low in vigour and fertility. These terraces, sometimes compared to Burgundy's Côte d'Or gravels, are considered central to the concentration and structure of Martinborough Pinot Noir.
regions.classification: Martinborough is a registered GI within the broader Wairarapa region of New Zealand, with no formal quality-tier system; reputation is built vineyard-by-vineyard and producer-by-producer rather than through a legal hierarchy.

subRegions.name: Te Muna Road
subRegions.notes: An emerging sub-district on similar gravel terraces just outside the original township plantings.

regions.styles: Pinot Noir is the defining style: medium to full-bodied, structured and savoury, with dark cherry fruit, firm tannins and strong ageing potential, often likened to red Burgundy. Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris are more aromatic and fruit-driven than the reds from the same district, and small volumes of well-regarded Chardonnay are also produced.
notes: A small group of pioneer producers, including Ata Rangi, Dry River and Martinborough Vineyard, established the region's reputation in the 1980s.
Martinborough's gravel terraces are often compared to Burgundy's Côte d'Or for their suitability to Pinot Noir.
Yields here are typically very low, contributing to concentration but limiting overall production volume.
The district sits in the rain shadow of the Tararua Ranges, which helps keep rainfall low.

regions.name: Constantia
regions.summary: Constantia, on the Cape Peninsula just south of Cape Town, is South Africa's oldest wine-producing area, historically famous for the sweet Vin de Constance that was prized across 18th- and 19th-century European courts. Today it is best known for cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc alongside a modern revival of its historic sweet wine style.
regions.climate: A cool maritime climate cooled by both the Atlantic Ocean and False Bay, with higher rainfall than most of the Cape winelands and strong, drying south-easterly winds known locally as the 'Cape Doctor'. These conditions keep summer temperatures moderate and support the freshness and aromatic intensity found in the region's white wines.
regions.soils: Vineyards are planted on decomposed granite soils on the slopes of Table Mountain and the Constantiaberg, generally well-drained and of moderate fertility, suited to producing aromatic, structured whites.
regions.classification: Constantia is a Wine of Origin (WO) ward, one of South Africa's smallest and most historic, sitting within the Cape Town district; there is no further internal sub-division given its small size.
regions.styles: Modern Constantia is dominated by fresh, aromatic, cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc with pronounced herbaceous and tropical notes. The historic style, revived since the 1980s, is Vin de Constance, a naturally sweet, unfortified Muscat wine of great concentration and ageing potential, made without fortification by late-harvesting and natural cessation of fermentation.
notes: Constantia is South Africa's oldest wine region, with Groot Constantia founded in 1685.
Vin de Constance was famously enjoyed by figures including Napoleon and referenced in 19th-century literature such as Jane Austen's novels.
The historic sweet wine style nearly disappeared before being revived by Klein Constantia in the 1980s.
The 'Cape Doctor' wind that cools the region also helps reduce fungal disease pressure in the vineyards.

regions.name: Walker Bay (Hemel-en-Aarde)
regions.summary: Walker Bay, centred on the town of Hermanus, is South Africa's leading cool-climate region for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, anchored by the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley. Pioneered in the 1970s, it has become the benchmark Cape region for Burgundian varieties.
regions.climate: A cool maritime climate strongly influenced by the cold Benguela current and direct exposure to the Atlantic Ocean, giving one of the coolest growing seasons in the Cape winelands. Sea breezes moderate summer heat and extend the ripening period, allowing grapes to retain acidity while developing complexity, conditions particularly favourable to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
regions.soils: Soils vary through the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley from clay-rich shale near the coast to more decomposed shale and sandstone further inland and at higher elevation, with distance from the sea and soil type both used to distinguish its three wards.
regions.classification: Walker Bay is a Wine of Origin (WO) district containing several wards, most notably the three Hemel-en-Aarde wards — Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge — each delimited by its distinct distance from the coast, elevation and soil composition.

subRegions.name: Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
subRegions.notes: The original, coolest and closest-to-sea ward, planted first in the 1970s.

subRegions.name: Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
subRegions.notes: Further inland and slightly warmer, with clay-rich soils.

subRegions.name: Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge
subRegions.notes: Higher elevation, shale-based soils producing structured, age-worthy wines.

regions.styles: Pinot Noir here is elegant and perfumed with red-fruit and savoury, earthy character, while Chardonnay is complex and mineral with careful use of oak. Sauvignon Blanc offers a cooler, more restrained counterpart, and small volumes of Pinotage and Syrah are also produced.
notes: Tim Hamilton Russell established the first vineyards in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley in the 1970s, seeking the Cape's coolest possible sites.
The three Hemel-en-Aarde wards are delimited largely by their distance from the ocean and elevation.
Walker Bay is widely regarded as South Africa's foremost Pinot Noir and Chardonnay region.
The name Hemel-en-Aarde is Afrikaans for 'heaven and earth'.

regions.name: Naoussa & Nemea
regions.summary: Naoussa and Nemea are Greece's two most important red wine PDOs, each built around a single indigenous grape: Xinomavro in the northern region of Naoussa and Agiorgitiko in the Peloponnesian region of Nemea. Together they represent Greece's benchmark structured red wines, ranging from powerful and tannic to soft and approachable.
regions.climate: Naoussa, on the slopes of Mount Vermio in Macedonia, has a continental climate moderated by elevation, with cold winters and warm summers that allow the late-ripening Xinomavro to reach full phenolic maturity. Nemea, in the north-eastern Peloponnese, has a Mediterranean climate strongly shaped by altitude, with vineyards planted from around 250 to over 800 metres; lower sites are warmer and riper while higher sites remain cooler, giving producers a wide stylistic range from a single appellation.
regions.soils: Naoussa's vineyards sit on a mix of clay, sandstone and limestone-influenced soils across varied slopes, contributing to the wide range of Xinomavro styles found within the appellation. Nemea's soils shift with elevation, from richer, more fertile ground on the valley floor to poorer, sandier and limestone-influenced soils on higher slopes that produce more structured, age-worthy Agiorgitiko.
regions.classification: Both are PDO (Protected Designation of Origin) appellations under Greece's EU-based wine law. Naoussa PDO is reserved for red wines made entirely from Xinomavro, while Nemea PDO is reserved for red wines made entirely from Agiorgitiko; within Nemea, informal altitude bands (low, mid and high-elevation vineyards) are used by producers to signal style even though they are not formally codified sub-zones.

subRegions.name: Naoussa
subRegions.notes: Northern Greek PDO for structured, tannic, age-worthy Xinomavro, often compared to Nebbiolo.

subRegions.name: Nemea
subRegions.notes: Peloponnesian PDO for Agiorgitiko, ranging from soft and fruity to concentrated and age-worthy depending on vineyard altitude.

regions.styles: Naoussa Xinomavro is high in tannin and acidity, medium in colour, with red fruit, tomato, olive and dried herb notes that develop leather and spice with age, drawing frequent comparisons to Nebbiolo. Nemea Agiorgitiko is softer and more approachable, typically medium to full-bodied with ripe red and black fruit, though wines from the highest, coolest vineyards show noticeably more structure and ageing potential. Both regions also produce lighter, fruit-forward styles for earlier drinking alongside their more serious, oak-aged bottlings.
notes: Xinomavro is often compared to Nebbiolo for its combination of high acidity, high tannin and relatively pale colour.
Nemea's wide range of vineyard elevations, from roughly 250 to over 800 metres, lets producers craft everything from easy-drinking to serious, age-worthy Agiorgitiko from one appellation.
Naoussa was one of Greece's first officially delimited wine appellations, designated in 1971.
Agiorgitiko is one of Greece's most widely planted red grapes and is also used to make rosé and, occasionally, sweet styles.

regions.name: Dealu Mare & Cotnari
regions.summary: Two of Romania's most historically important wine areas: Dealu Mare, a hilly red-wine belt in the south known for Fetească Neagră and international varieties, and Cotnari in the northeast, famous for centuries as a source of sweet, botrytis-influenced white wines. Together they represent Romania's strongest claims to quality winemaking recognized within Europe.
regions.climate: Dealu Mare sits on south-facing hills at the southern edge of the Carpathians, benefiting from good sun exposure and drainage while being sheltered from cold northern winds; a warm, temperate continental climate allows reliable ripening of red grapes. Cotnari, further north and at higher latitude, has a cooler continental climate with autumn morning mists rising from nearby valleys that encourage noble rot, historically prized for sweet wine production. Both areas experience cold winters and warm summers typical of inland Romania, with elevation and aspect used to moderate frost and ripening risk.
regions.soils: Dealu Mare's hillsides feature clay and loess-influenced soils over limestone and sandy subsoils, giving structure to red wines while aiding drainage on slopes. Cotnari's vineyards lie on chalky, clay-limestone soils that help retain moisture balance needed for the slow ripening and botrytis development central to its sweet wine tradition.
regions.classification: Both regions fall under Romania's DOC (Denumire de Origine Controlată) system established after EU accession, with sub-designations indicating harvest and ripeness conditions (such as late-harvest or noble-rot affected grapes) for sweeter styles. Dealu Mare DOC covers red and some white still wines from its hillside communes, while Cotnari DOC is a long-established, tightly defined appellation focused almost exclusively on its traditional sweet white blend.

subRegions.name: Dealu Mare
subRegions.notes: Rolling hills producing Romania's most respected red wines from Fetească Neagră and Bordeaux varieties.

subRegions.name: Pietroasele
subRegions.notes: A noted sub-zone within Dealu Mare historically associated with sweet Tămâioasă Românească.

subRegions.name: Cotnari
subRegions.notes: A single historic appellation in the northeast producing sweet, aromatic white wines from indigenous grapes, sometimes affected by noble rot.

regions.styles: Dealu Mare produces full-bodied, dark-fruited red wines, with Fetească Neagră offering deep color and dark plum, spice character, often blended with or compared to Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from the same hills. Cotnari's signature wine is a golden, sweet white blend of Grasă de Cotnari, Tămâioasă Românească, Frâncușă, and Fetească Albă, showing honeyed, floral, apricot-like flavors with good aging potential due to natural acidity balancing residual sugar. Both regions also produce lighter, drier styles for everyday consumption alongside their flagship wines.
notes: Fetească Neagră ('black maiden grape') is one of Romania's most distinctive indigenous red varieties and is closely associated with Dealu Mare.
Cotnari's sweet wine tradition predates phylloxera and was historically compared favorably to Tokaji by European royalty.
Dealu Mare benefits from foehn-like warm winds descending the Carpathian foothills, aiding ripening.
Tămâioasă Românească is a musk-scented, aromatic grape related to the Muscat family, used in both Dealu Mare and Cotnari.

regions.name: Thracian Valley
regions.summary: The Thracian Lowlands are Bulgaria's most important red wine region, historically linked to some of the oldest winemaking traditions in Europe. The area is best known for the indigenous Mavrud grape as well as strong plantings of international red varieties.
regions.climate: The Thracian Valley lies in southern Bulgaria between the Balkan Mountains to the north and the Rhodope Mountains to the south, giving it a warm, sheltered continental climate with hot, dry summers well suited to ripening thick-skinned red grapes. The surrounding mountain ranges help protect vineyards from extreme northern cold and moderate rainfall, while the Maritsa River valley provides some humidity and cooling influence in parts of the region. This combination of heat and mountain shelter makes the valley Bulgaria's most reliable region for full-bodied red wine production.
regions.soils: Soils vary across the valley but commonly include fertile alluvial deposits near the Maritsa River alongside clay and stonier soils on higher ground closer to the mountains, the latter generally favored for quality red wine production. Mavrud in particular is associated with warmer, well-drained sites where its thick skins can ripen fully.
regions.classification: The Thracian Lowlands form one of Bulgaria's two broad EU-recognized Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) zones (alongside the Danube Plain in the north), within which smaller Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) wine areas and specific village or estate names can appear. Quality red wines from well-regarded communes such as those near Asenovgrad, Sakar, and Stambolovo are often marketed with more specific local names in addition to the broader regional designation.

subRegions.name: Asenovgrad area
subRegions.notes: A traditional center for Mavrud production near the Rhodope foothills.

subRegions.name: Sakar
subRegions.notes: A warm eastern sub-zone known for robust red wines, including Mavrub and Bordeaux varieties.

subRegions.name: Stambolovo
subRegions.notes: A sub-zone associated with Merlot and other red varieties benefiting from a warm mesoclimate.

regions.styles: The Thracian Valley is known primarily for deeply colored, full-bodied, tannic red wines. Mavrud produces dense, dark-fruited wines with notable structure and aging potential, often needing time to soften. International varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and Syrah are widely planted and made in both varietal and blended styles, generally ripe and full-bodied given the warm climate; some lighter whites and rosés are also produced but are secondary to the region's red wine reputation.
notes: Mavrud is a late-ripening, thick-skinned indigenous grape considered one of Bulgaria's signature varieties.
The region's wine history is linked to ancient Thrace, one of the earliest documented wine-producing cultures in Europe.
Bulgaria's modern wine industry saw major foreign investment and quality-focused revival after the fall of communism, with the Thracian Valley at the center of this resurgence.
Rubin is a Bulgarian crossing of Nebbiolo and Syrah, developed locally and grown alongside Mavrud.

regions.name: Primorska (Goriška Brda)
regions.summary: Primorska is Slovenia's westernmost wine region, bordering Italy's Friuli-Venezia Giulia, and includes the hilly Brda (Goriška Brda) district known for aromatic whites, skin-contact 'orange' wines, and a strong cross-border winemaking culture shared with neighboring Collio in Italy.
regions.climate: Primorska benefits from a Mediterranean-influenced climate moderated by proximity to the Adriatic Sea, giving it warmer, drier conditions than Slovenia's more continental interior regions. The Brda hills add elevation and varied aspect, moderating summer heat and helping preserve acidity in white grapes, while the Vipava Valley further south experiences the cooling influence of the Burja, a strong cold wind from the mountains. This mix of Mediterranean warmth and localized cooling effects supports both ripe, textured whites and increasingly serious reds.
regions.soils: The region's most distinctive soil is 'ponca' (or 'opoka'), a marl of alternating sandstone and limestone layers found in Brda and shared with the adjoining Collio area of Italy, valued for producing mineral, structured white wines. Other parts of Primorska, such as the Karst plateau, feature reddish terra rossa soils over limestone, associated with the dense red wines made from Refošk.
regions.classification: Slovenia's wine law recognizes Primorska as one of the country's main wine-growing regions, divided into official districts including Goriška Brda, Vipava Valley, Kras, and Slovenian Istria, each of which can appear on labels as a protected designation. Higher quality wines typically carry a district or vineyard name alongside varietal labeling, and Slovenia also uses a traditional PTP (recognized traditional designation) category for certain historic wine styles.

subRegions.name: Goriška Brda
subRegions.notes: Hilly district on the Italian border known for Rebula and skin-contact white winemaking.

subRegions.name: Vipava Valley
subRegions.notes: Influenced by the cooling Burja wind, producing both fresh whites and structured reds.

subRegions.name: Kras (Karst)
subRegions.notes: Limestone plateau known for Teran, a Refošk-based red wine with high acidity.

subRegions.name: Slovenian Istria
subRegions.notes: Coastal district near the Adriatic producing Malvazija-based whites and Refošk reds.

regions.styles: Primorska, and Brda in particular, is known for textured, often skin-contact ('orange') white wines made from Rebula, alongside fresher, more conventionally vinified Sauvignon Blanc and Malvazija. Reds based on Refošk (called Teran in the Kras district) are deeply colored, high in acidity, and traditionally rustic, though modern winemaking has produced smoother, more polished examples. International varieties like Merlot and Chardonnay are also grown, generally in a fuller, riper style reflecting the region's Mediterranean influence.
notes: Goriška Brda shares its 'ponca' soil and much of its winemaking culture with Italy's Collio, the two areas separated only by a national border drawn after World War II.
Orange/skin-contact white winemaking, using extended skin maceration for white grapes, has strong historical roots in this region and neighboring Friuli.
Teran, the Kras district's signature Refošk-based red, has been the subject of a long-running naming dispute with Croatia over use of the term.
Slovenia's wine regions are otherwise mostly continental (Podravje, Posavje), making Primorska distinct as the country's Mediterranean-influenced zone.

regions.name: Tikveš
regions.summary: Tikveš is North Macedonia's largest and most important wine region, producing the great majority of the country's wine. It is best known for Vranec, a deeply colored indigenous red grape that is the country's signature variety.
regions.climate: Tikveš lies in a warm basin in central North Macedonia, sheltered by surrounding mountains that create a modified continental climate with strong Mediterranean influence carried up the Vardar river valley from the Aegean. Summers are hot and dry, and the basin's enclosed position limits rainfall, making irrigation useful in some vineyard sites; this warmth allows thorough ripening of both red and aromatic grape varieties.
regions.soils: The region's vineyards are planted on a mix of alluvial and clay-limestone soils across the Tikveš basin, generally well-drained and suited to the vigorous, heat-tolerant Vranec vine, with some higher, stonier sites reserved for more concentrated wines.
regions.classification: North Macedonia's wine law is still developing an EU-aligned system of protected geographical designations, with Tikveš recognized as the country's principal named wine region; wines are commonly labeled by region and variety rather than through a more elaborate tiered appellation hierarchy. Individual producer estates and their vineyard holdings within Tikveš are often used as informal quality markers.
regions.styles: Tikveš is best known for Vranec-based red wines, which are typically deep in color, full-bodied, and rich in dark fruit character, ranging from everyday drinking styles to more concentrated, oak-aged examples with aging potential. Smederevka, the country's most widely planted white grape, produces light, neutral, easy-drinking whites, while Temjanika (a Muscat-family grape) offers more aromatic, floral styles. Rosé wines from Vranec are also commonly produced and popular domestically.
notes: Tikveš accounts for the large majority of North Macedonia's total wine production, making it the dominant region in the country by volume.
Vranec is genetically related to Montenegro's Vranac and is the flagship red grape across much of the western Balkans.
The Vardar river valley acts as a corridor for warm Mediterranean air to reach this inland basin, moderating what would otherwise be a purely continental climate.
North Macedonia was a major bulk wine supplier within the former Yugoslav market and is now shifting toward more quality-focused, estate-bottled production.

regions.name: Šumadija
regions.summary: Šumadija, in central Serbia south of Belgrade, is one of the country's best-known wine regions, historically associated with the indigenous red grape Prokupac and Serbia's traditional rosé-style wine, Ružica.
regions.climate: Šumadija has a moderate continental climate shaped by its rolling, forested hill country, with warm summers and cold winters typical of inland Serbia. Elevation and aspect across its hilly terrain provide some relief from summer heat and help protect against frost, while the region's name (meaning 'wooded area') reflects the forest cover that historically moderated local conditions around the vineyards.
regions.soils: Vineyards in Šumadija are typically planted on a mix of clay, sand, and limestone-influenced soils across hilly terrain, generally well-drained, which suits the region's traditional focus on structured red and rosé wines from Prokupac.
regions.classification: Serbia's wine sector operates under a developing geographical indication system aligned with EU practice, with Šumadija recognized as one of the country's principal named wine districts; labeling generally combines region, variety, and producer rather than a more elaborate tiered classification. Individual sub-areas and producer estates within Šumadija are often used to signal quality informally.

subRegions.name: Oplenac
subRegions.notes: A well-known sub-area historically tied to the Serbian royal family and Prokupac plantings.

subRegions.name: Topola
subRegions.notes: A traditional winemaking town within Šumadija associated with Prokupac and rosé production.

regions.styles: Prokupac, Šumadija's signature red grape, is traditionally used to make Ružica, a deeply colored, dry rosé style long associated with the region, as well as medium- to full-bodied red wines with earthy, dark-fruited character. International varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot are also grown for red wine, while Tamjanika (a Muscat-family grape) and other whites like Chardonnay provide aromatic and neutral white styles respectively. Modern producers increasingly blend Prokupac with international varieties to add structure and market appeal.
notes: Prokupac is considered Serbia's own indigenous grape and was historically the country's most widely planted variety before international grapes gained ground.
Ružica, a traditional Serbian dry rosé, has a long history in Šumadija predating modern rosé trends elsewhere in Europe.
Oplenac, within Šumadija, is closely tied to Serbia's Karađorđević royal dynasty, which historically supported local viticulture.
Serbia's wine industry is undergoing a quality-focused revival after decades of bulk production during the socialist Yugoslav era.

regions.name: Codru & Ştefan Vodă (Purcari)
regions.summary: Moldova is one of Eastern Europe's oldest and most significant wine-producing countries, with Codru in the central hills and Ştefan Vodă in the southeast (home to the historic Purcari winery) among its most recognized wine areas. The country is known for both indigenous grapes and internationally styled red blends that gained reputation in the export market, particularly to Russia and, more recently, Western Europe.
regions.climate: Moldova has a temperate continental climate moderated by its position between the Prut and Dniester rivers and by the generally rolling, hilly terrain that provides varied aspect and drainage. Codru, in the country's forested central plateau, benefits from higher elevation and tree cover that moderates temperature extremes, while Ştefan Vodă in the southeast, closer to the Black Sea's influence, is generally warmer, aiding the ripening of red varieties. Overall the climate allows for a wide range of styles, from fresh whites in cooler pockets to fuller reds in warmer areas.
regions.soils: Central Codru features a mix of clay, chernozem (black earth), and limestone-influenced soils across hilly, forested terrain, generally fertile and well-suited to varied plantings. Ştefan Vodă, closer to the Dniester valley, has soils with more chalk and limestone influence, historically associated with the structured red blends for which Purcari is known.
regions.classification: Moldova has established a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) system with several defined regions, including Codru, Ştefan Vodă, and Valul lui Traian, within which specific estates and vineyards may be named. Purcari, one of Moldova's oldest and most internationally recognized wineries, is located within the Ştefan Vodă PGI and is often used as a de facto quality marker for the area.

subRegions.name: Codru
subRegions.notes: Central, hilly, forested PGI zone with a wide range of grape plantings and a moderating climate.

subRegions.name: Ştefan Vodă
subRegions.notes: Southeastern PGI region near the Dniester, home to the historic Purcari winery and known for structured red blends.

regions.styles: Moldova's most internationally known wines are structured red blends, exemplified by Purcari's Negru de Purcari, combining Cabernet Sauvignon, Saperavi, and Rara Neagră into a full-bodied, dark-fruited style with aging potential. Fetească Neagră produces deeply colored, spicy reds with good structure, while Fetească Albă yields light, aromatic, off-dry to dry white wines. The country also has a long tradition of sparkling wine production alongside its still wines.
notes: Moldova has one of the highest ratios of vineyard area to population in the world and a winemaking history stretching back thousands of years.
Purcari's Negru de Purcari red blend has a long export history and was historically served to European royalty, contributing to the winery's reputation.
Fetească Neagră, Rara Neagră, and Fetească Albă are indigenous varieties shared culturally and linguistically with neighboring Romania.
The Soviet era saw Moldova developed into a major bulk wine supplier for the USSR, and much of the industry has since shifted toward quality and export-focused production.

regions.name: Commandaria
regions.summary: Commandaria is a sweet dessert wine made in a defined zone of villages on the southern slopes of the Troodos Mountains in Cyprus, widely cited as one of the oldest named wines still produced today, with a documented history stretching back many centuries. It is made from sun-dried Xynisteri and Mavro grapes and has long been associated with religious and ceremonial use.
regions.climate: The Commandaria zone lies on south-facing slopes of the Troodos foothills at moderate elevation, giving it a Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers well suited to ripening grapes to high sugar levels. The region's dryness and sun exposure are essential to the traditional production method, in which harvested grapes are further sun-dried outdoors after picking to concentrate sugars before fermentation.
regions.soils: Vineyards in the zone are generally planted on chalky, limestone-influenced soils typical of the Troodos foothills, which provide good drainage, a factor important for the health of vines grown for late, concentrated ripening.
regions.classification: Commandaria is a legally protected Designation of Origin (PDO), restricted to production within a defined zone of villages on the southern Troodos slopes, using only the two permitted indigenous grape varieties and traditional sun-drying and production methods. This makes it one of the most tightly regulated and geographically specific wine names in the region.
regions.styles: Commandaria is a sweet, amber to deep brown fortified or naturally sweet wine (depending on producer method), with concentrated flavors of dried fruit, raisins, caramel, and nuts, and typically high alcohol and residual sugar. It is capable of extended aging, with older examples developing oxidative, nutty, and dried-fruit complexity comparable to other historic sweet wines of the Mediterranean.
notes: Commandaria is frequently cited as the world's oldest wine name still in continuous production, with references to the wine and its production zone dating back to medieval times.
The wine takes its name from the medieval Grande Commanderie of the Knights Hospitaller, who controlled the region and its wine production.
Traditional production involves sun-drying harvested grapes on mats before pressing, concentrating sugars in a manner similar to passito or straw wine methods elsewhere.
Only Xynisteri (white) and Mavro (red) grapes, both indigenous to Cyprus, are permitted in Commandaria production.

regions.name: Areni (Vayots Dzor)
regions.summary: Vayots Dzor, in southern Armenia, is home to the village of Areni and is considered one of the cradles of winemaking, with archaeological evidence of ancient wine production found nearby. The region is best known today for Areni Noir, Armenia's flagship indigenous red grape, grown at high elevation in a dramatic mountain landscape.
regions.climate: Vayots Dzor sits at high elevation within Armenia's mountainous terrain, giving it a continental climate with large diurnal temperature swings that help preserve acidity and aromatic freshness in the grapes despite intense summer sun. The region's high-altitude vineyards, among the highest in the world for commercial viticulture, and low humidity help protect against many vine diseases, while winters can be severe, requiring hardy vine training and site selection.
regions.soils: Vineyards around Areni are planted on volcanic and stony, well-drained soils typical of the surrounding mountain terrain, which contribute to the concentration and mineral character found in wines from the area.
regions.classification: Armenia's formal wine appellation system is still developing, with geographical indications and protected designations being established in recent years as part of efforts to gain international recognition; Areni and the broader Vayots Dzor area are among the first regions to be promoted as a distinct, quality-focused zone within this emerging framework.
regions.styles: Areni Noir produces medium to full-bodied red wines with bright acidity, red fruit character, and firm tannins, often compared stylistically to Pinot Noir or Nebbiolo due to its combination of structure and elegance; both fresh, fruit-forward and more serious, oak-aged examples are produced. Voskehat, a notable indigenous white grape, produces fresh, floral, medium-bodied white wines.
notes: The Areni-1 cave complex near the village contains what is widely reported as the world's oldest known winery site, with wine-making equipment dated to roughly six thousand years ago.
Areni Noir vineyards are planted at some of the highest elevations used for commercial winemaking anywhere in the world.
Armenia's modern wine industry has seen significant international investment and revival in the past two decades, building on a winemaking history that predates most of Europe's.
Armenia is also historically known for brandy production, which for much of the Soviet era overshadowed its still wine industry.

regions.name: Cappadocia & Central Anatolia
regions.summary: Cappadocia, in central Turkey, is one of the country's most historic wine regions, known for its dramatic volcanic landscape and ancient underground wine cellars carved into soft rock. Along with other Anatolian wine areas, it forms part of a wine culture with roots reaching back thousands of years in a region considered part of the broader Caucasus/Near East origins of viticulture.
regions.climate: Cappadocia and much of central Anatolia have a high-elevation continental climate with hot, dry summers and cold winters, and significant diurnal temperature variation that helps preserve acidity in the grapes. The region's inland, semi-arid conditions and low humidity reduce disease pressure, while elevation moderates what would otherwise be excessive summer heat for fine wine production.
regions.soils: Cappadocia's vineyards are notably planted on volcanic, tuff-derived soils formed by ancient eruptions, the same soft volcanic rock famously carved into cave dwellings and wine cellars in the region; these soils are generally well-drained and contribute distinctive mineral character to the wines.
regions.classification: Turkey has been developing a geographical indication system for wine in recent years, with some Anatolian areas beginning to register protected regional names, though much of the country's wine is still labeled primarily by producer and grape variety rather than a fully developed appellation hierarchy. Cappadocia is recognized informally and increasingly formally as a distinct historic wine tourism and production area within this evolving framework.

subRegions.name: Nevşehir area
subRegions.notes: Heart of the Cappadocia wine region, known for ancient cave cellars and the Emir grape.

subRegions.name: Elazığ / Diyarbakır (Southeastern Anatolia)
subRegions.notes: Traditional home of Öküzgözü and Boğazkere, Turkey's most planted quality red grapes.

regions.styles: Central Anatolian and Cappadocian wines include fresh, light-bodied whites from the indigenous Emir grape, historically used in the region's ancient winemaking. Red wines from Öküzgözü tend to be lighter, fruity, and aromatic, while Boğazkere produces tannic, full-bodied, structured reds often built for aging; the two are frequently blended to balance each other's character. Kalecik Karası, from further north in Anatolia, gives lighter, fragrant red wines.
notes: Anatolia is considered one of the earliest regions in the world associated with grape domestication and winemaking, alongside the wider Caucasus and Near East.
Cappadocia's soft volcanic tuff rock, famous for cave dwellings, was historically also carved into underground cellars for wine storage and aging.
Turkey's population is majority Muslim, and domestic wine consumption is comparatively low relative to production, with much of the industry historically export- and tourism-oriented.
Öküzgözü ('bull's eye') and Boğazkere ('throat scratcher') are named descriptively in Turkish for the appearance and tannic grip of the grapes, respectively.

regions.name: Odesa (Black Sea Coast)
regions.summary: The Odesa region, along Ukraine's Black Sea coast, is one of the country's most established wine areas, with a winemaking history shaped by both indigenous and international grape varieties and a coastal, steppe climate. It has traditionally been associated with both still and sparkling wine production, drawing on the moderating influence of the Black Sea.
regions.climate: The Odesa coastal region has a temperate continental climate strongly moderated by proximity to the Black Sea, which tempers summer heat and winter cold compared to Ukraine's more extreme continental interior. Warm, relatively long growing seasons and ample sunshine support ripening of both white and red varieties, while sea breezes help reduce disease pressure and moderate humidity near the coast.
regions.soils: Vineyards near Odesa are generally planted on chernozem (black earth) and calcareous soils typical of the Black Sea steppe, fertile and well-suited to viticulture, with coastal areas benefiting from additional drainage and moderated temperatures close to the sea.
regions.classification: Ukraine's wine appellation system has historically been less formalized than in EU countries, with wines commonly labeled by region, producer, and grape variety; efforts to establish a Protected Geographical Indication framework aligned with EU practice have been underway in recent years, with coastal areas near Odesa among the regions expected to benefit from clearer geographic labeling.

subRegions.name: Shabo
subRegions.notes: A coastal wine village near Odesa with a long winemaking history and modern production focus.

regions.styles: The Odesa region produces a range of still wines, including fresh, dry whites from Rkatsiteli and Aligoté, as well as fuller reds from Cabernet Sauvignon and indigenous crossings such as Odesa Black. The area also has a notable tradition of sparkling wine production using the Black Sea coast's moderated climate to preserve acidity in base wines. Overall, styles tend toward approachable, fruit-driven wines rather than highly structured, long-aging examples.
notes: The Black Sea's moderating influence is central to viticulture in this region, distinguishing it from Ukraine's harsher continental interior.
Odesa Black is a Ukrainian-bred teinturier-type red grape used both for blending and as a varietal wine.
Shabo, near Odesa, has a winemaking history linked to earlier Swiss and German colonist settlement in the area during the 19th century.
Ukraine's wine industry, including the Odesa area, has faced significant disruption due to the ongoing war, affecting both production and export logistics in recent years.

regions.name: Valle de Guadalupe
regions.summary: Valle de Guadalupe, in Baja California near Ensenada, is Mexico's leading fine-wine region and the heart of its modern wine renaissance. It produces the large majority of Mexico's quality wine and has become a major food-and-wine tourism destination since the 1990s.
regions.climate: The valley has a Mediterranean climate cooled by its proximity to the Pacific Ocean, with morning fog and afternoon sea breezes moderating what would otherwise be hot, semi-arid conditions. Rainfall is low and largely confined to winter, so irrigation is essential for viticulture. Diurnal temperature swings help preserve acidity, while the surrounding hills give a range of mesoclimates and exposures.
regions.soils: Soils are generally sandy, granitic, and alluvial, offering good drainage in a region where water management is critical. Poor, low-fertility soils on the valley's slopes help naturally limit vigor and yields.
regions.classification: Mexico does not have a French-style appellation hierarchy with legally defined quality tiers; wine labeling relies on a general Denominación de Origen framework and, more informally, on the recognized geographic name "Valle de Guadalupe" itself, which functions as a marketing and provenance indicator rather than a strict regulated appellation.

subRegions.name: San Antonio de las Minas
subRegions.notes: A warmer, lower sub-area known for early plantings and some of the region's pioneering wineries.

subRegions.name: El Porvenir / Francisco Zarco
subRegions.notes: Central part of the valley with a dense concentration of boutique wineries and tasting rooms.

subRegions.name: Valle de Calafia
subRegions.notes: A cooler, higher-elevation zone increasingly planted for fresher styles.

regions.styles: The region is best known for bold, full-bodied red blends built around Bordeaux and Rhône varieties, often oak-aged and high in alcohol. Rosé and some traditional-method sparkling wine are also produced, and a newer generation of producers is pushing toward fresher, less extracted styles. Overall the wines trend toward ripe fruit and generous body, reflecting the warm, sun-drenched growing conditions.
notes: Mexico has the oldest continuous winemaking history in the Americas, dating to Spanish colonial vine plantings in the 16th century, though Valle de Guadalupe's fine-wine identity is a late-20th-century development.
L.A. Cetto is one of the largest and most internationally recognized producers based in the valley.
The region sits only about 100 km south of the US border, making it a popular day-trip destination from San Diego.
Wine tourism, boutique hotels, and a farm-to-table restaurant scene have grown alongside the wineries since the 1990s.

regions.name: Ica Valley
regions.summary: The Ica Valley, on Peru's arid southern coast, is the country's principal wine and pisco-producing region and one of the oldest sites of viticulture in South America. It is better known internationally for pisco, the grape brandy distilled from many of its same vineyards, than for still table wine.
regions.climate: Ica has a true desert climate, among the driest in South America, with viticulture dependent almost entirely on irrigation drawn from Andean rivers and aquifers. The cool offshore Humboldt Current moderates coastal temperatures despite the region's low latitude, and clear skies give intense sunshine with relatively cool nights. Water scarcity, rather than heat alone, is the defining challenge for growers.
regions.soils: Soils are predominantly sandy and alluvial, deposited by rivers descending from the Andes, giving generally free-draining conditions typical of coastal desert oases.
regions.classification: Peru does not have a formal quality-tier appellation system for still wine comparable to European models. Pisco, by contrast, is protected by its own Denominación de Origen, which covers Ica among a small number of designated coastal valleys and restricts production to specified grape varieties and methods.

subRegions.name: Ica (city area)
subRegions.notes: The historic core of the valley and the traditional center of both wine and pisco production.

subRegions.name: Ocucaje
subRegions.notes: A desert sub-zone known for some of the valley's oldest vineyards and pisco bodegas.

subRegions.name: Subtanjalla
subRegions.notes: A smaller cultivation area within the wider Ica oasis.

regions.styles: Still wines from Ica are generally simple, fruity, and made in both dry and off-dry styles for largely domestic consumption. The valley's greater fame rests on pisco, a clear, unaged grape brandy produced in aromatic (Italia, Torontel, Moscatel) and non-aromatic (Quebranta, Negra Criolla) styles.
notes: Peru's viticultural history predates that of Chile and Argentina, with Spanish colonists establishing vineyards on the coast in the mid-16th century.
Quebranta is a grape variety unique to Peru, believed to be a natural mutation that arose there after Spanish introduction.
Much of the valley's grape production is destined for pisco distillation rather than still table wine.
Peru and Chile have a long-running dispute over the historical origin and naming rights of pisco.

regions.name: Tarija / Valle Central
regions.summary: Centered on the city of Tarija in southern Bolivia, this region is home to some of the highest-altitude commercial vineyards in the world. It is best known for intensely colored, high-acid Tannat and for Singani, Bolivia's protected national grape spirit.
regions.climate: Vineyards here are planted at extreme elevation, commonly well above 1,700 meters and in places above 2,000-2,500 meters, giving intense ultraviolet exposure and very large diurnal temperature swings. The high-altitude, semi-arid conditions bring low humidity, which limits fungal disease pressure, while cool nights preserve acidity despite the region's relatively low latitude.
regions.soils: Soils are generally sandy and alluvial with good drainage, typical of valley floors and terraces cut by rivers descending from the Andes.
regions.classification: Bolivia has no French-style appellation hierarchy for wine. Singani, the grape brandy distilled mainly from Moscatel de Alejandría, does carry a protected geographic denomination restricting its production to specified high-altitude Bolivian regions, including areas around Tarija.

subRegions.name: Valle de la Concepción
subRegions.notes: One of the most planted and highest-profile wine-producing valleys near Tarija.

subRegions.name: Uriondo / San Lorenzo
subRegions.notes: Additional high-altitude growing areas within the broader Tarija wine zone.

subRegions.name: Cinti Valley
subRegions.notes: A historic, more remote high-altitude valley associated with some of Bolivia's oldest viticulture, extending toward Chuquisaca.

regions.styles: Still wines are typically full-bodied, deeply colored reds with high natural acidity, led by Tannat, alongside a small volume of whites and rosés. Singani, a clear unaged brandy, is Bolivia's signature spirit and is consumed far more widely than the country's still wine.
notes: Vineyards in the Valle de la Concepción area are among the highest-altitude commercial vineyards in the world.
Singani has a legally protected denomination of origin restricting its production to Bolivia.
Bolivia's wine industry is small and largely oriented toward domestic consumption rather than export.
The combination of intense sunlight and cool nights at altitude gives the wines notably vivid color and acidity for their latitude.

regions.name: Meknès
regions.summary: Meknès, in north-central Morocco near the Middle Atlas foothills, is the country's principal wine region and the historic center of its wine industry, which was rebuilt on a large scale under the French Protectorate in the early-to-mid 20th century.
regions.climate: The region has a Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers, moderated by proximity to the Middle Atlas Mountains, which provide cooling elevation and some hillside sites. Winters are mild and wetter, and vineyard sites on higher ground benefit from cooler nights that help preserve freshness in the grapes.
regions.soils: Soils are largely clay-limestone, similar in character to parts of the southern Rhône, with gravelly patches in some vineyard areas that aid drainage.
regions.classification: Morocco operates an Appellation d'Origine Garantie (AOG) system modeled on the French AOC framework, alongside broader Vin de Pays-style designations. The Guerrouane AOG, covering hillside vineyards around Meknès, is the region's principal recognized appellation.

subRegions.name: Guerrouane
subRegions.notes: The main AOG zone in the Meknès area, known for red blends from hillside vineyards.

subRegions.name: Zerhoune
subRegions.notes: A hillside growing area near Meknès associated with quality red wine production.

subRegions.name: Beni M'Tir
subRegions.notes: A foothill zone benefiting from elevation for cooler growing conditions.

regions.styles: The region is best known for full-bodied, Rhône-style red blends built on Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Grenache, and Cinsault, generally warm, ripe, and moderately tannic. Some rosé is also produced, and a handful of producers make wines with genuine ageing potential.
notes: Morocco's modern wine industry was largely established under the French Protectorate (1912-1956), which planted much of the country's vineyard land.
Morocco is a majority-Muslim country where wine remains legal and is produced primarily for domestic tourism, export, and local non-Muslim consumption.
Several of Morocco's largest wine producers are based in or around Meknès.
Historically the region supplied large volumes of bulk blending wine to France before Moroccan independence.

regions.name: Cap Bon
regions.summary: The Cap Bon peninsula in northeastern Tunisia is the country's leading wine region, historically celebrated for Muscat-based wines from around the town of Kelibia. Tunisian winemaking traces back to Phoenician and Carthaginian times, making it one of the oldest wine-producing areas in the Mediterranean.
regions.climate: The peninsula has a Mediterranean climate with strong maritime influence, since vineyards are surrounded on most sides by the sea. This moderates summer heat compared with more inland Tunisian sites and provides consistent breezes, while rainfall is concentrated in the mild winter months.
regions.soils: Soils are mixed, ranging from sandy coastal soils near the shore to clay-limestone further inland, both of which support the region's red and Muscat plantings.
regions.classification: Tunisia has operated an Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée (AOC) system since the mid-20th century, modeled on the French system. The Muscat de Kelibia AOC, on Cap Bon, is one of the country's best-known appellations and is specifically tied to Muscat-based wines from that area.

subRegions.name: Kelibia
subRegions.notes: Home to the Muscat de Kelibia AOC, Tunisia's most famous appellation for aromatic Muscat wines.

subRegions.name: Grombalia
subRegions.notes: A wine-producing area on the peninsula known for both red and rosé production.

regions.styles: Cap Bon is particularly known for dry and off-dry Muscat white wines with pronounced floral and grapey aromatics, as well as rosé, a historically important Tunisian style. Reds from Carignan and Grenache blends tend to be full-bodied and robust.
notes: Tunisia's winemaking history dates back over two millennia to the Phoenician and Carthaginian periods.
French colonial rule (1881-1956) substantially expanded Tunisian vineyard area and modernized production.
Tunisia is a majority-Muslim country, and its wine industry, while much reduced since independence, continues to produce mainly for export and tourism.
Muscat de Kelibia is one of the most internationally recognized Tunisian wine names.

regions.name: Nashik
regions.summary: Nashik, in the state of Maharashtra, is widely regarded as the "wine capital of India" and produces the majority of the country's quality wine. Its rapid growth since the late 1990s, led by pioneering producers, has made it central to India's emerging domestic wine industry.
regions.climate: Nashik sits on the Deccan Plateau at moderate elevation, which helps offset India's generally tropical heat and gives cooler nights favorable for grape growing. The growing season must be managed around the monsoon, since rainfall during the vine's growth cycle poses a significant disease and dilution risk, making careful timing of pruning and harvest important.
regions.soils: The region has a mix of black volcanic (regur) soils, characteristic of the Deccan Plateau, and red lateritic soils in places, requiring careful site selection and drainage management for viable viticulture.
regions.classification: India does not have a formal quality-tier appellation system comparable to European models; wine production is regulated primarily through state excise and licensing laws rather than a designated hierarchy, though geographic indication (GI) tags have begun to be used for areas such as Nashik.

subRegions.name: Nashik Valley
subRegions.notes: The core vineyard area and the most densely planted zone around the city of Nashik.

subRegions.name: Dindori
subRegions.notes: A nearby taluka with a growing concentration of vineyards and wineries.

subRegions.name: Niphad
subRegions.notes: Another vineyard area within Nashik district contributing to the region's production.

regions.styles: Wines are generally fresh, fruit-forward, and made in an approachable New World style, spanning reds, whites, rosés, and traditional-method sparkling wine. Most production is aimed at India's rapidly growing but still small domestic wine market.
notes: Sula Vineyards, founded in the late 1990s, is widely credited with pioneering Nashik's modern wine industry.
Moët Hennessy's Indian sparkling wine venture, Chandon India, is also based in the region.
India's per-capita wine consumption remains very low by international standards, so the industry is still in an early stage of development.
Growers must plan the vine cycle carefully around the monsoon to avoid rain during ripening.

regions.name: Coteaux de Mascara
regions.summary: Coteaux de Mascara, in northwestern Algeria, is one of the country's most historic wine regions and was central to Algeria's role as one of the world's largest wine exporters during the French colonial era. Production has declined sharply since Algerian independence but the region retains its historic appellation status.
regions.climate: The region has a Mediterranean climate, with vineyards planted on hillsides (coteaux) that provide some elevation and moderate the heat of the surrounding semi-arid plains. Summers are hot and dry, with rainfall concentrated in the cooler winter months.
regions.soils: Soils are predominantly clay-limestone on the hillside sites that give the region its name, historically valued for producing robust, well-colored red wines.
regions.classification: Algeria retains an AOC-style appellation system established under French rule, and Coteaux de Mascara is one of the country's longest-recognized appellations, alongside others such as Coteaux de Tlemcen and Dahra. The system regulates permitted grape varieties and production area but is less extensively codified than its French counterpart.
regions.styles: The region is traditionally known for robust, deeply colored, high-alcohol dry red wines, historically prized for blending into other wines. Styles remain predominantly full-bodied reds, with quality improving in recent decades among a small number of producers.
notes: In the early-to-mid 20th century, Algeria was one of the world's largest wine exporters, with much of its production shipped to France for blending.
Vineyard area and wine production collapsed dramatically after Algerian independence in 1962, due to both agricultural reorganization and cultural shifts.
Algeria is a majority-Muslim country, and its remaining wine industry is small, oriented mainly toward export and limited domestic demand.
Coteaux de Mascara wines were historically valued for their deep color and high natural alcohol levels.

regions.name: Prince Edward County
regions.summary: Prince Edward County is a cool-climate wine region on a peninsula bordered by Lake Ontario in southeastern Ontario, notable for its limestone-influenced soils and for the extreme winter protection its vines require. It is recognized as one of Canada's most distinctive small, quality-focused wine appellations.
regions.climate: The region has a cool continental climate, moderated to a degree by the surrounding waters of Lake Ontario, which help extend the growing season and reduce frost risk relative to inland sites. Winters can still be severe enough that vinifera vines must be buried under soil for protection, a defining practical challenge of viticulture here. The relatively short, cool growing season favors early-ripening, high-acid varieties.
regions.soils: Vineyards sit on a shallow limestone bedrock (alvar) with thin topsoil in many areas, similar in character to other cool-climate limestone regions, which is credited with contributing to the wines' minerality and structure.
regions.classification: Prince Edward County is a designated appellation within the Vintners Quality Alliance (VQA) Ontario system, which sets rules on permitted grape sourcing, minimum ripeness, and labeling for wines bearing the appellation name.
regions.styles: The region is best known for elegant, high-acid Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, along with aromatic Riesling, and a growing amount of traditional-method sparkling wine. Wines are generally lighter-bodied and cool-climate in character, prized for freshness and site expression rather than power.
notes: Vines must be hilled up with soil each autumn and uncovered in spring to survive the region's harsh winters, a labor-intensive practice distinctive to the County.
Prince Edward County was recognized as a distinct VQA appellation in the 2000s, making it one of Ontario's newer designated wine regions alongside Niagara Peninsula and Lake Erie North Shore.
Its shallow limestone soils are often compared to those of Chablis or the Niagara Escarpment.
The region is a small, boutique-scale producer by volume but has earned a strong critical reputation for its Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Paarl
regions.summary: Paarl is one of South Africa's oldest and most historic wine districts, centred on the town beneath the granite domes of Paarl Mountain. It is home to KWV, the cooperative that shaped South African wine for most of the 20th century, and produces everything from full-bodied reds to fortified wines and brandy.
regions.climate: Warm, Mediterranean-continental climate, generally less maritime-influenced than Stellenbosch since Paarl sits further inland from False Bay. The surrounding mountains (Paarl Mountain, Klein Drakenstein, Du Toitskloof) create rain-shadow effects and a range of mesoclimates, while the Berg River offers some moderation on the valley floor. Higher-altitude mountain slopes provide cooler pockets favoured for premium grape growing, while lower, warmer sites suit bulk and fortified production.
regions.soils: Decomposed granite dominates the mountain slopes of Paarl Mountain and Simonsberg, giving well-drained, moderately fertile soils well suited to red varieties. Table Mountain sandstone-derived soils and deep alluvial valley-floor soils are also found, the latter typically used for irrigated, higher-yielding vineyards.
regions.classification: Paarl is a Wine of Origin (WO) District within the Coastal Region of the Western Cape geographical unit. It contains several recognized wards, including Simonsberg-Paarl and Voor Paardeberg, which denote distinct terroir zones, though much wine is still labelled simply under the broader district name. As with all WO labelling, 100% of the grapes must originate from the stated area.

subRegions.name: Simonsberg-Paarl
subRegions.notes: Granite-soil slopes on the Simonsberg mountain favouring structured red Bordeaux varieties.

subRegions.name: Voor Paardeberg
subRegions.notes: A drier, warmer westward ward known for old-vine Chenin Blanc and Rhône varieties.

regions.styles: Paarl produces a broad stylistic range: age-worthy, full-bodied reds from Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz and Pinotage; characterful old-vine Chenin Blanc; rich fortified dessert wines; and premium brandy. Overall the wines tend toward riper, fuller expressions given the warmer inland climate.
notes: KWV's headquarters and historic cellars are in Paarl, and the cooperative governed South African wine production under a quota system for much of the 20th century.
Paarl is regarded as South Africa's brandy capital, home to some of the country's largest brandy cellars.
The town and mountain take their name from the Dutch word for 'pearl', describing the granite outcrop's sheen after rain.
Paarl was a centre of the country's earliest cooperative wine-industry structures.

regions.name: Franschhoek
regions.summary: Franschhoek ('French Corner') is a small, dramatically mountain-ringed valley settled by French Huguenot refugees in the late 17th century, a heritage still celebrated in its name and farm titles. Today it is known for old-vine Semillon, excellent Cap Classique sparkling wine, and a dense concentration of boutique wineries and fine dining.
regions.climate: Warm Mediterranean climate, moderated by the high mountains (Franschhoek, Groot Drakenstein, Wemmershoek) that enclose the valley on three sides, forming a cul-de-sac. Altitude and mountain proximity give cooler nights and a wider diurnal temperature range than many lower-lying Cape districts, while some maritime cooling filters in from False Bay through the Franschhoek Pass.
regions.soils: Weathered granite-derived soils dominate the valley slopes, with pockets of Table Mountain sandstone and alluvial soils on the valley floor. These are generally well-drained, moderate-fertility soils, with red or white varieties favoured according to aspect and elevation.
regions.classification: Franschhoek Valley is a Wine of Origin ward within the Paarl District of the Coastal Region. Local producers established their own identity and marketing body (Franschhoek Vignerons) to promote the valley, though legally it remains a ward rather than an independent district, and WO rules require full traceability of grape origin for labelling.
regions.styles: The valley is particularly noted for old-vine Semillon, producing rich, waxy, age-worthy white wines among South Africa's finest of the variety, alongside excellent traditional-method Cap Classique sparkling wines suited to the cooler mesoclimate. Structured Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz-based reds and well-regarded Chardonnay round out production.
notes: Named for the French Huguenot refugees who settled the valley from 1688 fleeing religious persecution in France.
Many farms still carry French names, such as La Motte, Chamonix and La Bourgogne, reflecting this heritage.
The valley holds some of South Africa's oldest surviving Semillon vineyards.
Franschhoek is widely regarded as South Africa's food-and-wine tourism capital, with an unusually high density of acclaimed restaurants for its size.

regions.name: Elgin
regions.summary: Elgin is South Africa's premier cool-climate ward, an apple-growing valley in the Overberg reinvented from the 1980s-90s as a source of elegant Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
