regions.soils: Soils are variable and include wind-blown loess, volcanic and basalt-derived material, and alluvial deposits along the Snake River, generally well-drained, with the fine, silty loess being a particularly notable regional feature.
regions.classification: Snake River Valley AVA, established in 2007, is a large, high-elevation appellation straddling southwestern Idaho and a small part of eastern Oregon, and is the base for the great majority of Idaho's wine production. There is no further internal sub-appellation structure.
regions.styles: A wide range of styles is produced given the AVA's relative youth and varied plantings, from crisp, aromatic Riesling and other whites to structured, full-bodied reds such as Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec that benefit from high sunlight exposure and cool nights. Wines generally show ripe fruit balanced by retained acidity, a direct result of the region's pronounced diurnal temperature shift.
notes: The Snake River Valley AVA is one of the highest-elevation AVAs in the United States, with much of its vineyard land above 2,500 feet.
The AVA crosses state lines, including a small portion of eastern Oregon along with southwestern Idaho.
Idaho's wine industry is still comparatively young and small relative to neighboring Washington and Oregon, but has grown quickly in recent decades.
The region's high-desert conditions mean irrigation is typically necessary for viticulture.

regions.name: Arizona (Verde Valley & Willcox)
regions.summary: Arizona's wine industry centers on two high-elevation growing areas: the Verde Valley/Sedona area in central Arizona and the Willcox area in the southeastern high desert. Both rely on elevation rather than latitude to create viable growing conditions in an otherwise hot, arid state.
regions.climate: Both areas rely on high elevation, with Willcox vineyards generally around 4,000 to 5,000 feet and Verde Valley somewhat lower, to offset Arizona's southern latitude and desert aridity. The result is a high-desert climate with intense sunlight, low humidity, large diurnal swings between warm days and cool nights, and low disease pressure. Late-summer monsoon rains bring a risk of harvest-time moisture, and irrigation is essential given generally low annual rainfall.
regions.soils: Willcox has sandy, well-drained alluvial soils typical of a high desert basin, while Verde Valley has more volcanic and sedimentary-influenced soils, including some limestone and basalt-derived material. Both areas' soils are generally low in fertility and rocky or sandy, favoring vine stress and fruit concentration.
regions.classification: Willcox AVA, established in 2016, covers the major growing area in southeastern Arizona and is now the source of the majority of the state's wine grapes by planted acreage. The Verde Valley area, while historically and currently significant for Arizona wine, is more associated with wine-trail branding and tourism than with a single dedicated federal AVA. Arizona's modern wine industry is young, having developed largely since the 1980s.

subRegions.name: Willcox AVA
subRegions.notes: Southeastern Arizona's high-desert basin, the state's largest source of wine grapes by planted acreage.

subRegions.name: Verde Valley
subRegions.notes: Central Arizona area near Sedona and Cottonwood, one of the state's earliest modern winegrowing areas and a major wine-tourism hub.

regions.styles: Warm-climate, Mediterranean and Rhône-leaning styles dominate: Syrah, Grenache and other Rhône reds show ripe, spicy, full-bodied character, while Malvasia Bianca and Viognier provide aromatic whites. Overall the state's wines tend toward bold, sun-ripened fruit balanced by the acid-retaining effect of high-elevation diurnal temperature swings.
notes: Arizona's modern wine industry is relatively young, having grown substantially since pioneering plantings in the 1980s.
Elevation, not latitude, is what makes Arizona viticulture possible - most vineyards sit at 3,500 to 5,000-plus feet to escape the desert heat of the valleys below.
Willcox AVA, recognized in 2016, is now the source of the majority of Arizona's wine grapes.
Late-summer monsoon rains are a distinctive regional viticultural risk, potentially bringing humidity and disease pressure at a sensitive point in the season.

regions.name: Missouri (Hermann)
regions.summary: Hermann, Missouri, on the banks of the Missouri River, is the historic heart of Missouri wine production and was one of the most important wine regions in the United States before Prohibition. Today it is known for cold-hardy hybrid and native American grape varieties, especially Norton, Missouri's official state grape.
regions.climate: Hermann has a humid continental climate with cold winters, hot, humid summers and real risk of extreme winter cold, conditions that historically made classic vinifera varieties difficult to grow and favored cold-hardy native American and French-American hybrid varieties instead. The Missouri River provides some moderating benefit to air drainage on vineyard sites close to its banks.
regions.soils: The best vineyard sites lie on bluffs above the Missouri River, with well-drained loess (wind-blown silt) soils over limestone bedrock; lower-lying areas nearer the river have alluvial soils.
regions.classification: The Hermann AVA lies within Missouri's historic river-hills wine country, part of a state industry that also includes the larger Ozark Highlands and Ozark Mountain AVAs. Missouri's modern industry centers on cold-hardy hybrid and native varieties rather than vinifera, a direct reflection of the region's climate constraints, and there is no formal quality tier above AVA status.
regions.styles: Norton, Missouri's signature grape, produces robust, distinctive red wines with dark fruit, earthy and sometimes smoky character and naturally high acidity. Aromatic and often semi-sweet white wines come from Vignoles and Vidal Blanc, while sweeter styles from native Catawba and related varieties reflect the region's long tradition of sweeter wine production. Overall the style profile is shaped by cold-hardy varieties rather than classic vinifera.
notes: Before Prohibition, Missouri, and Hermann in particular, was one of the largest wine-producing regions in the US, sometimes compared by nineteenth-century German immigrant settlers to the Rhine Valley.
Norton, also called Cynthiana, is Missouri's official state grape and one of the few native American Vitis aestivalis varieties used for quality dry red wine.
American rootstock, including material sourced through Missouri, played a role in helping combat the phylloxera epidemic that devastated European vineyards in the late nineteenth century.
The nearby Augusta AVA, also in Missouri's river hills, was the first AVA ever recognized in the United States, in 1980, predating even Napa Valley.

regions.name: New Mexico
regions.summary: New Mexico has the oldest continuous winegrowing history in the United States, dating to Spanish missionaries in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, and today produces wine from high-elevation desert vineyards along the Rio Grande. The state is also historically notable for high-quality traditional-method sparkling wine.
regions.climate: New Mexico's vineyards sit in a high-elevation, arid to semi-arid desert climate, with many sites between roughly 4,000 and 6,000 feet. Intense sunlight, very low humidity and minimal rainfall mean irrigation is required, while large diurnal temperature swings help preserve acidity despite intense daytime heat. Spring frost and occasional extreme winter cold are notable viticultural hazards, especially at higher elevations.
regions.soils: Vineyards are generally planted on sandy, alluvial soils along the Rio Grande valley, well-drained and low in organic matter, typical of high desert river-valley terrain.
regions.classification: New Mexico has several federally recognized AVAs, including Mimbres Valley, Mesilla Valley (shared with Texas) and Middle Rio Grande Valley. The state's wine industry, while historically the oldest in the country, remains small in scale today, and there is no formal quality tier above the AVA level.

subRegions.name: Mimbres Valley AVA
subRegions.notes: Southern New Mexico high-desert AVA around Deming, a historic center of the state's wine production.

subRegions.name: Mesilla Valley AVA
subRegions.notes: Shared with far West Texas along the Rio Grande near Las Cruces, one of the few AVAs to span two states.

subRegions.name: Middle Rio Grande Valley AVA
subRegions.notes: Covers vineyard areas further north along the river, around Albuquerque.

regions.styles: A broad range of still wine styles is produced, from crisp whites such as Chardonnay and Riesling to full-bodied reds such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. New Mexico is also historically notable for high-quality traditional-method sparkling wine, pioneered by Gruet Winery, which remains one of the state's best-known specialties alongside its still varietal wines.
notes: New Mexico has the oldest continuous winegrowing history in what is now the United States, with vines planted by Spanish missionaries as early as the late 1500s or early 1600s.
Gruet Winery, founded by a Champagne-region French family, established New Mexico's modern reputation for high-quality traditional-method sparkling wine beginning in the 1980s.
High elevation, with much of the state's vineyard land well above 4,000 feet, is what makes viticulture viable despite New Mexico's southern, desert setting.
The Mesilla Valley AVA is one of relatively few AVAs that spans two states, straddling the New Mexico-Texas border.

regions.name: Lombardy
regions.summary: Lombardy, Italy's wealthy industrial heartland around Milan, is a diverse wine region best known internationally for Franciacorta, Italy's most prestigious traditional-method sparkling wine, but it also produces distinctive mountain reds from Nebbiolo in Valtellina and everyday wines in volume from Oltrepò Pavese.
regions.climate: Lombardy spans a wide climatic range from the pre-Alpine lake zones to high Alpine valleys. Around Lake Iseo, Franciacorta benefits from a relatively mild mesoclimate with morning fog and lake breezes that moderate summer heat while retaining the high acidity needed for sparkling wine base. Valtellina, in the far north against the Swiss border, is a narrow, steep Alpine valley where vines are planted on sun-facing terraces to capture enough warmth for Nebbiolo to ripen at altitude. Oltrepò Pavese, in the south near Pavia, has a milder, more continental hill climate suited to higher-volume production.
regions.soils: Glacial moraine left by ancient glaciers dominates around Lake Iseo, a free-draining mix of sand, gravel, clay and limestone that varies considerably from vineyard to vineyard. Valtellina's terraced slopes are built on thin, poor schist and granite soils held in place by centuries of dry-stone walls. Oltrepò Pavese has more fertile clay and limestone hill soils, generally supporting higher yields than the other two zones.
regions.classification: Franciacorta DOCG governs both the geographic zone and a strict traditional-method production process, with minimum lees-ageing requirements exceeding Champagne's for equivalent categories; still wine from the same zone is labelled separately as Curtefranca DOC. In Valtellina, Nebbiolo (locally called Chiavennasca) reaches its two top tiers in Valtellina Superiore DOCG, with five named sub-zones, and the passito-style, part-dried-grape Sforzato di Valtellina DOCG. Oltrepò Pavese DOC covers a wide range of still and sparkling styles, including metodo classico sparkling wine from Pinot Nero.

subRegions.name: Franciacorta
subRegions.notes: Lombardy's flagship sparkling wine zone near Lake Iseo; styles include non-vintage, the softer no-Pinot-Nero Satèn, vintage Millesimato, and extended-ageing Riserva.

subRegions.name: Valtellina
subRegions.notes: Steep, terraced Alpine valley on the Swiss border where Nebbiolo (Chiavennasca) produces structured, high-acid reds; the Superiore sub-zones include Sassella, Grumello, Inferno, Valgella, and Maroggia.

subRegions.name: Oltrepò Pavese
subRegions.notes: Hilly zone south of Pavia producing large volumes of still and sparkling wine, including Pinot Nero used both for still reds and as a metodo classico sparkling base.

regions.styles: Franciacorta is predominantly brut-style traditional-method sparkling wine with a fine mousse and toasty, brioche-like character from extended lees ageing. Valtellina reds are pale but structured and high in acid, with red cherry, rose, and tar notes recalling Barolo in miniature, while Sforzato is a richer, part-dried-grape style with raisined fruit and higher alcohol. Oltrepò Pavese ranges from everyday still reds and whites to increasingly serious metodo classico sparkling wine from Pinot Nero.
notes: Franciacorta DOCG's minimum lees-ageing requirements are longer than Champagne's for equivalent non-vintage and vintage categories.
Satèn is a Franciacorta-specific style term for a lower-pressure blanc de blancs, not used elsewhere in Italian sparkling wine law.
Franciacorta developed as a serious sparkling wine zone largely from the 1960s onward, notably through the Berlucchi winery, making it younger than many other DOCGs.
Valtellina's terraces are so steep in places that some vineyard work is still done using a monorail cart system rather than tractors.
Oltrepò Pavese is one of Italy's largest sources of Pinot Nero, much of it destined for sparkling wine base rather than varietal still red.

regions.name: Lazio
regions.summary: Lazio, the region surrounding Rome, was for centuries one of Italy's most famous white wine areas thanks to Frascati, grown in the volcanic Castelli Romani hills southeast of the capital. A 20th-century reputation for cheap, mass-market wine has given way in recent decades to a renewed focus on quality whites and Lazio's own native red, Cesanese.
regions.climate: A warm Mediterranean climate moderated by both the sea and volcanic hill elevation. The Castelli Romani hills southeast of Rome, the remnant of an ancient volcanic complex, catch cooling breezes and offer greater diurnal temperature variation than the Roman plain, helping preserve freshness in the region's white grapes. Further north, vineyards around Lake Bolsena benefit from the lake's moderating influence, while the hill town of Piglio, east of Rome, sits at higher elevation favouring the region's principal red grape.
regions.soils: The Alban Hills around Frascati are volcanic, rich in tuff, pozzolana (volcanic ash), and lapilli layered over lava rock, giving the local whites a faint mineral edge. Similar volcanic ash and tuff soils surround Lake Bolsena further north. Around Piglio, soils are a mix of volcanic and clay-limestone material better suited to structured red wine.
regions.classification: Frascati DOC covers standard dry, off-dry and sweet whites, while Frascati Superiore DOCG requires a higher minimum percentage of Malvasia, lower yields, and slightly higher alcohol; a separate Cannellino di Frascati DOCG designates a traditional sweet, late-harvest style. Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone DOC, around Lake Bolsena, is another historic white wine zone with a similarly Malvasia/Trebbiano-based blend. Cesanese del Piglio DOCG, Lazio's only DOCG for red wine, is built on the native Cesanese grape.

subRegions.name: Frascati and Castelli Romani hills
subRegions.notes: The historic core zone southeast of Rome, with vineyards on volcanic slopes; Grottaferrata and Monte Porzio Catone are other towns within the DOC/DOCG boundary.

subRegions.name: Montefiascone
subRegions.notes: Hill town by Lake Bolsena giving its name to Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone, tied to a well-known medieval legend about a wine-scouting bishop's servant.

subRegions.name: Piglio
subRegions.notes: Hill zone east of Rome and home to Cesanese del Piglio DOCG, Lazio's sole red DOCG, from the native Cesanese grape.

regions.styles: Standard Frascati is pale, light-bodied, dry, and simple, with delicate stone fruit, almond, and floral notes for early drinking; Superiore versions show more concentration and texture, and Cannellino di Frascati is a luscious, honeyed sweet style now made in tiny quantities. Est! Est!! Est!!! is a similarly light, dry white. Cesanese del Piglio reds are medium-bodied with dark cherry fruit, soft tannins, and a faintly bitter, herbal finish, available in still, off-dry (amabile), and sometimes semi-sparkling versions.
notes: Frascati was for centuries one of the most famous and widely exported Italian white wines, closely tied to Rome's dining culture, though its international reputation faded through the later 20th century amid overproduction of thin, mass-market versions.
The volcanic tuff and pozzolana soils of the Alban Hills are the same porous volcanic rock historically used by the ancient Romans as a building material.

Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone's name comes from a legend of a bishop's servant marking inns with good wine "Est!" ("it is [here]"), tripling the exclamation for the best he found at Montefiascone.
Cesanese del Piglio, granted DOCG status in 2008, is one of the few Italian DOCGs dedicated to a native central-Italian red grape grown almost nowhere else.

regions.name: Basilicata
regions.summary: Basilicata, in Italy's mountainous, sparsely planted deep south, is a small wine region whose reputation rests almost entirely on Aglianico del Vulture, grown on the slopes of the extinct volcano Monte Vulture. It produces some of southern Italy's most age-worthy reds from the Aglianico grape, long compared to Piedmont's Nebbiolo for its structure and ageing potential.
regions.climate: A high-altitude, semi-continental climate unusual for such a southerly latitude: vineyards on Monte Vulture's slopes, often planted between 400 and 700 metres, benefit from cooler nights and a longer, slower ripening season than surrounding Basilicata lowlands. This altitude moderates what would otherwise be a very hot Mediterranean climate, allowing the late-ripening Aglianico to retain acidity while developing complex phenolic ripeness.
regions.soils: Volcanic soils derived from Monte Vulture's ancient eruptions dominate, rich in minerals and often layered with lava, tuff, and ash over limestone and clay at lower elevations. These well-draining soils are credited with giving Aglianico del Vulture its characteristic mineral, almost smoky edge alongside its firm tannin and dark fruit.
regions.classification: Aglianico del Vulture DOC covers standard red wines from the Aglianico grape, while Aglianico del Vulture Superiore DOCG, Basilicata's only DOCG, requires higher minimum alcohol, longer mandatory ageing including time in wood, and lower yields, applying only to wines from the most favoured vineyard sites on the volcano's slopes. There is no formal cru system beneath the DOCG, though single-vineyard bottlings from named sites are increasingly common among quality producers.

subRegions.name: Monte Vulture slopes
subRegions.notes: The core, higher-elevation volcanic zone producing the most structured, age-worthy Superiore-level wines.

subRegions.name: Barile and Rionero in Vulture
subRegions.notes: Historic winemaking towns at the heart of the DOC/DOCG, both with a long tradition of cellars cut into volcanic tuff.

regions.styles: Aglianico del Vulture reds are deeply coloured, full-bodied, and tannic in youth, with dark cherry and plum fruit, notes of leather, tobacco, and volcanic minerality, and the ability to age for a decade or more in the best vintages. Basic DOC bottlings can be approachable within a few years, while Superiore DOCG wines are built for extended cellaring, often needing several years to soften.
notes: Aglianico del Vulture Superiore is Basilicata's only DOCG, reflecting the region's relatively small and historically under-recognised wine industry.
Historic cellars in towns like Barile are carved directly into the volcanic tuff rock beneath the towns.
Aglianico is genetically distinct from, but stylistically often compared to, Nebbiolo for its high acidity and firm tannin.
Despite Basilicata's southern, Mediterranean latitude, Monte Vulture's altitude gives the region one of southern Italy's coolest, latest-ripening red wine sites.
